Applying Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_307 to $Y$, $\mathcal E$ and $P=\mathbf P_Y(\mathcal E)=\operatorname{Proj}(\operatorname{Sym}_{\mathcal O_Y}\mathcal E)$ (all over $\mathbb F_q$, with $\ell\ne p$), we obtain for every $n\ge 0$ a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism
\[
\Phi_n:\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}H^{n-2i}(Y)\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;H^n(P),\qquad (x_0,\dots,x_r)\longmapsto\sum_{i=0}^{r}\pi^*x_i\cup c^{\,i},
\]
with the convention $H^m(Y)=0$ for $m<0$, and this isomorphism carries the operator $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}q^{i}F_Y$ on the source onto $F_P$ on the target; i.e.
\[
\Phi_n\circ\Big(\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}q^{i}F_Y\Big)=F_P\circ\Phi_n .
\]
(Concretely, this is the identity $F_P(\pi^*x\cup c^i)=\pi^*(F_Yx)\cup (F_Pc)^i=\pi^*(F_Yx)\cup(q^ic)^i=q^i\,\pi^*(F_Yx)\cup c^i$, using that $\pi$ and $c$ are $\mathbb F_q$-rational up to the Tate twist, which is exactly the content of the equivariance supplied by lemma_307.)

Step 2 (each summand operator is semisimple). Fix $i\in\{0,\dots,r\}$ and $n\ge 0$. The space $H^{n-2i}(Y)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ (Step 0, and it is $0$ when $n-2i<0$, in which case there is nothing to prove), and $F_Y$ restricts to a semisimple automorphism of it by the hypothesis of the lemma (applied to the degree $n-2i\ge 0$). The scalar $q^i$ is a positive rational number, hence an element of $\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$, and $q^iF_Y$ is an invertible $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operator on $H^{n-2i}(Y)$. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_248 (semisimplicity is unchanged under multiplication by a scalar of $\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$), $q^iF_Y$ is semisimple on $H^{n-2i}(Y)$.

Step 3 (the direct sum is semisimple). The source $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}H^{n-2i}(Y)$ is a finite direct sum of finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, and $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}q^{i}F_Y$ is a direct sum of invertible operators, each semisimple by Step 2. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9 (a direct-sum operator is semisimple if and only if each summand operator is), $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}q^{i}F_Y$ is semisimple on $\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}H^{n-2i}(Y)$.

Step 4 (transport across $\Phi_n$). The isomorphism $\Phi_n$ intertwines $\bigoplus_i q^iF_Y$ with $F_P$ (Step 1), both spaces being finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ and both operators invertible. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8, semisimplicity is invariant under such an intertwining isomorphism; hence $F_P$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

Step 5 (conclusion). Step 4 holds for every integer $n\ge 0$, which is precisely the required conclusion: the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $(\mathrm{id}_{P_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for all $n\ge 0$. By Step 0 (eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5) this is the same as diagonalisability after extending scalars to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. $\blacksquare$

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ℓ≠p be prime, let m≥1, let k be an algebraic closure of F_q, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let F=(id_{X_k}×Spec σ)^*, σ(c)=c^{q^m}, be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. For 0≤n≤2d, if α∈overline{Q}_ℓ^× is an eigenvalue of F on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ℓ), then q^{md}/α is an eigenvalue of F on H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ℓ).
proof:
Proof. Put Q=q^m. Then Q=p^{am} is a prime power and k=overline F_Q. The given operator F is exactly the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius (id_{X_k} x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^Q.

First note that the relevant cohomology groups are finite-dimensional and that F is invertible. Applying lemma_45_finite_frob to the proper F_Q-scheme X and the constant sheaf Q_ell with its natural Frobenius structure gives finite-dimensionality of H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) for every n. Applying lemma_6a gives that F is a Q_ell-linear automorphism of each H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell); hence every eigenvalue alpha in overline Q_ell is nonzero.

If d=0, then a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension 0 over F_Q is Spec F_Q. Thus H^0_et(X_k,Q_ell)=Q_ell, H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)=0 for n>0, and F acts as the identity on H^0. The only possible n with 0<=n<=2d is n=0, the only eigenvalue is alpha=1, and Q^0/1=1 is again an eigenvalue on H^0. Hence assume from now on that d>=1.

Let V=H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell), W=H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell), and write F_V and F_W for the restrictions of F to V and W. Fix a nonzero element xi in Q_ell(-d). By lemma_271 applied with q replaced by Q, the perfect Poincare pairing <v,w>=tr_X(v cup w) into Q_ell(-d) gives a Q_ell-linear isomorphism Psi: W -> V^vee=Hom_Q_ell(V,Q_ell), defined by <v,w>=Psi(w)(v) xi, and it satisfies
Psi o F_W = Q^d (F_V^{-1})^vee o Psi.
Since Q^d=q^{md}, set c=q^{md} in Q_ell^*. Then
F_W = c Psi^{-1} (F_V^{-1})^vee Psi,
so F_W is conjugate over Q_ell to T:=c(F_V^{-1})^vee.

We now use a purely linear algebra fact. Let S be an invertible linear operator on a finite-dimensional K-vector space U, let c in K^*, and let alpha be an eigenvalue of S over an algebraic closure. Then c/alpha is an eigenvalue of c(S^{-1})^vee. Indeed, choose a basis of U and let A be the matrix of S. The matrix of S^{-1} is A^{-1}, and the matrix of the dual operator is the transpose of A^{-1}. Since A is invertible, alpha is nonzero. If N=dim_K U, then
 det(t I - A^{-1}) = det(A^{-1}) det(t A - I).
Evaluating at t=alpha^{-1} gives
det(alpha^{-1} I - A^{-1}) = det(A^{-1}) det(alpha^{-1} A - I) = det(A^{-1}) alpha^{-N} det(A-alpha I)=0,
because alpha is a root of det(t I-A). Hence alpha^{-1} is an eigenvalue of A^{-1}. Transposition does not change the characteristic polynomial, so alpha^{-1} is also an eigenvalue of (A^{-1})^T. Finally, multiplication by c scales eigenvalues by c: if (B-alpha^{-1}I)^r v=0, then (cB-c alpha^{-1}I)^r v=0. Therefore c/alpha is an eigenvalue of c(A^{-1})^T, proving the fact.

Apply the fact with K=Q_ell, U=V, and S=F_V. Since alpha is an eigenvalue of F_V, c/alpha is an eigenvalue of T. Because F_W is conjugate to T, they have the same characteristic polynomial over Q_ell and hence the same eigenvalues over overline Q_ell. Therefore c/alpha=q^{md}/alpha is an eigenvalue of F_W on H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell). This is exactly the desired conclusion.

statement: Let \(p\) be a prime, let \(Q=p^{b}\) be a power of \(p\), let \(m\ge 2\) be an integer with \(p\nmid m\), and let \(C\subset\mathbb P^{2}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}\) be the closed subscheme defined by \(u^{m}+v^{m}=w^{m}\). Then \(C\) is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(\mathbb F_{Q}\).
proof:
Throughout write L := \(\mathbb F_{Q}\) (a field of characteristic \(p\)), \(R := L[u,v,w]\) for the polynomial ring with its standard \(\mathbb N\)-grading (\(\deg u=\deg v=\deg w=1\)), and
\[
F := u^{m}+v^{m}-w^{m}\in R_{m},\qquad C := \operatorname{Proj} R/(F)\subset \mathbb P^{2}_{L}=\operatorname{Proj}R ,
\]
the closed subscheme cut out by the homogeneous ideal \((F)\). Note \(m\ge 2\) and \(p\nmid m\), so \(m\in L^{\times}\). The proof has four parts: projectivity (Step 2), smoothness of relative dimension 1 (Step 4), geometric connectedness (Steps 5–8), and the conclusion (Step 9).

**Step 1 (The three affine charts).** Let \(S:=R/(F)\) and denote by \(\bar u,\bar v,\bar w\) the images of \(u,v,w\); these are homogeneous of degree 1 and are nonzero, since \(\deg F=m\ge2\) so no linear form lies in \((F)\). For a homogeneous \(G\in S_{d}\), \(d\ge1\), the lemma \(\text{Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma\_proj\_principal\_open\_affine}\) gives a canonical isomorphism of open subschemes \(D_{+}(G)\cong \operatorname{Spec} S_{(G)}\), where \(S_{(G)}=(S_{G})_{0}\). Since \(\bar u,\bar v,\bar w\) generate \(S_{+}\), the three opens \(D_{+}(\bar u),D_{+}(\bar v),D_{+}(\bar w)\) cover \(C\). Computing the degree-zero parts (localise \(R\) at the variable and divide \(F\) by its \(d\)-th power):
\[
S_{(\bar w)}\cong L[x,y]/(x^{m}+y^{m}-1),\ x=\tfrac{u}{w},\ y=\tfrac{v}{w};\quad
S_{(\bar u)}\cong L[s,t]/(1+s^{m}-t^{m}),\ s=\tfrac{v}{u},\ t=\tfrac{w}{u};\quad
S_{(\bar v)}\cong L[p,q]/(p^{m}+1-q^{m}),\ p=\tfrac{u}{v},\ q=\tfrac{w}{v}.
\]
(For instance, \(R_{w}=L[x,y,w,w^{-1}]\) and its degree-zero part is \(L[x,y]\); the kernel of \(L[x,y]\twoheadrightarrow S_{(\bar w)}\) is generated by \(F/w^{m}=x^{m}+y^{m}-1\). The other two are identical.)

**Step 2 (Projectivity and non-emptiness).** \(C\to\operatorname{Spec}L\) is the composition of the closed immersion \(C\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^{2}_{L}\) with the projective morphism \(\mathbb P^{2}_{L}\to\operatorname{Spec}L\); a closed subscheme of a projective \(L\)-scheme is projective over \(L\) (the restriction of \(\mathcal O(1)\) is still ample, and a closed immersion is of finite type). Hence \(C\) is projective, in particular proper and of finite type, hence separated, over \(L\). Also \(C(L)\ne\emptyset\): \((1\!:\!0\!:\!1)\) satisfies \(1^{m}+0^{m}-1^{m}=0\).

**Step 3 (The Jacobian criterion, classical form used).** We use the following standard one-equation Jacobian criterion, which we recall with its proof for completeness. *Let \(K\) be a field, \(n\ge1\), \(0\ne g\in K[X_{1},\dots,X_{n}]\), \(A=K[X_{1},\dots,X_{n}]/(g)\), and let \(\mathfrak p\subset A\) be a prime such that some partial \(\partial g/\partial X_{j}\) has nonzero image in \(A/\mathfrak p\). Then \(A_{\mathfrak p}\) is smooth of relative dimension \(n-1\) over \(K\).* Indeed, say \(\partial g/\partial X_{n}\notin\mathfrak p\) and put \(B=K[X_{1},\dots,X_{n-1}]\). Then \(B[X_{n},(\partial g/\partial X_{n})^{-1}]/(g)\) is a *standard étale* \(B\)-algebra, hence étale over \(B\) (classical: it is of finite presentation, \(\Omega^{1}=0\) because \(dg\) becomes \(0=(\partial g/\partial X_{n})dX_{n}\) after inverting \(\partial g/\partial X_{n}\), and it is flat by the standard monogenic-flatness argument for \(B[X]/(g)\) at a simple root); \(A_{\mathfrak p}\) is a localisation of this algebra, hence étale over \(B_{\mathfrak p\cap B}\). Étale morphisms are smooth of relative dimension 0, \(B_{\mathfrak p\cap B}\) is smooth of relative dimension \(n-1\) over \(K\) (localisation of a polynomial ring), and smoothness is preserved by composition with relative dimensions adding. \(\square\)

**Step 4 (Smoothness of relative dimension 1).** The partial derivatives of \(F\) are \(m\,u^{m-1},\ m\,v^{m-1},\ -m\,w^{m-1}\). We check the criterion chart by chart, using that \(m\in L^{\times}\) and \(m-1\ge1\).
* Chart \(w\): \(f=x^{m}+y^{m}-1\), partials \(m x^{m-1}, m y^{m-1}\). If a prime \(\mathfrak p\subset S_{(\bar w)}\) contained both, then \(x,y\in\mathfrak p\), so \(1=(x^{m}+y^{m})-(x^{m}+y^{m}-1)\in\mathfrak p\), impossible.
* Chart \(u\): \(f=1+s^{m}-t^{m}\), partials \(m s^{m-1},-m t^{m-1}\); both in \(\mathfrak p\) would give \(s,t\in\mathfrak p\) and \(1=(1+s^{m}-t^{m})-s^{m}+t^{m}\in\mathfrak p\), impossible.
* Chart \(v\): identical, with \(p,q\).
Thus at every point of every chart some partial is a unit in the local ring, and Step 3 (with \(n=2\)) shows each chart is smooth of relative dimension \(2-1=1\) over \(L\) at every prime. Smoothness is local on the source and the three charts cover \(C\), so \(C\) is **smooth of relative dimension 1 over \(L\)**. Consequences: \(C\) is regular, of finite type over \(L\), every local ring of \(C\) has Krull dimension 1, and each connected component of \(C\) is equidimensional of dimension 1.

**Step 5 (Four ring-theoretic facts).**
(S1) *Polynomial rings over a UFD are UFDs (Gauss).* Since \(\Omega\) is a field, \(\Omega[x]\) is Euclidean, hence a PID and a UFD; iterating, \(\Omega[u,v,w]\) is a UFD.
(S2) *In a UFD every irreducible element is prime.* If \(\pi\) is irreducible and \(\pi\mid ab\), write \(a,b\) as products of irreducibles; uniqueness of factorisation in \(ab\) forces \(\pi\) to be associate to an irreducible factor of \(a\) or of \(b\).
(S3) *Gauss.* For a UFD \(A\) with fraction field \(K\): (i) a product of primitive polynomials of \(A[y]\) is primitive — if a prime \(\pi\in A\) divided all coefficients of \(ab\), then in \((A/\pi)[y]\), which is a domain because \(\pi\) is prime, one would have \(\bar a\bar b=0\) with \(\bar a,\bar b\ne0\); (ii) consequently, if \(f\in A[y]\) is monic and \(f=gh\) in \(K[y]\) with \(g,h\) monic, then \(g,h\in A[y]\): writing \(g=a/\lambda\), \(h=b/\mu\) with \(a,b\) primitive and \(\lambda,\mu\in A\setminus\{0\}\), we get \(ab=\lambda\mu f\), whose left side is primitive by (i) while the right side has all coefficients divisible by \(\lambda\mu\); hence \(\lambda\mu\) is a unit, so \(\lambda,\mu\) are units. Together these give the usual form: a primitive \(f\in A[y]\) irreducible in \(K[y]\) is irreducible in \(A[y]\).
(S4) *Eisenstein.* Let \(A\) be a UFD, \(\pi\in A\) prime, \(K=\operatorname{Frac}A\), and \(f=y^{d}+a_{d-1}y^{d-1}+\cdots+a_{0}\in A[y]\) with \(d\ge1\), \(a_{i}\in(\pi)\) for \(i\le d-1\), \(a_{0}\notin(\pi^{2})\). Then \(f\) is irreducible in \(K[y]\). Proof: if \(f=gh\) in \(K[y]\) with \(0<\deg g,\deg h<d\), take \(g,h\) monic, so \(g,h\in A[y]\) by (S3)(ii). Reducing modulo \((\pi)\), which is a prime ideal so \((A/\pi)[y]\) is a domain, gives \(\bar g\bar h=y^{d}\); since \(y\) is prime in \((A/\pi)[y]\) (quotient \(\cong A/\pi\), a domain), \(\bar g=c\,y^{\alpha}\), \(\bar h=c'\,y^{\beta}\) with \(cc'=1\). As \(\deg g,\deg h\ge1\) and \(\alpha+\beta=d=\deg g+\deg h\), one has \(\alpha,\beta\ge1\) (if \(\alpha=0\) then \(\deg h=d=\deg f\), forcing \(\deg g=0\)). Hence \(\pi\) divides both constant terms of \(g\) and \(h\), so \(\pi^{2}\mid a_{0}\), contradiction. \(\square$

**Step 6 (Eisenstein at \(x-1\): irreducibility of \(f=y^{m}+(x^{m}-1)\)).** Let \(\Omega\) be an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(p\) (we use only \(m\ge2\) and \(m\ne0\) in \(\Omega\), i.e. \(p\nmid m\)). In \(\Omega[x]\) one has
\[
x^{m}-1=(x-1)\,q(x),\qquad q(x)=1+x+\cdots+x^{m-1},\qquad q(1)=m\ne0\in\Omega ,
\]
so \(x-1\mid x^{m}-1\) but \((x-1)^{2}\nmid x^{m}-1\). The element \(\pi:=x-1\) is prime in the UFD \(\Omega[x]\), because \(\Omega[x]/(x-1)\cong\Omega\) is a field. Now view
\[
f:=y^{m}+(x^{m}-1)\in \Omega[x][y]:
\]
it is monic of degree \(m\ge2\) in \(y\), the coefficients of \(y^{m-1},\dots,y\) are \(0\in(\pi)\), and the constant term \(x^{m}-1\) lies in \((\pi)\setminus(\pi^{2})\). By (S4) \(f\) is irreducible in \(\operatorname{Frac}(\Omega[x])[y]\), and being monic it is primitive, so (S3) gives: **\(f\) is irreducible in \(\Omega[x,y]\).**

**Step 7 (Irreducibility of \(F_{\Omega}=u^{m}+v^{m}-w^{m}\) in \(T:=\Omega[u,v,w]\)).** Give \(T\) the total-degree grading; \(T\) is a domain with \(T_{0}=\Omega\).
(a) *The dehomogenisation map on a graded piece.* \(\operatorname{ev}_{w}:T\to\Omega[u,v]\), \(G\mapsto G(u,v,1)\), sends the monomial \(u^{i}v^{j}w^{k}\) to \(u^{i}v^{j}\). For each \(d\), the monomials with \(i+j+k=d\) are a \(\Omega\)-basis of \(T_{d}\) and their images are the monomials \(u^{i}v^{j}\) with \(i+j\le d\), a basis of the space \(\Omega[u,v]_{\le d}\) of polynomials of total degree \(\le d\). Hence \(\operatorname{ev}_{w}:T_{d}\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\Omega[u,v]_{\le d}\) is a \(\Omega\)-linear isomorphism; in particular \(\operatorname{ev}_{w}(G)\ne0\) for \(0\ne G\in T_{d}\). Writing \(G=\sum_{i+j\le d}c_{ij}u^{i}v^{j}w^{d-i-j}\) we see moreover that \(\operatorname{ev}_{w}(G)=c\in\Omega^{\times}\) **iff** \(G=c\,w^{d}\). (We deliberately assert nothing about degrees of dehomogenisations: \(\operatorname{ev}_{w}\) does not preserve degree, e.g. \(\operatorname{ev}_{w}(w^{d})=1\); only non-vanishing and this constant case are used.)
(b) \(F_{\Omega}\in T_{m}\) is homogeneous and \(\operatorname{ev}_{w}(F_{\Omega})=u^{m}+v^{m}-1\), which is exactly the polynomial \(f\) of Step 6 after renaming \(x\mapsto u,\ y\mapsto v\); it is irreducible in \(\Omega[u,v]\).
(c) *Factors are homogeneous.* Let \(0\ne G\in T\) be written \(G=G_{r_{0}}+\cdots+G_{r_{s}}\) with \(r_{0}<\cdots<r_{s}\) and \(G_{r_{i}}\in T_{r_{i}}\setminus\{0\}\) its nonzero homogeneous components, and similarly \(H=H_{t_{0}}+\cdots+H_{t_{u}}\). Because \(T\) is a graded domain, the component of \(GH\) of degree \(r_{0}+t_{0}\) is \(G_{r_{0}}H_{t_{0}}\ne0\) (it is the only term of that degree) and the component of degree \(r_{s}+t_{u}\) is \(G_{r_{s}}H_{t_{u}}\ne0\). If \(GH\) is homogeneous of degree \(D\), all other components vanish, so \(r_{0}+t_{0}=D=r_{s}+t_{u}\); with \(r_{0}\le r_{s}\) and \(t_{0}\le t_{u}\) this forces \(r_{0}=r_{s}\) and \(t_{0}=t_{u}\), i.e. \(G\) and \(H\) are homogeneous.
(d) *Conclusion of irreducibility.* Suppose \(F_{\Omega}=GH\) with \(G,H\) nonunits of \(T\). By (c) both are homogeneous, say \(G\in T_{r}\), \(H\in T_{s}\), \(r+s=m\); since \(T_{0}^{\times}=\Omega^{\times}\) consists of units of \(T\), nonunit homogeneous elements have positive degree, so \(r,s\ge1\). By (a), \(\operatorname{ev}_{w}(G)\ne0\) and \(\operatorname{ev}_{w}(H)\ne0\), and \(\operatorname{ev}_{w}(G)\operatorname{ev}_{w}(H)=\operatorname{ev}_{w}(F_{\Omega})=u^{m}+v^{m}-1\), irreducible by (b). Hence one of them, say \(\operatorname{ev}_{w}(G)\), is a unit of \(\Omega[u,v]\), i.e. a nonzero constant. By (a), \(G=c\,w^{r}\) with \(c\in\Omega^{\times}\) and \(r\ge1\); thus \(w\mid F_{\Omega}\) in \(T\). But the image of \(F_{\Omega}\) in \(T/(w)\cong\Omega[u,v]\) is \(u^{m}+v^{m}\ne0\) (the monomial \(u^{m}\) is nonzero), so \(F_{\Omega}\notin(w)\), contradiction. Therefore **\(F_{\Omega}\) is irreducible in \(T\)**.

**Step 8 (Geometric connectedness).** Let \(\Omega/L\) be any field extension. Base change of the closed immersion \(C\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^{2}_{L}\) along \(\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to\operatorname{Spec}L\) is the closed immersion of \(\mathbb P^{2}_{\Omega}=\operatorname{Proj}\Omega[u,v,w]\) defined by the extended ideal \((F_{\Omega})\); that is, \(C_{\Omega}:=C\times_{L}\Omega\cong\operatorname{Proj}S_{\Omega}\) with \(S_{\Omega}:=\Omega[u,v,w]/(F_{\Omega})\).
(i) First take \(\Omega\) algebraically closed (of characteristic \(p\)). By Step 7(d) \(F_{\Omega}\) is irreducible, and by (S1)+(S2) the principal ideal \((F_{\Omega})\) is prime in the UFD \(T\). So \(S_{\Omega}\) is an integral domain, \(\mathbb N\)-graded, with \((S_{\Omega})_{0}=\Omega\) and \((S_{\Omega})_{+}\ne0\) (the image of \(u\) is nonzero, as \(\deg F_{\Omega}=m\ge2\)). We claim \(\operatorname{Proj}S_{\Omega}\) is integral. The zero ideal is homogeneous and prime and does not contain \((S_{\Omega})_{+}\), so it is a point \(\eta\) of \(\operatorname{Proj}S_{\Omega}\); every nonempty basic open \(D_{+}(G)\) (\(G\in (S_{\Omega})_{+}\) homogeneous) has \(G\ne0\), hence \(\eta\in D_{+}(G)\), so \(\eta\) lies in every nonempty open and \(\{\eta\}\) is dense: the space is irreducible. By \(\text{Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma\_proj\_principal\_open\_affine}\), \(D_{+}(G)=\operatorname{Spec}(S_{\Omega})_{(G)}\), and \((S_{\Omega})_{(G)}\) is a subring of the localisation \((S_{\Omega})_{G}\) of the domain \(S_{\Omega}\), hence a domain; so each \(D_{+}(G)\) is an integral scheme. Since these form an open cover, every local ring of \(\operatorname{Proj}S_{\Omega}\) is a domain. Irreducible + all local rings domains means \(C_{\Omega}=\operatorname{Proj}S_{\Omega}\) is **integral**, in particular nonempty and connected.
(ii) Now let \(\Omega/L\) be arbitrary and choose an algebraic closure \(\overline{\Omega}\). By (i), \(C_{\overline{\Omega}}\) is connected. The projection \(\pi:C_{\overline{\Omega}}\to C_{\Omega}\) is the base change of \(\operatorname{Spec}\overline{\Omega}\to\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\), hence faithfully flat and quasi-compact (\(C_{\Omega}\) is quasi-compact, being of finite type over a field). If \(C_{\Omega}=U\sqcup V\) were a decomposition into two nonempty open-and-closed subsets, then \(C_{\overline{\Omega}}=U_{\overline{\Omega}}\sqcup V_{\overline{\Omega}}\) would be such a decomposition as well; both pieces are nonempty, because for an affine open \(\operatorname{Spec}B\subseteq U\) with \(B\ne0\) one has \(B\otimes_{\Omega}\overline{\Omega}\ne0\) (the tensor product of two nonzero vector spaces over the field \(\Omega\) is nonzero). This contradicts the connectedness of \(C_{\overline{\Omega}}\). Hence \(C_{\Omega}\) is connected.
Since \(\Omega/L\) was arbitrary and \(C_{\Omega}\ne\emptyset\) (it contains the image of \((1\!:\!0\!:\!1)\)), \(C\) is **geometrically connected** over \(L\).

**Step 9 (Conclusion).** Take \(\Omega=\overline{L}\) in Step 8(i): \(C_{\overline{L}}\) is integral. The morphism \(C_{\overline{L}}\to C\) is surjective (faithfully flat), so \(C\), being the continuous surjective image of an irreducible space, is irreducible; and \(C\) is reduced because \(C\) is regular by Step 4. Thus \(C\) is integral. By Step 4 it is of finite type over \(L\) with all local rings of dimension 1, so \(\dim C=1\); by Step 2 it is separated and projective over \(L\). Therefore \(C\) is an integral separated scheme of finite type of dimension 1 over \(\mathbb F_{Q}\) — a curve — which is smooth (Step 4), projective (Step 2) and geometrically connected (Step 8). This is exactly the statement: the Fermat curve \(C=\{u^{m}+v^{m}=w^{m}\}\subset\mathbb P^{2}_{\mathbb F_{Q}}\) is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(\mathbb F_{Q}\). \(\qed\)

(Remarks on the use of the hypotheses: \(p\nmid m\) is used twice, to make \(m\) a unit so that the partials \(m u^{m-1},m v^{m-1},-m w^{m-1}\) vanish simultaneously only at \(u=v=w=0\) (Step 4), and to ensure \(q(1)=m\ne0\), i.e. that \(x-1\) divides \(x^{m}-1\) exactly once, in Step 6. The condition \(m\ge2\) is used to make \(F_{\Omega}\) a nonunit of degree \(\ge2\), so that in Step 7(d) the exponent \(r\) is \(\ge1\) and \(w\mid F_{\Omega}\) is a genuine contradiction, and so that Eisenstein applies to a polynomial of degree \(\ge2\).) No statement about the Fermat surface, the blow-up, or Frobenius semisimplicity is used or proved here.

statement: Let \ell be a prime, let V be a finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space, let T:V\to V be a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear endomorphism, and let R\ge 0 be a real number. Suppose V has a finite filtration 0=V_0\subset V_1\subset\cdots\subset V_s=V by T-stable subspaces such that for every j=1,\dots,s, every embedding \iota:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C, and every eigenvalue \alpha of the induced endomorphism on (V_j/V_{j-1})\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, one has |\iota(\alpha)|\le R. Then for every embedding \iota:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C and every eigenvalue \alpha of T on V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, one has |\iota(\alpha)|\le R.
proof:
The statement is purely linear-algebraic; the prime $\ell$, the field $\mathbb Q_\ell$ and the real number $R\ge 0$ play no role beyond providing the ground field and the bound. We argue with a basis adapted to the filtration and the resulting block-triangular shape of the matrix of $T$.

Notation. For a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $W$ and a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear endomorphism $u$, write $\chi(u,W):=\det(X\cdot \mathrm{id}_W-u)\in\mathbb Q_\ell[X]$ for the characteristic polynomial (a monic polynomial of degree $\dim W$; if $W=0$ it is the empty determinant, $\chi(u,0)=1$).

Step 0 (vacuous case). If $V=0$, then $V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell=0$ has no eigenvalues at all, so the conclusion "every eigenvalue $\alpha$ satisfies $|\iota(\alpha)|\le R$" is vacuously true. Henceforth assume $V\neq 0$; then $s\ge 1$.

Step 1 (the induced endomorphisms on the graded pieces). For each $j\in\{1,\dots,s\}$ put $\mathrm{Gr}_j:=V_j/V_{j-1}$ and let $T_j:\mathrm{Gr}_j\to \mathrm{Gr}_j$ be defined by $T_j(v+V_{j-1}):=T(v)+V_{j-1}$. This is well defined and $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear: if $v-v'\in V_{j-1}$, then, since $V_{j-1}$ is $T$-stable by hypothesis, $T(v)-T(v')=T(v-v')\in T(V_{j-1})\subset V_{j-1}$, so $T(v)+V_{j-1}=T(v')+V_{j-1}$. Let $n_j:=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathrm{Gr}_j$. Note $\sum_{j=1}^s n_j=\sum_j(\dim V_j-\dim V_{j-1})=\dim V_s-\dim V_0=\dim V$.

Step 2 (a basis adapted to the filtration). For each $j$ choose vectors $e_{j,1},\dots,e_{j,n_j}\in V_j$ whose residue classes $\bar e_{j,k}:=e_{j,k}+V_{j-1}$ form a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-basis of $\mathrm{Gr}_j$ (possible when $n_j\ge 1$; if $n_j=0$ the family is empty). We claim that for every $j$, the concatenated family $B_j:=(e_{1,1},\dots,e_{1,n_1},e_{2,1},\dots,e_{2,n_2},\dots,e_{j,1},\dots,e_{j,n_j})$ is a basis of $V_j$. Proof by induction on $j$. For $j=1$: $V_1/V_0=V_1$, so $B_1$ is already a basis of $V_1$. Inductive step: assume $B_{j-1}$ is a basis of $V_{j-1}$, and let $E_j:=\mathrm{span}(B_j)$. Then $E_j\supset \mathrm{span}(B_{j-1})=V_{j-1}$, and the image of $E_j$ in $V_j/V_{j-1}=\mathrm{Gr}_j$ contains all $\bar e_{j,k}$, hence is all of $\mathrm{Gr}_j$. Thus $E_j+V_{j-1}=V_j$, and since $V_{j-1}\subset E_j$ this gives $E_j=V_j$. Finally $|B_j|=\sum_{i\le j}n_i=\dim V_j$, so $B_j$ is a basis of $V_j$. In particular $B:=B_s$ is a basis of $V$.

Step 3 (block upper-triangular shape). Order $B$ by increasing $j$ (block $j$ consisting of $e_{j,1},\dots,e_{j,n_j}$) and let $M$ be the matrix of $T$ in this basis. Fix $j,k$. Since $e_{j,k}\in V_j$ and $V_j$ is $T$-stable, $T(e_{j,k})\in V_j=\mathrm{span}(B_j)$; so in the expansion
$$T(e_{j,k})=\sum_{i=1}^{s}\ \sum_{b=1}^{n_i} c^{(i,b)}_{(j,k)}\, e_{i,b}$$
all coefficients with $i>j$ vanish. Thus $M$ is block upper triangular with respect to the decomposition $\dim V=n_1+\cdots+n_s$. Moreover, reducing the displayed equality modulo $V_{j-1}$, all terms with $i<j$ vanish (they lie in $V_{j-1}$), and we obtain
$$T_j(\bar e_{j,k})=\sum_{b=1}^{n_j} c^{(j,b)}_{(j,k)}\,\bar e_{j,b}.$$
Since the $\bar e_{j,b}$ form a basis of $\mathrm{Gr}_j$, the $j$-th diagonal block of $M$ is exactly the matrix $M_j$ of $T_j$ in that basis.

Step 4 (characteristic polynomial of a block upper-triangular matrix). We show $\det(X I_{\dim V}-M)=\prod_{j=1}^{s}\det(X I_{n_j}-M_j)$. The matrix $X I-M$ is again block upper triangular, with diagonal blocks $X I_{n_j}-M_j$. We argue by induction on $s$ (the case $s=0$ or $s=1$ being immediate). Consider the Leibniz expansion of the determinant, $\det=\sum_{\sigma\in \mathfrak S_N}\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_a (X I-M)_{a,\sigma(a)}$, $N=\sum n_j$. Rows belonging to the last block (indices in $I_s:=\{n_1+\cdots+n_{s-1}+1,\dots,N\}$) have all entries zero outside the column set $I_s$, because blocks below the diagonal are zero. Hence a permutation $\sigma$ contributes a nonzero product only if $\sigma(I_s)=I_s$; then also $\sigma(I_s^c)=I_s^c$, so $\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)=\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma|_{I_s})\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma|_{I_s^c})$ (no extra sign, as $\sigma$ preserves both subsets) and the sum factorises as the product of the determinant of the $I_s\times I_s$ block, namely $\det(XI_{n_s}-M_s)$, and the determinant of the complementary block, which is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks $XI_{n_1}-M_1,\dots,XI_{n_{s-1}}-M_{s-1}$; the induction hypothesis applies to it. (Empty blocks, $n_j=0$, contribute the factor $1$ and cause no difficulty.) Combining Step 3 with the definition of the characteristic polynomial we obtain the key identity in $\mathbb Q_\ell[X]$:
$$\chi(T,V)=\prod_{j=1}^{s}\chi(T_j,\mathrm{Gr}_j). \qquad (\ast)$$

Step 5 (descent of the identity to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$). Let $\bar V:=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, $\bar T:=T\otimes\mathrm{id}$, $\overline{\mathrm{Gr}}_j:=\mathrm{Gr}_j\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ and $\bar T_j:=T_j\otimes\mathrm{id}$. The basis $B$ of $V$ induces the basis $\bar B=\{e\otimes 1:e\in B\}$ of $\bar V$, and the matrix of $\bar T$ in $\bar B$ is the very same matrix $M$, now regarded as having entries in $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$; likewise $\bar M_j=M_j$. Therefore $\chi(\bar T,\bar V)$ is the image of $\chi(T,V)$ under the inclusion $\mathbb Q_\ell[X]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[X]$, and similarly $\chi(\bar T_j,\overline{\mathrm{Gr}}_j)$ is the image of $\chi(T_j,\mathrm{Gr}_j)$. Hence $(\ast)$ remains valid over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$:
$$\chi(\bar T,\bar V)=\prod_{j=1}^{s}\chi(\bar T_j,\overline{\mathrm{Gr}}_j)\quad\text{in }\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[X].\qquad (\ast\ast)$$

Step 6 (eigenvalues are roots of the characteristic polynomial). Since $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is algebraically closed, $\chi(\bar T,\bar V)=\prod_{\alpha}(X-\alpha)$ with the product over the eigenvalues of $\bar T$ counted with multiplicity: indeed $\bar T$ admits an upper-triangular matrix over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ (put it in Jordan/rational form; algebraic closedness gives a full flag of $\bar T$-stable subspaces, built inductively by choosing an eigenvector, which exists because $\chi(\bar T,\bar V)$ has a root), and the diagonal entries of such a triangular matrix are precisely the eigenvalues and equal the roots of the characteristic polynomial. The same holds for each $\bar T_j$. In particular, the roots in $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ of $\chi(\bar T_j,\overline{\mathrm{Gr}}_j)$ are exactly the eigenvalues of the induced endomorphism on $(V_j/V_{j-1})\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.

Step 7 (conclusion). Let $\iota:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$ be an embedding and let $\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ be an eigenvalue of $\bar T$ on $\bar V$. By Step 6, $\chi(\bar T,\bar V)(\alpha)=0$. Evaluating $(\ast\ast)$ at $\alpha$ in the field $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ (which has no zero divisors) gives $\prod_j \chi(\bar T_j,\overline{\mathrm{Gr}}_j)(\alpha)=0$, so $\chi(\bar T_j,\overline{\mathrm{Gr}}_j)(\alpha)=0$ for some $j\in\{1,\dots,s\}$; necessarily $n_j\ge 1$, since a factor equal to $1$ does not vanish. By Step 6 applied to $\mathrm{Gr}_j$, $\alpha$ is an eigenvalue of $\bar T_j$ on $(V_j/V_{j-1})\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. The hypothesis of the lemma, applied to this index $j$ and this embedding $\iota$, yields $|\iota(\alpha)|\le R$. As $\iota$ and $\alpha$ were arbitrary, the conclusion holds for every embedding and every eigenvalue of $T$ on $V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.

Remark (equivalent formulation, not needed above). The same argument is the length-$s$ iteration of the short-exact-sequence case: for $0\to W\to V\to V/W\to 0$ with $W$ $T$-stable one has $\chi(T,V)=\chi(T|_W,W)\,\chi(T_{V/W},V/W)$, so the multiset of eigenvalues on $V$ is the union (with multiplicity) of those on $W$ and on $V/W$; no semisimplicity, purity, duality or Frobenius-specific input is used anywhere.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimensions \(d\ge1\) and \(e\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and use it to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\xi_X\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(\xi_Y\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be cycle classes of \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-rational very ample divisors, and suppose cup product with \(\xi_X\) (resp. \(\xi_Y\)) induces isomorphisms \(H^{d-n}\to H^{d+n}\) (resp. \(H^{e-j}\to H^{e+j}\)) in the expected degrees. Let \(p_1,p_2\) be the projections of \(X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}Y\), let \(\eta=p_1^*\xi_X+p_2^*\xi_Y\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), and let \(L_\eta\) be cup product with \(\eta\). Then \(L_\eta^{d+e-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d+2e-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every integer \(n\) with \(0\le n\le d+e\).
proof:
Write $Q:=q^{m}=p^{am}$, so that $Q$ is again a prime power and $\mathbb F_{Q}=\mathbb F_{q^{m}}$; since $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q}$ is algebraically closed and algebraic over $\mathbb F_{Q}$ we also have $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{Q}$. Put $P:=X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^{m}}}Y$, and abbreviate $H^{n}(X):=H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})$, $H^{n}(Y):=H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})$, $H^{n}(P):=H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})$. The fixed nonzero element of $\mathbb Q_{\ell}(1)$ is used, as the statement prescribes, to view the cycle classes $\xi_X,\xi_Y$ as classes in $H^{2}(X),H^{2}(Y)$; hence $\eta=p_{1}^{*}\xi_X+p_{2}^{*}\xi_Y\in H^{2}(P)$ is well defined.

Step 1: finite dimensionality. $X$, $Y$ and $P$ are projective, hence proper, varieties over $\mathbb F_{Q}$. Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob (with the prime power $Q$ in place of its $q$, and with $K=\mathbb Q_{\ell}$ the constant sheaf, which carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure) to each of $X$, $Y$, $P$, every group $H^{n}(X)$, $H^{n}(Y)$, $H^{n}(P)$ is finite dimensional over $\mathbb Q_{\ell}$.

Step 2: vanishing above twice the dimension. $X_k$ (resp. $Y_k$) is a projective scheme over the algebraically closed field $k$, equidimensional of dimension $d$ (resp. $e$). By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_projective_cohomology_vanishes_above_twice_dimension, $H^{r}(X)=0$ for all $r>2d$ and $H^{s}(Y)=0$ for all $s>2e$. Also $H^{r}(-)=0$ for $r<0$, since $\mathrm{\acute et}$ cohomology is the right derived functor of global sections on a topos. Thus $\bigoplus_{r\ge0}H^{r}(X)=\bigoplus_{r=0}^{2d}H^{r}(X)$ and similarly for $Y$.

Step 3: the two graded Lefschetz spaces. Define $V=\bigoplus_{r=0}^{2d}V_{r}$ by $V_{r}:=H^{r}(X)$ and $W=\bigoplus_{s=0}^{2e}W_{s}$ by $W_{s}:=H^{s}(Y)$; these are finite dimensional by Step 1 (Step 2 gives the range). Let $L_{V}:V\to V$ be cup product with $\xi_X$ and $L_{W}:W\to W$ cup product with $\xi_Y$. Since $\deg\xi_X=\deg\xi_Y=2$ and cup product is $\mathbb Q_{\ell}$-bilinear and compatible with the grading, $L_{V}(V_{r})\subseteq V_{r+2}$ and $L_{W}(W_{s})\subseteq W_{s+2}$ (with $V_{r+2}=0$, $W_{s+2}=0$ if the index exceeds $2d$, $2e$). The hypothesis of the lemma says exactly that cup product with $\xi_X$ (resp. $\xi_Y$) gives isomorphisms $H^{d-n}\xrightarrow{\sim}H^{d+n}$ (resp. $H^{e-j}\xrightarrow{\sim}H^{e+j}$) in the expected degrees, i.e. $L_{X}^{d-n}:H^{n}(X)\to H^{2d-n}(X)$ is an isomorphism for every $0\le n\le d$ and $L_{Y}^{e-j}:H^{j}(Y)\to H^{2e-j}(Y)$ for every $0\le j\le e$. Substituting $r=d-n$ (so $0\le r\le d$ and $2d-r=d+n$) this reads: $L_{V}^{d-r}:V_{r}\xrightarrow{\sim}V_{2d-r}$ for every $0\le r\le d$, and $L_{W}^{e-s}:W_{s}\xrightarrow{\sim}W_{2e-s}$ for every $0\le s\le e$.

Step 4: K\"unneth identification of the total cohomology of $P$. Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_146 with the prime power $Q$ in place of its $q$: for each $t\ge0$ the map
$$\kappa_{t}:\bigoplus_{i+j=t}H^{i}(X)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_{\ell}}H^{j}(Y)\longrightarrow H^{t}(P),\qquad a\otimes b\longmapsto p_{1}^{*}a\cup p_{2}^{*}b,$$
is an isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_{\ell}$-vector spaces. By Step 2 the summands with $i>2d$ or $j>2e$ vanish, so the source of $\kappa_t$ is canonically $(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_{\ell}}W)_{t}:=\bigoplus_{i+j=t}V_{i}\otimes W_{j}$. Thus the $\kappa_t$ assemble to an isomorphism of graded vector spaces $\kappa:V\otimes W\xrightarrow{\sim}H^{*}(P)$ with $\kappa((V\otimes W)_{t})=H^{t}(P)$.

Step 5: $\kappa$ intertwines $L_{V}\otimes\mathrm{id}+\mathrm{id}\otimes L_{W}$ with $L_{\eta}$. Let $a\in V_{i}=H^{i}(X)$ and $b\in W_{j}=H^{j}(Y)$. Using functoriality of the cup product with respect to pullback ($f^{*}(u\cup v)=f^{*}u\cup f^{*}v$), associativity, bilinearity, and graded commutativity (the class $p_{2}^{*}\xi_Y$ has degree $2$, so moving it past $p_{1}^{*}a$ contributes the sign $(-1)^{2i}=+1$), we compute in $H^{i+j+2}(P)$:
$$\begin{aligned} L_{\eta}\bigl(\kappa(a\otimes b)\bigr)&=(p_{1}^{*}\xi_X+p_{2}^{*}\xi_Y)\cup p_{1}^{*}a\cup p_{2}^{*}\\ &=p_{1}^{*}(\xi_X\cup a)\cup p_{2}^{*}b\;+\;p_{1}^{*}a\cup p_{2}^{*}(\xi_Y\cup b)\\ &=\kappa\bigl((L_{V}\otimes\mathrm{id})(a\otimes b)+(\mathrm{id}\otimes L_{W})(a\otimes b)\bigr).\end{aligned}$$
Since pure tensors span $V\otimes W$, this gives $L_{\eta}\circ\kappa=\kappa\circ T$ on $V\otimes W$, where $T:=L_{V}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{W}+\mathrm{id}_{V}\otimes L_{W}$. By induction on $N$, $L_{\eta}^{N}\circ\kappa=\kappa\circ T^{N}$ for every $N\ge0$. Moreover $T$ raises the degree by $2$ (each of the two summands does), so $T^{N}$ maps $(V\otimes W)_{t}$ into $(V\otimes W)_{t+2N}$, and correspondingly $L_{\eta}^{N}$ maps $H^{t}(P)$ into $H^{t+2N}(P)$.

Step 6: the linear algebra. We now invoke Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_tensor_product_lefschetz with $K=\mathbb Q_{\ell}$ (characteristic $0$), with its $m$ equal to $d$ and its $n$ equal to $e$, and with $V,W,L_{V},L_{W}$ as in Step 3. Its hypotheses are exactly the grading conditions and the isomorphism properties verified in Step 3, and $V,W$ are finite dimensional by Step 1. Its conclusion is: for every integer $t$ with $0\le t\le d+e$, the operator
$$T^{\,d+e-t}:(V\otimes W)_{t}\longrightarrow (V\otimes W)_{2d+2e-t}$$
is an isomorphism (note $t+2(d+e-t)=2d+2e-t$).

Step 7: conclusion. Fix $n$ with $0\le n\le d+e$. The diagram
$$\require{AMScd} \begin{CD} (V\otimes W)_{n} @>{T^{\,d+e-n}}>> (V\otimes W)_{2d+2e-n} \\ @V{\kappa_{n}}^{\sim}VV @VV{\kappa_{2d+2e-n}}^{\sim}V \\ H^{n}(P) @>{L_{\eta}^{\,d+e-n}}>> H^{2d+2e-n}(P) \end{CD}$$
commutes by Step 5. Its two vertical arrows are isomorphisms by Step 4 (and $2d+2e-n\ge 0$, so the lower right group is in the K\"unneth range), and the top arrow is an isomorphism by Step 6. Hence the bottom arrow, $L_{\eta}^{\,d+e-n}:H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^{m}}}Y)_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})\to H^{2d+2e-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^{m}}}Y)_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})$, is an isomorphism. As $n$ ranges over all integers with $0\le n\le d+e$, this is precisely the required statement. $\blacksquare$

statement: Let \(N\cong\mathbb Z^d\) be a lattice with dual lattice \(M\), let \(P\subset M_{\mathbb R}\) be a lattice polytope of dimension \(d\), and let \(\Sigma\) be the normal fan of \(P\) in \(N_{\mathbb R}\), assumed smooth. For a maximal cone \(\sigma\in\Sigma\), let \(u_1^\sigma,\dots,u_d^\sigma\) be its ray generators, let \(m_\sigma\) be the vertex of \(P\) determined by \(\langle m_\sigma,w\rangle=\min_{m\in P}\langle m,w\rangle\) for all \(w\in\sigma\), and for \(v\in N\) write \(v=\sum_{i=1}^{d}c_i^\sigma(v)\,u_i^\sigma\). Suppose \(c_i^\sigma(v)\neq 0\) for every maximal cone \(\sigma\) and every \(i\), and set \(\tau_-(\sigma)=\operatorname{cone}\{u_i^\sigma : c_i^\sigma(v)<0\}\). Then for maximal cones \(\sigma\ne\sigma'\) with \(\sigma'\supseteq\tau_-(\sigma)\) one has \(\langle m_{\sigma'},v\rangle>\langle m_\sigma,v\rangle\).

  "proof": "We prove the statement exactly as written (with the strict inequality $\\langle m_{\\sigma'},v\\rangle>\\langle m_{\\sigma},v\\rangle$). The library contains no polyhedral or fan-theoretic results, so the proof is self-contained; it is organised in five parts. Throughout, $N\\cong\\mathbb Z^{d}$, $M=\\operatorname{Hom}_{\\mathbb Z}(N,\\mathbb Z)$, $N_{\\mathbb R}=N\\otimes_{\\mathbb Z}\\mathbb R$, $M_{\\mathbb R}=M\\otimes_{\\mathbb Z}\\mathbb R$, and $\\langle\\,,\\rangle:M_{\\mathbb R}\\times N_{\\mathbb R}\\to\\mathbb R$ is the extended perfect pairing. Since $M$ is free abelian, $M\\to M_{\\mathbb R}$, $m\\mapsto m\\otimes 1$, is injective, so we view $M\\subset M_{\\mathbb R}$; likewise $N\\subset N_{\\mathbb R}$. Perfectness means: $m\\in M_{\\mathbb R}$ satisfies $\\langle m,w\\rangle=0$ for all $w\\in N_{\\mathbb R}$ iff $m=0$, and every $\\mathbb R$-linear functional on $M_{\\mathbb R}$ is $\\langle\\,\\cdot\\,,w\\rangle$ for a unique $w\\in N_{\\mathbb R}$.\n\nThe polytope $P$ is the convex hull of finitely many points of $M$; write $V=\\{v_1,\\dots,v_s\\}$ for its set of vertices (extreme points). Then $P=\\operatorname{conv}(V)$, $V$ is finite, and $v\\in V$ iff $v\\notin\\operatorname{conv}(V\\setminus\\{v\\})$: indeed, writing $P=\\operatorname{conv}(S)$ with $|S|$ minimal, every extreme point of $P$ lies in $S$ (an extreme point written as a convex combination of points of $S$ must equal one of them), and each $s\\in S$ is extreme (otherwise $s$ is a convex combination of points of $P=\\operatorname{conv}(S)$, hence of points of $S\\setminus\\{s\\}$, contradicting minimality of $S$); thus $V=S$ is the minimal generating set. Since $\\dim P=d$, $\\operatorname{aff}(P)=M_{\\mathbb R}$.\n\n**Part 0. The case $d=0$.** Then $N_{\\mathbb R}=0$ and the only cone of $\\Sigma$ is $\\{0\\}$, so there are no pairs of distinct maximal cones and the claim is vacuous. We assume $d\\ge1$ from now on.\n\n**Part 1. Faces of $P$.** For $w\\in N_{\\mathbb R}$ put $\\mu(w):=\\min_{m\\in P}\\langle m,w\\rangle$ (the minimum exists because $P$ is compact) and\n$$F(w):=\\{\\,m\\in P:\\langle m,w\\rangle=\\mu(w)\\,\\}.$$\nCall $F(w)$ a *face* of $P$ (an *exposed* face); $P=F(0)$ is a face.\n\n**1.1 Lemma.** $\\mu(w)=\\min_{1\\le j\\le s}\\langle v_j,w\\rangle$, and $F(w)=\\operatorname{conv}\\{v\\in V:\\langle v,w\\rangle=\\mu(w)\\}$. In particular every face is non-empty, is the convex hull of the vertices it contains, and $P$ has only finitely many faces.\n*Proof.* A linear function on $\\operatorname{conv}(V)$ attains its minimum at a vertex, giving the first equality. If $x\\in F(w)$, write $x=\\sum_j\\lambda_jv_j$ with $\\lambda_j\\ge0$, $\\sum_j\\lambda_j=1$; then $\\mu(w)=\\langle x,w\\rangle=\\sum_j\\lambda_j\\langle v_j,w\\rangle\\ge\\sum_j\\lambda_j\\mu(w)=\\mu(w)$, so equality holds throughout and every $v_j$ with $\\lambda_j>0$ lies in $F(w)$. Hence $F(w)$ is the convex hull of the vertices it contains; the reverse inclusion is immediate since $F(w)$ is convex and contains them. A face is determined by its vertex set, and there are only $2^s$ subsets. $\\square$\n\n**1.2 Lemma.** If $F(w_1)\\cap F(w_2)\\ne\\emptyset$, then $F(w_1)\\cap F(w_2)=F(w_1+w_2)$; hence the intersection of two faces with a common point is again a face.\n*Proof.* Put $\\mu_i=\\mu(w_i)$. For all $m\\in P$, $\\langle m,w_1+w_2\\rangle\\ge\\mu_1+\\mu_2$, so $\\mu(w_1+w_2)\\ge\\mu_1+\\mu_2$; choosing $m^\\ast\\in F(w_1)\\cap F(w_2)$ gives equality $\\mu(w_1+w_2)=\\mu_1+\\mu_2$. Then $m\\in F(w_1+w_2)$ iff $\\langle m,w_1\\rangle+\\langle m,w_2\\rangle=\\mu_1+\\mu_2$, and since each term is $\\ge$ the corresponding $\\mu_i$, this holds iff $m\\in F(w_1)\\cap F(w_2)$. $\\square$\n\n**1.3 Lemma (strict separation, minimum convention).** Let $A,B\\subset M_{\\mathbb R}$ be non-empty, compact, convex, with $A\\cap B=\\emptyset$. Then there is $w\\in N_{\\mathbb R}$ with $\\sup_{x\\in A}\\langle x,w\\rangle<\\inf_{y\\in B}\\langle y,w\\rangle$.\n*Proof.* Choose any inner product $(\\cdot\\mid\\cdot)$ on $M_{\\mathbb R}$ with norm $\\|\\cdot\\|$. The compact set $A\\times B$ contains a pair $(a,b)$ minimising $\\|x-y\\|$; $a\\ne b$ since $A\\cap B=\\emptyset$. Let $\\xi:=b-a\\ne0$ and let $w\\in N_{\\mathbb R}$ be the unique element with $\\langle z,w\\rangle=(z\\mid\\xi)$ for all $z\\in M_{\\mathbb R}$ (perfectness). For $x\\in A$, $t\\mapsto\\|(a+t(x-a))-b\\|^2$ on $[0,1]$ is $\\ge\\|a-b\\|^2$ and equals it at $t=0$, so its right derivative at $0$ is $\\ge0$: $2(a-b\\mid x-a)\\ge0$, i.e.\\ $(x-a\\mid\\xi)\\le0$, i.e.\\ $\\langle x,w\\rangle\\le\\langle a,w\\rangle$. For $y\\in B$, $t\\mapsto\\|a-(b+t(y-b))\\|^2$ has right derivative $-2(a-b\\mid y-b)\\ge0$ at $0$, so $(y-b\\mid\\xi)\\le0$, i.e.\\ $\\langle y,w\\rangle\\ge\\langle b,w\\rangle$. Finally $\\langle a,w\\rangle-\\langle b,w\\rangle=(a-b\\mid b-a)=-\\|b-a\\|^2<0$. Hence $\\sup_A\\langle\\cdot,w\\rangle\\le\\langle a,w\\rangle<\\langle b,w\\rangle\\le\\inf_B\\langle\\cdot,w\\rangle$. $\\square$\n\n**1.4 Lemma (vertices are exposed).** For each vertex $v$ of $P$ there is $w\\in N_{\\mathbb R}$ with $F(w)=\\{v\\}$.\n*Proof.* $A:=\\{v\\}$ and $B:=\\operatorname{conv}(V\\setminus\\{v\\})$ are non-empty compact convex sets (as $v$ is a vertex and $d\\ge1$, $V\\setminus\\{v\\}\\ne\\emptyset$) and are disjoint because $v\\notin\\operatorname{conv}(V\\setminus\\{v\\})$. Lemma 1.3 gives $w$ with $\\langle v,w\\rangle<\\langle y,w\\rangle$ for all $y\\in B$, hence for all vertices $\\ne v$. By 1.1, $F(w)$ is the convex hull of the vertices at which $\\langle\\cdot,w\\rangle$ attains its minimum over $V$, namely $v$ alone; so $F(w)=\\{v\\}$. $\\square$\n\n**1.5 Lemma (exposed faces = abstract faces).** Let $G\\subseteq P$ be convex with the property that $x,y\\in P$, $t\\in(0,1)$, $tx+(1-t)y\\in G$ imply $x,y\\in G$. Then $G=F(w)$ for some $w$.\n*Proof.* If $G=P$, take $w=0$. Assume $G\\ne P$. First, $G=\\operatorname{conv}(G\\cap V)$:

write $x\in G$ as a convex combination $x=\sum_{j=1}^r\lambda_j p_j$ of vertices $p_j\in V$ with all $\lambda_j>0$, and argue by induction on $r$. If $r=1$ there is nothing to prove. If $r>1$, put
$$
y=\sum_{j=2}^r\frac{\lambda_j}{1-\lambda_1}p_j\in P.
$$
Then $x=\lambda_1p_1+(1-\lambda_1)y$ is a non-trivial convex combination of two points of $P$ lying in $G$, so the face property gives $p_1,y\in G$. By induction applied to $y$, which is a convex combination of $r-1$ vertices, we get $p_2,\dots,p_r\in G$. Thus every vertex occurring in a convex representation of a point of $G$ lies in $G$, and hence $G=\operatorname{conv}(G\cap V)$.

If $G\ne P$, set $V_G=G\cap V$. Then $V_G$ is a proper non-empty subset of $V$. We first show that
$$
\operatorname{aff}(G)\cap\operatorname{conv}(V\setminus V_G)=\varnothing.
$$
Suppose $z$ lies in the intersection. Since $z\in\operatorname{aff}(G)$, we may write
$$
z=\sum_{p\in V_G}\alpha_p p,\qquad \sum_{p\in V_G}\alpha_p=1,
$$
with real coefficients $\alpha_p$. Since $z\in\operatorname{conv}(V\setminus V_G)$, we may also write
$$
z=\sum_{q\in V\setminus V_G}\beta_q q,\qquad \beta_q\ge0,\quad \sum_q\beta_q=1.
$$
Let $P_+=\{p\in V_G:\alpha_p>0\}$ and $P_-=\{p\in V_G:\alpha_p<0\}$. Then
$$
\sum_{q\in V\setminus V_G}\beta_q q+\sum_{p\in P_-}(-\alpha_p)p
=
\sum_{p\in P_+}\alpha_p p.
$$
The sum of the coefficients on the right is
$$
S=\sum_{p\in P_+}\alpha_p,
$$
and the sum of the coefficients on the left is
$$
1+\sum_{p\in P_-}(-\alpha_p).
$$
But $\sum_{P_+}\alpha_p+\sum_{P_-}\alpha_p=1$, so indeed
$$
S=1+\sum_{p\in P_-}(-\alpha_p)>0.
$$
Dividing by $S$, the right-hand side becomes a convex combination of vertices in $G$, hence lies in $G$. The left-hand side is a convex combination of vertices of $P$ whose support contains every $q$ with $\beta_q>0$. Since $G$ is a face and the common point lies in $G$, all vertices appearing on the left must lie in $G$. This is impossible because $\sum_q\beta_q=1$ and every such $q$ lies outside $G$. Therefore the intersection is empty.

Now separate the affine subspace $L=\operatorname{aff}(G)$ from the compact convex set $B=\operatorname{conv}(V\setminus V_G)$. Choose a pair $(a,b)\in L\times B$ minimizing the Euclidean distance $\|x-y\|$ (existence follows from closedness of $L$ and compactness of $B$). Since $L\cap B=\varnothing$, $a\ne b$. Let $\xi=b-a\ne0$, and let $w\in N_{\mathbb R}$ be the unique element such that $\langle z,w\rangle=(z\mid\xi)$ for all $z\in M_{\mathbb R}$, where $(\cdot\mid\cdot)$ is the chosen inner product.

For any $x\in L$, the function $t\mapsto\|a+t(x-a)-b\|^2$ has a global minimum at $t=0$, so its derivative at $0$ vanishes:
$$
0=2(a-b\mid x-a)=-2(\xi\mid x-a),
$$
hence $\langle x,w\rangle=\langle a,w\rangle$ for every $x\in L$. For any $y\in B$, the function $t\mapsto\|a-(b+t(y-b))\|^2$ has a minimum at $t=0$ on $[0,1]$, so its right derivative is non-negative:
$$
0\le -2(a-b\mid y-b)=2(\xi\mid y-b),
$$
hence $\langle y,w\rangle\ge\langle b,w\rangle$. Finally,
$$
\langle b,w\rangle-\langle a,w\rangle=(\xi\mid\xi)=\|\xi\|^2>0.
$$
Thus $w$ is constant on $G$ and strictly larger on every vertex outside $G$. Consequently the minimum of $\langle\cdot,w\rangle$ on $P$ is attained exactly on $G$, and by Lemma 1.1 we get $F(w)=G$. This proves Lemma 1.5. $\square$

**Part 2. The normal fan and the vertex attached to a maximal cone.** For a non-empty face $F$ of $P$ put
$$
N(F):=\{w\in N_{\mathbb R}:F\subseteq F(w)\}.
$$
With the minimum convention, the normal fan $\Sigma$ is the fan whose cones are precisely these $N(F)$. We record the elementary properties we need.

Because $F=\operatorname{conv}(V_F)$, where $V_F=F\cap V$, the condition $w\in N(F)$ is equivalent to
$$
\langle v,w\rangle\le\langle u,w\rangle\qquad
\text{for all }v\in V_F,\ u\in V.
$$
Hence $N(F)$ is a closed convex cone. If $F\subseteq G$, then clearly $N(G)\subseteq N(F)$.

The map $F\mapsto N(F)$ is injective on non-empty faces. Indeed, suppose $F\ne G$. If $F\not\subseteq G$, choose a vertex $v\in V_F\setminus V_G$. By Lemma 1.5 there is $w$ with $F(w)=G$. Then $w\in N(G)$. If also $w\in N(F)$, then $F\subseteq F(w)=G$, contradiction. The case $F\subsetneq G$ is symmetric. Thus $N(F)\ne N(G)$.

Now we identify the maximal cones. If $F$ is not a vertex, choose a vertex $v\in F$. Then $\{v\}\subsetneq F$, so $N(F)\subseteq N(\{v\})$. The inclusion is proper: by Lemma 1.4 choose $w$ with $F(w)=\{v\}$; then $w\in N(\{v\})$, but $w\notin N(F)$ because $F\not\subseteq\{v\}$. Hence $N(F)$ is not maximal.

Conversely, let $v\in V$. If $N(\{v\})\subseteq N(G)$ for some face $G$, choose $w$ exposing $\{v\}$, so $F(w)=\{v\}$. Then $w\in N(G)$, hence $G\subseteq F(w)=\{v\}$, and therefore $G=\{v\}$. Thus $N(\{v\})$ is maximal.

We conclude that the maximal cones of $\Sigma$ are exactly the cones
$$
\sigma_v:=N(\{v\}),\qquad v\in V,
$$
and that $v\mapsto\sigma_v$ is a bijection from the vertex set of $P$ to the set of maximal cones.

For a maximal cone $\sigma$, let $m_\sigma$ be the unique vertex with $\sigma=N(\{m_\sigma\})$. Then for every $w\in N_{\mathbb R}$,
$$
w\in\sigma
\iff m_\sigma\in F(w)
\iff \langle m_\sigma,w\rangle=\min_{m\in P}\langle m,w\rangle.
\tag{$\ddagger$}
$$
This proves both existence and uniqueness of the vertex $m_\sigma$ appearing in the statement. For completeness, here is the uniqueness argument in the form needed later. Suppose $m''\in P$ satisfies $\langle m'',w\rangle=\min_P\langle\cdot,w\rangle$ for every $w\in\sigma$. Let $H$ be the minimal face of $P$ containing $m''$; it exists because there are only finitely many faces, and the intersection of two faces with a common point is again a face by Lemma 1.2. For every $w$, one has $m''\in F(w)$ if and only if $H\subseteq F(w)$, since $F(w)$ is a face and $H$ is the smallest face containing $m''$. Therefore $\sigma\subseteq N(H)$. But $N(H)$ is a cone of $\Sigma$ and $\sigma$ is maximal, so $\sigma=N(H)$. On the other hand $\sigma=N(\{m_\sigma\})$, and injectivity of $F\mapsto N(F)$ gives $H=\{m_\sigma\}$, hence $m''=m_\sigma$.

**Part 3. Ray generators as a basis.** Since $\Sigma$ is smooth, the primitive ray generators of every cone extend to a $\mathbb Z$-basis of $N$. A maximal cone has exactly $d$ ray generators, so for a maximal cone $\sigma$ the vectors
$$
u_1^\sigma,\dots,u_d^\sigma
$$
form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of $N$. Consequently they form an $\mathbb R$-basis of $N_{\mathbb R}$, and every $v\in N$ has a unique expansion
$$
v=\sum_{i=1}^d c_i^\sigma(v)u_i^\sigma
$$
with coefficients $c_i^\sigma(v)\in\mathbb Z$.

**Part 4. The inequality.** Let $\sigma\ne\sigma'$ be maximal cones such that $\sigma'\supseteq\tau_-(\sigma)$. Write
$$
a=m_\sigma,\qquad b=m_{\sigma'},\qquad \delta=b-a\in M.
$$
Because distinct maximal cones correspond to distinct vertices, $\sigma\ne\sigma'$ implies $a\ne b$, so $\delta\ne0$.

For each $i$, the ray generator $u_i:=u_i^\sigma$ lies in $\sigma$. Applying $(\ddagger)$ to $\sigma$ and $w=u_i$, the vertex $a$ minimises $\langle\cdot,u_i\rangle$ on $P$. Since $b\in P$,
$$
\langle \delta,u_i\rangle=\langle b-a,u_i\rangle\ge0.
\tag{1}
$$

Now suppose $c_i^\sigma(v)<0$. Then $u_i\in\tau_-(\sigma)\subseteq\sigma'$. Applying $(\ddagger)$ to $\sigma'$ and $w=u_i$, the vertex $b$ minimises $\langle\cdot,u_i\rangle$ on $P$. Since $a\in P$,
$$
\langle \delta,u_i\rangle=\langle b-a,u_i\rangle\le0.
$$
Together with (1) this gives
$$
c_i^\sigma(v)<0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \langle\delta,u_i\rangle=0.
\tag{2}
$$

Since $\delta\ne0$ and $u_1,\dots,u_d$ form an $\mathbb R$-basis of $N_{\mathbb R}$, the pairing is non-degenerate; hence there exists an index $i_0$ with $\langle\delta,u_{i_0}\rangle\ne0$. By (1) this value is actually positive. By (2) its coefficient cannot be negative, and by hypothesis $c_{i_0}^\sigma(v)\ne0$. Therefore
$$
c_{i_0}^\sigma(v)>0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\langle\delta,u_{i_0}\rangle>0.
$$

Finally expand $v$ in the basis $u_i$:
$$
\langle\delta,v\rangle
=
\left\langle\delta,\sum_{i=1}^d c_i^\sigma(v)u_i\right\rangle
=
\sum_{i=1}^d c_i^\sigma(v)\langle\delta,u_i\rangle.
$$
For indices with $c_i^\sigma(v)<0$, the corresponding term is zero by (2). For indices with $c_i^\sigma(v)>0$, the factor $\langle\delta,u_i\rangle$ is non-negative by (1). At least one such index, namely $i_0$, contributes a strictly positive term. Hence
$$
\langle\delta,v\rangle>0.
$$
Substituting $\delta=m_{\sigma'}-m_\sigma$ gives
$$
\langle m_{\sigma'},v\rangle>\langle m_\sigma,v\rangle,
$$
which is exactly the required inequality. $\square$"
}

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(A\subset H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-span of the cycle classes of all Cartier divisors on \(S_k\), and let \(\beta\) be the Poincaré duality pairing on \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then the restriction \(\beta|_A\) is nondegenerate.
proof: Put X = S_k. Since S is smooth projective geometrically connected over F_{q^m}, the base change X is a smooth projective connected surface over the algebraically closed field k of characteristic p, and ell != p. Over an algebraically closed field, connected is the same as geometrically connected, so X is geometrically connected. Let c(D) denote the cycle class of a Cartier divisor D on X in H^2_et(X,Q_ell), under the fixed identification of Tate twists with Q_ell. Let NS = NS(X) = Pic(X)/Pic^0(X). By lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_205, NS is a finitely generated abelian group. The theorem Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_464 is stated for an intersection form on NS given by cup product of cycle classes followed by the Poincare duality trace; in particular, the cycle class of a Cartier divisor depends only on its class in NS and the induced map is additive. Hence c factors through NS and induces a Q_ell-linear map cbar: NS tensor_Z Q_ell -> H^2_et(X,Q_ell). Its image is exactly A, because A is by definition the Q_ell-span of the classes c(D) of Cartier divisors D. Let beta_0 be the Poincare pairing beta_0(x,y)=tr_0(x cup y), where tr_0 is the trace normalised by tr_0(cl(z))=1 for closed points z. Define B_0 on NS by B_0(D,E)=beta_0(c(D),c(E)). Lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_464 states that the R-bilinear extension of B_0 to NS tensor_Z R is nondegenerate, indeed of signature (1,rho-1), where rho is the rank of NS. The hypotheses of that lemma apply to X: X is smooth projective geometrically connected over the algebraically closed field k, ell != char(k), and rho >= 1 because an ample Cartier divisor has nonzero class in NS. Let M = NS/NS_tors. Torsion in NS pairs trivially: if t is torsion and n t = 0, then n B_0(t,e)=B_0(n t,e)=0 for every e, so B_0(t,e)=0. Thus B_0 descends to M. Choose a Z-basis e_1,...,e_rho of M and let G be the rho x rho Gram matrix (B_0(e_i,e_j)) with entries in Z. Nondegeneracy over R implies det(G) != 0 in R. Since det(G) is an integer, det(G) is nonzero in Q and hence in Q_ell. Therefore G is invertible over Q_ell, and the Q_ell-extension B_ell of B_0 to M tensor_Z Q_ell = NS tensor_Z Q_ell is nondegenerate. The beta appearing in the lemma is also a Poincare duality pairing H^2_et(X,Q_ell) x H^2_et(X,Q_ell) -> Q_ell. The trace tr_0 used for beta_0 is another Poincare duality trace. Since H^4_et(X,Q_ell) is one-dimensional, there exists a scalar lambda in Q_ell^* such that beta(x,y)=lambda beta_0(x,y) for all x,y in H^2_et(X,Q_ell). Consequently, for u,v in NS tensor_Z Q_ell, beta(cbar(u),cbar(v))=lambda B_ell(u,v). Now take x in A with beta(x,y)=0 for every y in A. Choose u in NS tensor_Z Q_ell with x=cbar(u). For any v in NS tensor_Z Q_ell, y=cbar(v) lies in A, so 0=beta(cbar(u),cbar(v))=lambda B_ell(u,v). Since lambda is nonzero, B_ell(u,v)=0 for all v. Nondegeneracy of B_ell gives u=0, hence x=0. Thus the right radical of beta restricted to A is zero. The pairing is symmetric because cup product of two degree-2 classes is graded-commutative with sign (-1)^(2*2)=1, so the left radical is also zero. Therefore beta|_A is nondegenerate.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(Y\subset X\) be a smooth effective divisor of pure dimension \(d-1\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) be the closed immersion, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and use it to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of \(Y\), and for \(n\ge0\) let \(i_!:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{n+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the Gysin homomorphism of the divisor \(Y\). Let \(n\ge0\) be an integer such that \(i^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is surjective. Then \(i^*(i_!\alpha)=\alpha\smile i^*\xi\) for every \(\alpha\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
proof:
Write H^n(Z) := H^n_{\acute et}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for Z \in \{X,Y\}, with k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q, and write H^*(Z) = \bigoplus_{n\ge0} H^n(Z) for the graded \mathbb Q_\ell-algebra with product given by cup product.

STEP 0 (the Gysin map of the statement is the trace-characterised one, so that lemma_439 applies). The fixed nonzero element u \in \mathbb Q_\ell(1) identifies every Tate twist \mathbb Q_\ell(r) with \mathbb Q_\ell by u^r \mapsto 1; this is the identification used in the statement, and it is the one used in eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_439_gysin_projection_formula_divisor. Composing the Poincar\'e duality trace with this identification gives, for Z \in \{X,Y\}, traces tr_Z : H^{2\dim Z}(Z) \to \mathbb Q_\ell (on Y the trace being the sum of the traces on the connected components of Y_k; no geometric connectedness of Y is needed). By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77(b), applied to the smooth projective geometrically connected X over \mathbb F_q with m = 1, the pairing H^{n+2}(X) \times H^{2d-2-n}(X) \to \mathbb Q_\ell, (b,c) \mapsto tr_X(b \cup c), is perfect for every n. Hence for each n there is AT MOST ONE \mathbb Q_\ell-linear map \varphi : H^n(Y) \to H^{n+2}(X) satisfying tr_X(\varphi(a) \cup b) = tr_Y(a \cup i^*b) for all a \in H^n(Y), b \in H^{2d-2-n}(X). The Gysin homomorphism of the smooth divisor Y \subset X (the map denoted i_! in the present statement) is exactly this map: it is the standard characterisation of the divisor Gysin map by compatibility with the Poincar\'e duality traces, and it is precisely how the map i_! is introduced in eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_439_gysin_projection_formula_divisor, whose hypotheses (q = p^a, \ell \neq p, X smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d \ge 1 over \mathbb F_q, Y \subset X a smooth effective divisor of pure dimension d-1 defined over \mathbb F_q, i the inclusion, k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q, u \in \mathbb Q_\ell(1) nonzero, \xi = cl(Y), i_! the trace-characterised Gysin map) are verbatim the hypotheses of the present lemma. We may therefore invoke that lemma.

STEP 1 (the surjectivity hypothesis produces a lift). Let n \ge 0 and let \alpha \in H^n(Y). By hypothesis i^* : H^n(X) \to H^n(Y) is surjective, so there exists x \in H^n(X) with i^*x = \alpha. (If \alpha = 0 one may take x = 0; the argument below is uniform in \alpha.)

STEP 2 (projection formula for the divisor). Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_439_gysin_projection_formula_divisor to the class x \in H^n(X) gives
    i_!(i^*x) = x \cup \xi .
Substituting \alpha = i^*x from Step 1, we obtain the explicit formula
    i_!\alpha = x \cup \xi \ \in H^{n+2}(X).

STEP 3 (pull back along i, using that i^* is a graded ring homomorphism). \'Etale cohomology is contravariantly functorial and the cup product is functorial: the pullback on the \acute etale topos, f^{-1}(-) \otimes f^{-1}(-) \to f^{-1}(- \otimes -) together with f^{-1}\mathbb Q_\ell \cong \mathbb Q_\ell, is an isomorphism of symmetric monoidal functors, so the induced map f^* : H^*(\,\cdot\,) on cohomology satisfies f^*(1) = 1 and f^*(p \cup q) = f^*p \cup f^*q for all homogeneous p,q, with NO Koszul sign (f^* has degree 0 and is a homomorphism, not a derivation). Applying this to f = i, p = x \in H^n(X) and q = \xi \in H^2(X), and using Step 2,
    i^*(i_!\alpha) \;=\; i^*(x \cup \xi) \;=\; i^*x \cup i^*\xi \;=\; \alpha \cup i^*\xi,
where the last equality is again Step 1. Both sides lie in H^{n+2}(Y), as required (\alpha has degree n and i^*\xi has degree 2). Since H^*(Y) is graded-commutative and i^*\xi is of even degree, \alpha \cup i^*\xi = i^*\xi \cup \alpha, so this is the usual self-intersection formula with no sign.

STEP 4 (the conclusion is independent of the auxiliary lift). The identity just proved involves only \alpha. For completeness, if x' \in H^n(X) is another lift of \alpha, then i^*(x - x') = 0, so Step 2 applied to x - x' (using \mathbb Q_\ell-linearity of i_!) gives (x - x') \cup \xi = i_!(i^*(x-x')) = i_!(0) = 0; hence x \cup \xi = x' \cup \xi and Step 3 yields the same value of i^*(i_!\alpha). Thus the argument is well posed.

This covers every integer n \ge 0 and every \alpha \in H^n_{\acute et}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), and establishes i^*(i_!\alpha) = \alpha \smile i^*\xi.

REMARKS ON THE HYPOTHESES USED. Ampleness/very-ampleness of Y is not used, nor is geometric connectedness of Y (the trace on Y_k is the sum of the component traces, exactly as in lemma_439). The only place the extra hypothesis of this lemma is used is Step 1: it is what lets one write \alpha as i^*x and thereby apply the projection formula of Step 2 directly, avoiding the circular attempt to extend im(i^*)-linearity of i^*i_! to all of H^*(Y).

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(Y\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(\mathcal E\) be a vector bundle of rank \(\rho\ge1\) on \(Y\) defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and let \(\pi:P=\mathbf P_Y(\mathcal E)\to Y\) be the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients. Suppose the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every integer \(n\ge0\). Then the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every integer \(n\ge0\).
proof:
We prove the statement by a direct instantiation of the already-proved lemma eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/7074f0 (the projective-bundle step for Frobenius semisimplicity over a prime-power field) with the prime field size replaced by q^m. No linear algebra and no finiteness statement has to be invoked by hand; they are contained in the proof of that lemma.

Step 1 (the auxiliary prime power). Put Q := q^m = p^{am}. Since a >= 1 and m >= 1, one has am >= 1, so Q is again a prime power, with the *same* underlying prime p. In particular the given prime ell satisfies ell != p, so ell is admissible as a coefficient prime for the prime power Q as well.

Step 2 (identification of the algebraic closures). Because F_q \subset F_{q^m} = F_Q \subset \overline{F}_q, the field k = \overline{F}_q is algebraic over F_Q (it is algebraic over F_q, and F_Q/F_q is finite) and is algebraically closed; hence k is an algebraic closure of F_Q. We therefore use k as the chosen algebraic closure \overline{F}_Q in what follows; base change of an F_Q-scheme to \overline{F}_Q and to k are the same operation, so the groups H^n_et(Y_k, Q_ell) and H^n_et(P_k, Q_ell) that appear in the target are literally the groups appearing in the instantiated lemma.

Step 3 (identification of the Frobenius operators). For an F_Q-scheme Z, the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius of Z_k is (id_{Z_k} \times Spec \sigma_Q)^*, where \sigma_Q(c) = c^Q = c^{q^m} for c \in k. This is exactly the operator the target calls "the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius". Thus the hypothesis and the conclusion we must obtain are statements about the very same endomorphisms that the instantiated lemma talks about; there is no change of operator to justify.

Step 4 (verification of the hypotheses of eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/7074f0, with q replaced by Q). That lemma reads, for a prime power q_0 = p^{a_0}, a prime ell != p, and k_0 = \overline{F}_{q_0}: if Y_0 is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over F_{q_0}, E_0 a vector bundle of rank r_0 + 1 >= 1 on Y_0, and \pi_0: P_0 = \mathbf{P}_{Y_0}(E_0) -> Y_0 the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients, then semisimplicity of the q_0-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^n_et((Y_0)_k, Q_ell) for every n >= 0 implies semisimplicity of the q_0-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^n_et((P_0)_k, Q_ell) for every n >= 0. We instantiate it with q_0 := Q = q^m (so a_0 := am), k_0 := k = \overline{F}_q, Y_0 := Y, E_0 := \mathcal E, r_0 := \rho - 1, and P_0 := P = \mathbf{P}_Y(\mathcal E). Each hypothesis is then satisfied:
  (i) q_0 = p^{am} is a prime power and ell != p (Steps 1); k_0 = \overline{F}_{q_0} by Step 2.
  (ii) Y is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over F_{q^m} = F_Q, by the hypothesis of the target lemma.
  (iii) \mathcal E is a vector bundle on Y defined over F_{q^m} = F_Q, again by hypothesis, and its rank is \rho >= 1, so \rho = r_0 + 1 with r_0 = \rho - 1 >= 0 an integer, as required.
  (iv) P = \mathbf{Y}_Y(\mathcal E) = \mathbf{P}_Y(\mathcal E) is precisely the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients of \mathcal E, with projection \pi: P -> Y, matching the lemma's P_0 = \mathbf{P}_{Y_0}(E_0).
  (v) The semisimplicity hypothesis: by assumption the q^m-power = Q-power arithmetic Frobenius (id_{Y_k} \times Spec \sigma)^*, \sigma(c) = c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_et(Y_k, Q_ell) for every integer n >= 0; this is exactly the required hypothesis with q_0 = Q.

Step 5 (conclusion). Applying eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/7074f0 with these data yields: the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius (id_{P_k} \times Spec \sigma)^*, \sigma(c) = c^Q = c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_et(P_k, Q_ell) for every integer n >= 0. By the identification in Step 3 this is verbatim the desired conclusion: the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_et(P_k, Q_ell) for every n >= 0.

Since n was arbitrary, the lemma is proved. (Equivalently, one could have cited the identical statement Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_375; only one of the two is used above.)

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\beta(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup y)\) be the Poincaré duality pairing on \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Let \(A\) be the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-span of the cycle classes of all Cartier divisors on \(S_k\), let \(T=A^\perp\), and let \(F\) be the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius. Suppose \(\beta|_A\) is nondegenerate. Then the restriction of \(\beta\) to \(T\) is a perfect pairing and \(F\) is a \(q^{2m}\)-similitude of it.
proof:
Let V = H^2_et(S_k,Q_l) and let V^vee denote the Q_l-linear dual of V. Apply lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77 to S, regarded as a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d = 2 over F_{q^m}. It gives the Poincare duality trace tr_S: H^4_et(S_k,Q_l) -> Q_l(-2) such that the pairing beta_0(x,y) = tr_S(x cup y) on V is perfect and satisfies beta_0(Fx,Fy) = q^{2m} beta_0(x,y) for all x,y in V, where F is the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. Under the fixed nonzero element of Q_l(1), which identifies Q_l(-2) with Q_l, beta_0 is exactly the beta in the statement. Hence beta is a perfect pairing on V, F is a q^{2m}-similitude of beta on V, and the map rho: V -> V^vee, y -> beta(-,y), is an isomorphism.

In particular V is finite-dimensional. Indeed, if dim V = kappa were infinite, then dim V^vee = |Q_l|^kappa >= 2^kappa > kappa, so rho could not be an isomorphism. Therefore A and T are finite-dimensional. Since S is smooth, Cartier divisors and Weil divisors coincide, so the subspace A in the statement is the same as the subspace considered in lemma eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/9db8b3.

We first prove that beta|_T is perfect. Define r: V -> A^vee by r(v)(a) = beta(a,v). Let l be any element of A^vee. Extend l to a linear functional L on V. Since rho is an isomorphism, there exists v in V such that L(x) = beta(x,v) for every x in V. Then r(v) = l, so r is surjective. Its kernel is exactly T = A^perp = {v in V : beta(a,v) = 0 for all a in A}. The restriction r|_A: A -> A^vee is injective because beta|_A is nondegenerate; since A is finite-dimensional, r|_A is an isomorphism. Hence for every v in V there exists a in A with r(a) = r(v), and then v - a lies in T. Thus V = A + T. Also A intersect T = ker(r|_A) = 0, so V = A direct sum T.

Now define s: T -> T^vee by s(t)(t') = beta(t',t). If s(t) = 0, then beta(t',t) = 0 for every t' in T, and beta(a,t) = 0 for every a in A because t lies in T. Since V = A + T, it follows that beta(x,t) = 0 for every x in V. Because rho is injective, t = 0. Thus s is injective. Since T is finite-dimensional, s is an isomorphism, so beta|_T is a perfect pairing.

By lemma eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/9db8b3, F(A) is contained in A and F(T) is contained in T. Since T is finite-dimensional and F|_T is injective (because F is an automorphism of V), F|_T is an automorphism of T. Finally, for x,y in T we have Fx,Fy in T, and the similitude identity on V gives beta(Fx,Fy) = q^{2m} beta(x,y). The scalar q^{2m} is nonzero in Q_l, so F is a q^{2m}-similitude of the perfect pairing beta|_T.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(\mathcal E\) be a vector bundle of rank \(2\) on \(S\) defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and let \(\pi:P=\mathbf P_S(\mathcal E)\to S\) be the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients. Then the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on \(H^3_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
proof:
Proof. Put Q=q^m=p^{am}. Let F_S and F_P denote the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms (id x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^Q, acting on H^*_et(S_k,Q_ell) and H^*_et(P_k,Q_ell). First, finite-dimensionality of the cohomology groups that occur, and invertibility of the corresponding Frobenius operators, follow from eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob applied to the proper F_Q-varieties S and P, with the constant sheaf Q_ell equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure.

Step 1. Semisimplicity on H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell). The surface S is smooth projective geometrically connected over F_Q. Applying eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/ec0b56 with q replaced by Q shows that F_S is semisimple on H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell).

Step 2. Semisimplicity on H^3_et(S_k,Q_ell). Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_519_poincare_duality_frobenius_semisimplicity to the smooth projective surface S over F_Q, with e=2 and n=1. It states that F_S is semisimple on H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell) if and only if F_S is semisimple on H^{2e-n}=H^3_et(S_k,Q_ell). By Step 1, F_S is semisimple on H^3_et(S_k,Q_ell).

Step 3. Projective bundle decomposition for P. The vector bundle E has rank rho=2. Choose a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) and use it to identify Tate twists with Q_ell, as required by Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_516. Apply that lemma with Y=S, q=Q, m=1, rho=2, and n=3. It gives a Q_ell-linear isomorphism
Phi: H^3_et(S_k,Q_ell) (+) H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell) -> H^3_et(P_k,Q_ell),
(alpha_0,alpha_1) -> pi^*alpha_0 + pi^*alpha_1 cup xi,
where xi=c_1(O_P(1)). Moreover, under Phi the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius F_P corresponds to the direct sum operator F_S (+) (Q F_S): the i=0 summand is acted on by Q^{1*0}F_S=F_S, and the i=1 summand is acted on by Q^{1*1}F_S=Q F_S.

Step 4. Semisimplicity of the summand operators. The operator F_S on H^3_et(S_k,Q_ell) is semisimple by Step 2. The operator F_S on H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell) is semisimple by Step 1. Since ell != p, the integer Q=q^m is not divisible by ell, hence Q is a nonzero element of Q_ell. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_248, a nonzero scalar multiple of a semisimple invertible operator is semisimple. Therefore Q F_S is semisimple on H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell).

Step 5. Semisimplicity of the direct sum. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9, the direct sum operator F_S (+) (Q F_S) on H^3_et(S_k,Q_ell) (+) H^1_et(S_k,Q_ell) is semisimple.

Step 6. Transport to P. The isomorphism Phi intertwines F_P with the semisimple direct sum operator from Step 5. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8, semisimplicity is preserved under such a Frobenius-equivariant isomorphism. Hence F_P is semisimple on H^3_et(P_k,Q_ell). This is exactly the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius, i.e. the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, on H^3_et(P_k,Q_ell).

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(A\) be the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-span in \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) of the cycle classes of all Cartier divisors on \(S_k\). Then there exists an integer \(r\ge1\) divisible by \(m\) such that \(A\) is the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-span of the cycle classes of the Cartier divisors on \(S_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\).
proof:
Let F = F_{q^m} and let k be an algebraic closure of F_q. Write Pic = Pic(S_k), Pic0 = Pic^0(S_k), and NS = Pic/Pic0. Let cl: Pic -> H^2_et(S_k,Q_ell(1)) -> H^2_et(S_k,Q_ell) be the cycle class map, where the second arrow is the chosen identification Q_ell(1) isomorphic to Q_ell. For a Cartier divisor D, cl(D)=cl(O(D)). The scheme S_k is integral because S is smooth, projective, and geometrically connected over a field. Since every line bundle on an integral noetherian scheme has a nonzero rational section, every line bundle is O(D) for some Cartier divisor D. Hence A is exactly the Q_ell-span of cl(Pic).

We first prove that cl(Pic0)=0. Let P=Pic^0_{S_k/k}; P is an abelian variety. For each n>=1 the multiplication-by-n map [n]:P->P is finite surjective, and since k is algebraically closed it is surjective on k-points. Thus Pic0=P(k) is divisible. Fix L in Pic0. For each r>=1 choose M_r in Pic0 with M_r^{⊗ell^r} isomorphic to L. Since ell!=p, ell^r is invertible in k, so the Kummer sequence 0 -> mu_{ell^r} -> G_m -> G_m -> 0 is exact on the etale site and gives a connecting homomorphism delta_r: Pic -> H^2_et(S_k,mu_{ell^r}). The ell-adic Chern class of L is the inverse limit of delta_r(L) in H^2_et(S_k,Z_ell(1)), and its image after tensoring with Q_ell is cl(L). Since delta_r is a homomorphism from multiplicative Pic to additive cohomology, delta_r(L)=delta_r(M_r^{⊗ell^r})=ell^r delta_r(M_r)=0, because multiplication by ell^r on H^2_et(S_k,mu_{ell^r}) is zero. Therefore cl(L)=0. Thus cl factors through NS.

By lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_205, NS is a finitely generated abelian group. Choose line bundles L_1,...,L_s whose classes generate NS. Then A is the Q_ell-span of cl(L_1),...,cl(L_s). If s=0 this span is 0.

We need a descent fact. Let X be a separated finite type scheme over a finite field F and let K/F be an algebraic extension. Every line bundle on X_K descends to X_E for some finite subextension E/F of K. Proof. Choose a finite affine open cover U_a of X defined over F. Since X is separated, each U_a∩U_b is affine. For each a, the line bundle is trivial on finitely many principal opens D(f_{a,alpha}) of U_a,K. The finite set of f_{a,alpha}, the elements h_{a,alpha} with sum h_{a,alpha}f_{a,alpha}=1, and the transition functions on overlaps D(f_{a,alpha}f_{b,beta}) are elements of finitely generated F-algebras after base change to K. Let E be the finite extension of F generated over F by all coefficients needed to write these elements and their inverses and cocycle equations; E/F is finite because K is algebraic over a finite field. The descended principal opens cover X_E, and the descended transition functions satisfy the cocycle condition because they do after the faithfully flat base change E->K. Gluing gives a line bundle L_E on X_E whose pullback to X_K is the original line bundle.

Apply this to X=S, F=F_{q^m}, K=k. For each i there is a finite extension E_i/F and a line bundle L_{i,E_i} on S_{E_i} whose base change to S_k is L_i. Since E_i is a finite subextension of k/F, E_i=F_{q^{m t_i}} for some t_i>=1. Put r=m lcm(t_1,...,t_s) if s>0, and r=m if s=0. Then each E_i embeds in F_{q^r}. Base change L_{i,E_i} to S_{F_{q^r}}, and choose a Cartier divisor D_{i,r} on S_{F_{q^r}} with O(D_{i,r})=L_{i,r}. Its base change to S_k is a Cartier divisor D_i with O(D_i)=L_i. Naturality of cycle classes gives cl(D_i)=cl(L_i). Hence each generator cl(L_i) lies in B_r, the Q_ell-span of cycle classes of Cartier divisors on S_{F_{q^r}}. Therefore A is contained in B_r.

Conversely, any Cartier divisor on S_{F_{q^r}} base changes to a Cartier divisor on S_k, and its cycle class is one of the classes spanning A. Thus B_r is contained in A. Hence A=B_r, and r is divisible by m and satisfies r>=1.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let l != p be prime, let m >= 1, and put k=bar F_q. Let f:Y -> X be a proper surjective generically finite morphism of degree d >= 1 between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension D over F_{q^m}. If the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_et(Y_k,Q_l) for every integer n >= 0, then it is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) for every integer n >= 0.
proof: Proof. Put Q=q^m, so Q=p^{am} and k=bar F_Q=bar F_q. Let F_Z denote the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius (id_Z x Spec sigma_Q)^* on H^n_et(Z_k,Q_l), where sigma_Q(c)=c^Q. We must show that F_X is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) for every n. If D=0, then a smooth projective geometrically connected zero-dimensional variety over F_Q is Spec F_Q. Hence X=Y=Spec F_Q and f is the identity. Then H^0_et(X_k,Q_l)=Q_l and H^n_et(X_k,Q_l)=0 for n>0; the Frobenius is the identity on Q_l and the zero operator on the zero spaces, hence semisimple. Thus assume D>=1. Fix n>=0. By lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob applied over F_Q to the proper smooth varieties X and Y, the vector spaces V_X=H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) and V_Y=H^n_et(Y_k,Q_l) are finite-dimensional over Q_l.
