By lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a, F_X and F_Y are invertible Q_l-linear operators on V_X and V_Y. First note that pullback along f commutes with arithmetic Frobenius. Let f_k:Y_k->X_k be the base change of f, and let Phi_Z=id_Z x Spec sigma_Q. Since f is defined over F_Q, the square with vertical maps f_k and horizontal maps Phi_Z commutes: f_k Phi_Y = Phi_X f_k. By functoriality of etale cohomology, (g h)^*=h^* g^*, so F_Y f^* = Phi_Y^* f_k^* = (f_k Phi_Y)^* = (Phi_X f_k)^* = f_k^* Phi_X^* = f^* F_X. Now apply lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_444 with the prime power Q in place of q and with N=d. It gives a Q_l-linear map f_*:V_Y->V_X such that f_* F_Y = F_X f_* and f_* f^* = d id_{V_X}. Set p=(1/d)f_*:V_Y->V_X and s=f^*:V_X->V_Y. Then p s = id_{V_X}. Hence s is injective, p is surjective, and U=s(V_X)=im(f^*) is a direct summand of V_Y via the idempotent e=s p: e^2=s(p s)p=s p=e and im(e)=U. The summand U is stable under F_Y. Indeed, p F_Y = F_X p because f_* F_Y=F_X f_*, and s F_X=F_Y s by the previous paragraph; hence F_Y e = F_Y s p = s F_X p = s p F_Y = e F_Y. Equivalently, for u=s(x), F_Y u = F_Y s(x)=s(F_X x) in U. By hypothesis, F_Y is semisimple on V_Y. Since U is an F_Y-stable direct summand, lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_35(ii) implies that F_Y restricted to U is semisimple. The map s:V_X->U is a Q_l-linear isomorphism, and it is F-equivariant: s F_X = F_Y|_U s. Therefore, by lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8, F_X is semisimple on V_X if and only if F_Y|_U is semisimple on U. Since the latter is semisimple, F_X is semisimple on V_X. As n was arbitrary, F_X is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) for every n>=0. This is exactly the desired conclusion for the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge 1\) and \(j\ge 0\) be integers, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge 1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), used to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). For \(r\ge 1\) let \(A_r\subseteq H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-span of the cycle classes of the codimension-\(j\) cycles on \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^{mr}}}\), and let \(A_\infty\) be the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-span of the cycle classes of all codimension-\(j\) cycles on \(X_k\). Then there exists an integer \(r\ge 1\) such that \(A_\infty=A_r\).
proof:
We prove that the span of the classes of codimension-$j$ cycles defined over $\overline{\mathbb F}_q$ is already the span of those defined over a single finite extension of $\mathbb F_{q^m}$.

**Notation.** Put $Q:=q^m=p^{am}$; this is a prime power, and $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q=\overline{\mathbb F}_{Q}$. For an integer $n\ge1$ write $\mathbb F_n:=\mathbb F_{Q^n}$ and $X_n:=X\times_{\mathbb F_Q}\mathbb F_n$. By transitivity of the fibre product, $X_n\times_{\mathbb F_n}k=X\times_{\mathbb F_Q}k=X_k$ for every $n$, since $\overline{\mathbb F}_{Q^n}=k$.

**Convention on cycle classes.** Fix $0\ne u\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ and set $\xi:=u^{\otimes j}\in\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$, which is nonzero; it gives the identification $v\mapsto v\otimes\xi$ of $H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ with $H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j))$ (the convention used in the surrounding lemmas). For $n\in\{1,2,\dots,\infty\}$ (with $\mathbb F_\infty:=k$, $X_\infty:=X_k$) and $Z\subseteq X_n$ a closed integral subscheme of pure codimension $j$, let $\mathrm{cl}_n(Z)\in H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ be the vector corresponding to the $\ell$-adic cycle class of the base change $Z_k:=Z\times_{\mathbb F_n}k\subseteq X_k$; for $n=\infty$ this is just the class of $Z$. This is legitimate because, as Steps 0 and 1 below show, $X_k$ is integral of dimension $d$ and every irreducible component of $Z_k$ has dimension $\dim Z=d-j$, so $Z_k$ is of pure codimension $j$ in $X_k$ and its fundamental class in $H^{2j}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j))$ is defined. For a codimension-$j$ cycle $z=\sum_a m_a Z_a$ on $X_n$ we put $\mathrm{cl}_n(z):=\sum_a m_a\,\mathrm{cl}_n(Z_a)$. Then $A_n=\sum_z\mathbb Q_\ell\,\mathrm{cl}_n(z)$ (sum over codimension-$j$ cycles $z$ on $X_n$) for $n\ge1$, and $A_\infty$ is defined analogously.

If $j>d$ there are no integral closed subschemes of $X_k$ of codimension $j$ (as $\dim X_k=d$ by Step 0), so $A_r=A_\infty=\{0\}$ for every $r$, and the lemma holds with $r=1$. Henceforth assume $0\le j\le d$.

**Step 0. $X_n$ and $X_k$ are integral of dimension $d$.** Let $L/\mathbb F_Q$ be any field extension ($L=\mathbb F_n$ or $L=k$). Then $X_L$ is smooth over $\mathbb F_Q$, hence regular, hence normal, and it is noetherian; it is connected because $X$ is geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_Q$. A connected noetherian normal scheme is integral: a noetherian normal ring is a finite direct product of normal domains (its localisations at the finitely many minimal primes are $0$-dimensional normal noetherian rings, hence fields, and the ring maps isomorphically onto the product of these localisations), so the irreducible components of an affine open are open and closed, and this globalises. Thus $X_L$ is integral. Since $X$ is smooth of pure dimension $d$ over the field $\mathbb F_Q$ and $X_L$ is connected, $X_L$ is smooth of relative dimension $d$ over $L$, so all its irreducible components have dimension $d$; being integral, $\dim X_L=d$.

**Step 1 (dimension lemma).** *Let $K\subset L$ be fields and $W$ an integral $K$-scheme of finite type of dimension $e$. Then every irreducible component of $W_L:=W\times_K L$ has dimension $e$.*

*(a) Affine case.* $W=\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $A$ a finitely generated $K$-domain. By Noether normalization there is an injective finite $K$-algebra map $R:=K[t_1,\dots,t_e]\hookrightarrow A$ (with $e=\operatorname{trdeg}_K\operatorname{Frac}(A)=\dim A$). Put $B:=A\otimes_K L$ and $R':=R\otimes_K L=L[t_1,\dots,t_e]$. Since $L$ is a free (hence flat) $K$-module, $R'\hookrightarrow B$ is injective, and $B$ is a finite $R'$-module (base change of a finite map); thus $B$ is integral over $R'$, and $R'$ is a noetherian domain of dimension $e$ (Krull's theorem on polynomial rings).

*$B$ is torsion-free over $R'$:* $A$ is torsion-free over the domain $R$ (it is a domain containing $R$), so $A\hookrightarrow V:=A\otimes_R\operatorname{Frac}(R)$, a $\operatorname{Frac}(R)$-vector space. $R'$ is free over $R$ (a $K$-basis of $L$ is an $R$-basis of $R'$), so tensoring with $R'$ over $R$ gives an injection $B=A\otimes_R R'\hookrightarrow V\otimes_R R'=V\otimes_{\operatorname{Frac}R}D$, where $D:=(R\setminus\{0\})^{-1}R'$ is a domain (a localisation of the domain $R'$) with $\operatorname{Frac}(D)=\operatorname{Frac}(R')$. The last term is a free $D$-module, hence $D$-torsion-free, hence $R'$-torsion-free (nonzero elements of $R'$ map to nonzero elements of $D$). Thus $B$ is $R'$-torsion-free.

Now let $\mathfrak q$ be a minimal prime of $B$ and $\mathfrak p:=\mathfrak q\cap R'$. The noetherian ring $B$ has $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}(B)$, so $\mathfrak q=\operatorname{Ann}_B(b)$ for some $0\ne b\in B$. If $\mathfrak p\ne(0)$, choose $0\ne f\in\mathfrak p$; then $fb=0$ with $f\in R'\setminus\{0\}$ and $b\ne0$, contradicting $R'$-torsion-freeness. Hence $\mathfrak p=(0)$, so $B/\mathfrak q$ is a domain containing $R'=L[t_1,\dots,t_e]$ and integral over it. For an integral extension of domains the Krull dimensions agree: lying over together with going-up gives $\dim B/\mathfrak q\ge\dim R'$, and incomparability (distinct primes of $B/\mathfrak q$ lying over one prime of $R'$ are incomparable) makes the contraction of a strictly increasing chain of primes of $B/\mathfrak q$ a strictly increasing chain of $R'$, giving $\le$. Hence $\dim(B/\mathfrak q)=\dim R'=e$. The irreducible components of $\operatorname{Spec}B=W_L$ are exactly the $V(\mathfrak q)\cong\operatorname{Spec}(B/\mathfrak q)$ with $\mathfrak q$ minimal, so all have dimension $e$.

*(b) General case.* Write $W=U_1\cup\dots\cup U_s$ as a finite union of nonempty affine opens ($W$ is noetherian). Each $U_i$ is integral of dimension $e$: for an integral scheme $Y$ of finite type over a field one has $\dim Y=\operatorname{trdeg}\kappa(Y)$ (standard consequence of Noether normalization and the dimension formula for finite extensions), and $\kappa(U_i)=\kappa(W)$. The $U_{i,L}$ form an open cover of $W_L$. Let $T$ be an irreducible component of $W_L$; then $T=\bigcup_i\,(T\cap U_{i,L})$. Since $T$ is irreducible and noetherian it cannot be a finite union of proper closed subsets, so $T\cap U_{i,L}$ is dense in $T$ for some $i$; it is nonempty and irreducible. If it were not an irreducible component of $U_{i,L}$, it would be strictly contained in an irreducible closed $S\subseteq U_{i,L}$; the closure $\overline S$ in $W_L$ is irreducible closed and contains $\overline{T\cap U_{i,L}}^{T}=T$, so $\overline S=T$ as $T$ is a component; and since $S$ is closed in the open $U_{i,L}$ we have $S=\overline S\cap U_{i,L}$, whence $S=T\cap U_{i,L}$, a contradiction. So $T\cap U_{i,L}$ is an irreducible component of $U_{i,L}=(U_i)_L$, and by (a) applied to the integral affine $K$-scheme $U_i$ of dimension $e$, $\dim(T\cap U_{i,L})=e$. Finally $T$ is integral of finite type over $L$ and $T\cap U_{i,L}$ is a nonempty open of it with the same function field, so $\dim T=\operatorname{trdeg}_L\kappa(T)=\dim(T\cap U_{i,L})=e$. This proves the dimension lemma. $\square$

**Step 2 (monotonicity and containment in $A_\infty$).** (i) $A_n\subseteq A_\infty$ for every $n\ge1$: for integral $Z\subseteq X_n$ of codimension $j$, $\mathrm{cl}_n(Z)=\mathrm{cl}_k(Z_k)$, and $Z_k$ has all its components of dimension $\dim Z=d-j$ by the dimension lemma (with $K=\mathbb F_n$, $L=k$), hence is a codimension-$j$ cycle on $X_k$; so $\mathrm{cl}_n(Z)\in A_\infty$.

(ii) $A_b\subseteq A_n$ whenever $b\mid n$. Then $\mathbb F_b\subset\mathbb F_n$ and $\pi:X_n\to X_b$ is the base change of $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_n\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_b$: a finite locally free morphism of relative dimension $0$, in particular flat. Let $Z\subseteq X_b$ be integral of codimension $j$, so $\dim Z=d-j$. The fibre product $W:=Z\times_{\mathbb F_b}\mathbb F_n=Z\times_{X_b}X_n$ is the base change of the integral $\mathbb F_b$-scheme $Z$ of finite type of dimension $d-j$ to the field $\mathbb F_n$, so by the dimension lemma every irreducible component $W_1,\dots,W_t$ of $W$ has dimension $d-j$; as $X_n$ is integral of dimension $d$ (Step 0), each $W_i$ is an integral closed subscheme of $X_n$ of codimension $j$. The flat pullback of the cycle $[Z]$ is
\[
\pi^*[Z]:=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\ \ell_i\,[W_i],\qquad \ell_i:=\operatorname{length}_{\mathcal O_{W,\eta_i}}\bigl(\mathcal O_{W,\eta_i}\bigr)\ge1,
\]
the standard definition of flat pullback of cycles along a flat morphism of relative dimension $0$; by the preceding paragraph this is a codimension-$j$ cycle on $X_n$. Flat pullback is functorial for towers of flat morphisms of pure relative dimension $0$ (the usual transitivity property, which follows from the definition above together with associativity of the fibre product and multiplicativity of lengths in towers of artinian local rings). Applying this to the tower $X_k\xrightarrow{\ \pi_k\ }X_n\xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }X_b$ gives $(\pi^*[Z])_k=Z_k$ as cycles on $X_k$. Therefore
\[
\mathrm{cl}_b(Z)=\mathrm{cl}_k(Z_k)=\mathrm{cl}_k\bigl((\pi^*[Z])_k\bigr)=\mathrm{cl}_n(\pi^*[Z])\in A_n,
\]
the last equality because $\pi^*[Z]$ is a codimension-$j$ cycle on $X_n$. By additivity, $A_b\subseteq A_n$.

**Step 3 (descent: $A_\infty=\bigcup_{n\ge1}A_n$).** The inclusion $\bigcup_n A_n\subseteq A_\infty$ is Step 2(i). For the reverse it suffices to treat the class of an integral closed subscheme $Z\subseteq X_k$ of codimension $j$. Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_104_descent with the prime power $Q=q^m$ in the role of its '$q$' (the lemma holds for every prime power): $X$ is of finite type over $\mathbb F_Q$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{Q}$, and $Z\subset X\times_{\mathbb F_Q}k=X_k$ is an integral closed subscheme. The lemma provides an integer $r\ge1$ and an integral closed subscheme $Z'\subset X\times_{\mathbb F_Q}\mathbb F_{Q^r}=X_r$ such that $Z'\times_{\mathbb F_{Q^r}}k\simeq Z$ as closed subschemes of $X_k$; and since $X$ is smooth of pure dimension $d$ over $\mathbb F_Q$, $Z'$ has the same codimension as $Z$, namely $j$. Hence $Z'$ contributes to $A_r$ and
\[
\mathrm{cl}_\infty(Z)=\mathrm{cl}_k(Z)=\mathrm{cl}_k\bigl(Z'\times_{\mathbb F_{Q^r}}k\bigr)=\mathrm{cl}_r(Z')\in A_r .
\]
By linearity, $A_\infty\subseteq\bigcup_{r\ge1}A_r$, and equality follows.

**Step 4 (an ascending chain, and its stabilisation).** The $A_r$ are not a chain in $r$ (inclusions of fields $\mathbb F_r\subset\mathbb F_n$ hold only when $r\mid n$), so set
\[
C_s:=A_{s!}\qquad(s=1,2,3,\dots).
\]
Since $s!\mid(s+1)!$, Step 2(ii) gives $C_s\subseteq C_{s+1}$: an ascending chain of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspaces of $H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Moreover $\bigcup_{s\ge1}C_s=A_\infty$: each $C_s=A_{s!}\subseteq A_\infty$ by Step 2(i), and conversely every $A_r\subseteq A_{r!}=C_r$ (as $r\mid r!$), so $\bigcup_r A_r\subseteq\bigcup_s C_s$, and Step 3 identifies $\bigcup_r A_r$ with $A_\infty$.

Now $X$ is projective, hence proper, over $\mathbb F_Q$. Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob with the prime power $Q$ in the role of its '$q$', with the proper $\mathbb F_Q$-variety $X$ and with $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ the constant sheaf equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure, we obtain that $H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$.

Therefore the non-decreasing sequence of integers $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}C_s$ is bounded above by $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, hence eventually constant: there is $N\ge1$ with $\dim C_N=\dim C_{N+1}$. The inclusion $C_N\subseteq C_{N+1}$ between spaces of equal finite dimension is an equality, and inductively $C_s=C_N$ for all $s\ge N$. Consequently
\[
A_\infty=\bigcup_{s\ge1}C_s=\bigcup_{s\ge N}C_s=C_N=A_{N!}.
\]
Taking $r:=N!\ge1$ gives $A_\infty=A_r$, which is the desired conclusion.

(No statement about Frobenius semisimplicity is made or needed here: the lemma only produces the single level $r$. The semisimplicity of the $q^m$-power Frobenius on $A_r$, and its stability under Frobenius, are supplied separately by eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/d9031b and eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_371.)

statement: Let K be a field, let A = K[u,v], let I = (u,v) ⊂ A, and let R = \bigoplus_{n \ge 0} I^n be the Rees algebra of I over A, with ut, vt \in R_1 the elements u, v placed in degree one. Then Proj R = D_+(ut) \cup D_+(vt), and the inclusions A \hookrightarrow R_{(ut)} and A \hookrightarrow R_{(vt)} into the degree-zero parts of the localisations identify R_{(ut)} with K[u,w] and R_{(vt)} with K[v,z] as A-algebras, where A \to K[u,w] sends u \mapsto u and v \mapsto uw, and A \to K[v,z] sends u \mapsto zv and v \mapsto v.
proof:
We work through the whole statement in explicit algebraic detail. No cohomology is involved; the only external input is the standard description of the principal open subsets of Proj (the proved lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_proj_principal_open_affine), used in Step 7.

STEP 0. Notation and the graded ring R.
Let A = K[u,v]; since K is a field, A is a Noetherian domain, and Frac(A) = K(u,v). Let I = (u,v) ⊂ A; for n ≥ 1 the ideal I^n is generated as an A-module by the monomials u^i v^{n-i}, 0 ≤ i ≤ n, and I^0 = A. The Rees algebra is
   R = ⊕_{n≥0} I^n t^n ⊂ A[t],
so R_n := I^n t^n; the product of a t^n ∈ R_n and b t^m ∈ R_m is ab t^{n+m} ∈ R_{n+m} because I^n I^m = I^{n+m}. Thus R is a commutative N-graded ring, R_0 = A, and since I^n is generated by the products of n elements of I, R is generated as an R_0-algebra by R_1 = I t = A·(ut) + A·(vt). Being a subring of the domain A[t], R is itself a domain, and the element ut ∈ R_1 is nonzero (and so is every nonzero element of R).
For a nonzero f ∈ I write S(f) := R_{ft} for the localisation of R at the multiplicative set {1, ft, (ft)^2, …}, and S(f)_0 := (R_{ft})_0 for its degree-zero subring; this is the ring the statement denotes R_{(ft)}. Since R is a domain and ft ≠ 0, the localisation map R → R_{ft} is injective, and its restriction to R_0 = A identifies A with a subring of S(f)_0 (elements a/1 of degree 0). This is the "inclusion A ↪ R_{(ft)}" of the statement.

STEP 1. The irrelevant ideal is generated by ut and vt.
Claim: R_+ := ⊕_{n≥1} R_n = (ut, vt) as an ideal of R. Indeed ut, vt ∈ R_1 ⊂ R_+. Conversely, for n ≥ 1, R_n = I^n t^n = Σ_{i=0}^{n} A·u^i v^{n-i} t^n = Σ_{i=0}^{n} A·(ut)^i (vt)^{n-i}; each generator (ut)^i(vt)^{n-i} with i + (n−i) = n ≥ 1 is divisible by ut (if i ≥ 1) or by vt (if i = 0, then n − i = n ≥ 1), hence lies in (ut, vt). So R_n ⊂ (ut,vt) for all n ≥ 1 and R_+ = (ut, vt).

STEP 2. Proj R = D_+(ut) ∪ D_+(vt) as a set, hence as open subschemes.
Let p ∈ Proj R. By definition p is a homogeneous prime ideal of R with R_+ ⊄ p. If p ∉ D_+(ut) ∪ D_+(vt), then ut ∈ p and vt ∈ p, so by Step 1 R_+ = (ut, vt) ⊂ p, a contradiction. Hence p ∈ D_+(ut) ∪ D_+(vt), which gives the set-theoretic equality. Since D_+(ut) and D_+(vt) are open subsets of Proj R (by definition of the Zariski topology on Proj), the equality holds for the induced open subschemes: Proj R is the union of the two opens D_+(ut) and D_+(vt).

STEP 3. Shape of the degree-zero part of S(f).
Fix 0 ≠ f ∈ I. Every element of S(f)_0 = (R_{ft})_0 can be written in the form x/(ft)^n with x ∈ R_n. Proof: an arbitrary element of R_{ft} is a finite sum Σ_j x_j/(ft)^{n_j} with x_j homogeneous of degree d_j; putting over the common denominator (ft)^{N} with N = max n_j and adjusting gives a single fraction y/(ft)^N with y = Σ_j x_j (ft)^{N−n_j} homogeneous of degree d_j + (N − n_j) = d_j + N − n_j... more precisely, choosing the representation so that each summand has degree 0 (which we may, since we are inside the degree-zero part), each x_j has d_j = n_j, so y is homogeneous of degree N, i.e. y ∈ R_N. Hence the claim, and then y = a t^N with a ∈ I^N.

STEP 4. The isomorphism φ_f : (R_{ft})_0 →∼ A[I/f] ⊂ Frac(A).
Here A[I/f] denotes the A-subalgebra of Frac(A) generated by {g/f : g ∈ I}; note f ≠ 0 so Frac(A) makes sense and f^n ≠ 0 for all n.

Definition. For a ∈ I^n and n ≥ 0 set φ_f(a t^n/(ft)^n) := a/f^n ∈ Frac(A). By Step 3 every element of (R_{ft})_0 has this form, so this defines a map on all of (R_{ft})_0 provided it is well defined.

Well defined. Suppose a t^n/(ft)^n = b t^m/(ft)^m in (R_{ft})_0 with a ∈ I^n, b ∈ I^m. By the definition of localisation there is k ≥ 0 with (ft)^k·(a t^n (ft)^m − b t^m (ft)^n) = 0 in R. Now R ⊂ A[t] is a domain and ft ≠ 0, so we may cancel (ft)^k and obtain a t^n (ft)^m = b t^m (ft)^n in A[t], that is
   a f^m t^{n+m} = b f^n t^{n+m},  hence  a f^m = b f^n  in A.      (*)
Dividing (*) by f^{n+m} in Frac(A) gives exactly
   a/f^n = b/f^m,
which is precisely the required equality of the two values. (Note that the equality to be checked is between a/f^n, the value attached to the representative with denominator (ft)^n, and b/f^m; the cross-multiplication criterion a/f^n = b/f^m ⇔ a f^m = b f^n is exactly (*).) So φ_f is well defined.

Ring homomorphism. Let x = a t^n/(ft)^n and y = b t^m/(ft)^m with a ∈ I^n, b ∈ I^m. Then
   x + y = (a t^n (ft)^m + b t^m (ft)^n)/(ft)^{n+m} = (a f^m + b f^n) t^{n+m}/(ft)^{n+m},
and a f^m + b f^n ∈ I^n I^m + I^m I^n = I^{n+m} (using f ∈ I), so this is a valid representative and
   φ_f(x+y) = (a f^m + b f^n)/f^{n+m} = a/f^n + b/f^m = φ_f(x) + φ_f(y).
Similarly xy = ab t^{n+m}/(ft)^{n+m} with ab ∈ I^{n+m}, so φ_f(xy) = ab/f^{n+m} = φ_f(x)φ_f(y); and φ_f(1·t^0/(ft)^0) = 1/1 = 1. Hence φ_f is a ring homomorphism (necessarily A-linear for the A-structure on (R_{ft})_0 given by a ↦ a/1 and on A[I/f] given by the inclusion A ⊂ Frac(A), because φ_f(a/1) = a/1 = a).

Injective. If φ_f(a t^n/(ft)^n) = a/f^n = 0 in Frac(A), then a = 0 in A (f^n ≠ 0 and A → Frac(A) is injective), hence a t^n = 0 in R_n and the element is 0 in R_{ft}.

Image. First, im φ_f ⊂ A[I/f]: for a ∈ I^n write a = Σ_ν c_{ν,1}···c_{ν,n} with c_{ν,j} ∈ I; then a/f^n = Σ_ν (c_{ν,1}/f)···(c_{ν,n}/f) ∈ A[I/f]. Conversely, A[I/f] is generated over A by the elements g/f, g ∈ I, and A ⊂ im φ_f (take n = 0), while g/f = φ_f(g t/(ft)) ∈ im φ_f. So im φ_f = A[I/f], and
   φ_f : (R_{ft})_0 →∼ A[I/f]   is an isomorphism of A-algebras.

STEP 5. The chart f = u.
We have I/u = {g/u : g ∈ (u,v)} generated as an A-module by u/u = 1 and v/u, hence
   A[I/u] = A[1, v/u] = A[v/u] = K[u, v/u] ⊂ K(u,v).
Let w := v/u. Consider the K-algebra homomorphism
   μ_u : K[U,W] → Frac(A),  U ↦ u,  W ↦ v/u.
Surjectivity onto K[u, v/u] is by definition of the latter as the K-subalgebra generated by u and v/u. For injectivity, take P = Σ_{i,j} c_{ij} U^i W^j ∈ K[U,W] with μ_u(P) = 0. Then Σ_{i,j} c_{ij} u^i (v/u)^j = Σ_{i,j} c_{ij} u^{i−j} v^j = 0 in K(u,v). Multiplying by a large power u^N clears denominators: Σ_{i,j} c_{ij} u^{N+i−j} v^j = 0 in K[u,v]. The monomials u^{N+i−j} v^j are pairwise distinct for distinct pairs (i,j) (the exponent pair (N+i−j, j) determines (i,j)), and the monomials of K[u,v] are K-linearly independent; hence all c_{ij} = 0. So μ_u is an isomorphism K[U,W] →∼ K[u,w] = A[I/u].
Transporting φ_u along μ_u gives an isomorphism of K-algebras
   (R_{ut})_0 →∼ K[u,w].
A-algebra structure: the composite A = K[u,v] → (R_{ut})_0 →∼ K[u,w] sends the class of u ∈ A to u (because φ_u(u/1) = u and μ_u^{-1}(u) = U), and sends v ∈ A to v = u·(v/u) = u w (because φ_u(v/1) = v ∈ A[I/u] and μ_u^{-1}(v) = μ_u^{-1}(u·v/u) = UW). Thus (R_{ut})_0 ≅ K[u,w] as an A-algebra via u ↦ u, v ↦ u w.

STEP 6. The chart f = v.
Symmetrically, I/v is generated by u/v and v/v = 1, so A[I/v] = A[u/v] = K[v, z] with z := u/v. The K-homomorphism
   μ_v : K[V,Z] → Frac(A),  V ↦ v,  Z ↦ u/v,
has image K[v, u/v] = A[I/v]; it is injective by the identical monomial argument, since μ_v(Σ c_{ij} V^i Z^j) = Σ c_{ij} u^j v^{i−j} and the exponent pairs (j, N+i−j) after clearing denominators determine (i,j). Hence μ_v is an isomorphism K[V,Z] →∼ A[I/v], and composing with φ_v gives (R_{vt})_0 ≅ K[v,z] as K-algebras. The A-structure: u ∈ A maps to φ_v(u/1) = u = (u/v)·v, whose preimage under μ_v is ZV; v maps to V. So A → K[v,z] is u ↦ z v, v ↦ v.

STEP 7. Scheme-theoretic form, and conclusion.
Apply the proved lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_proj_principal_open_affine to the graded ring S = R and the homogeneous elements F = ut and F = vt, both of degree d = 1 ≥ 1: it gives canonical isomorphisms of schemes over Spec R_0 = Spec A,
   D_+(ut) = Spec R_{(ut)}  and  D_+(vt) = Spec R_{(vt)},
under which the structure morphism D_+(ut) → Spec A (respectively D_+(vt) → Spec A) is induced by the inclusion A ↪ R_{(ut)} (respectively A ↪ R_{(vt)}) of Step 0. Combining with Steps 5 and 6 we obtain A-algebra isomorphisms
   R_{(ut)} = (R_{ut})_0 ≅ K[u,w]  (A → K[u,w]: u ↦ u, v ↦ u w),
   R_{(vt)} = (R_{vt})_0 ≅ K[v,z]  (A → K[v,z]: u ↦ z v, v ↦ v),
and Step 2 gives Proj R = D_+(ut) ∪ D_+(vt). This is exactly the statement: Proj R is covered by the two principal opens D_+(ut) and D_+(vt), and the degree-zero parts are the polynomial rings K[u,w] and K[v,z], with the asserted A-algebra structures.

STEP 8. Consistency check on the overlap (not required, but it verifies the glueing).
On D_+(ut) ∩ D_+(vt) = D_+((ut)(vt)) one inverts (ut)(vt) in R, so both w = v/u and z = u/v are inverted and zw = 1. Concretely, the image of (R_{ut})_0 in (R_{utvt})_0 is A[I/u][1/(v/u)]... writing it in the polynomial models: the localisation of K[u,w] at the element uw = v equals K[u,w,w^{-1}] (since inverting uw in K[u,w] inverts both u and w: u = (uw)/w becomes invertible once w is, and w = (uw)/u), and under the identification with K[v,z] = K[uz, z] one has u = zv and w = 1/z, so K[u,w,w^{-1}] = K[zv, 1/z, z] = K[v,z,z^{-1}], the localisation of K[v,z] at zv = u. The two transition maps are mutually inverse, confirming that Proj R is the scheme obtained from the two affine planes Spec K[u,w] and Spec K[v,z] by glueing along the punctured line via u ↦ zv, w ↦ 1/z: the blow-up of A^2_K = Spec A at the origin (u,v), whose two standard charts are exactly the ones computed above. Note in particular that the structure map to Spec A is not smooth — the fibre over the origin V(I) is D_+(w) ∪ D_+(z) ≅ P^1_K, of dimension 1, while the fibres away from the origin are points — which is consistent with the fact that the assertion proved here is only the chart computation.

All steps are justified: Step 1 and Step 2 by the explicit generation of R_+ and the definition of Proj; Step 3 by the definition of localisation of a graded ring; Step 4 by the cross-multiplication identity (*) proved above; Steps 5 and 6 by the monomial-independence injectivity argument; Step 7 by the cited lemma. This completes the proof.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let l != p be prime, let w be an integer, and let V be a finite-dimensional Q_l-vector space with T in GL(V). Suppose that for every embedding iota: overline{Q}_l -> C and every eigenvalue alpha of T on V tensor_{Q_l} overline{Q}_l, one has |iota(alpha)| = q^{w/2}. If W subset V is a T-stable subspace, then for every embedding iota and every eigenvalue beta of the automorphism induced by T on W tensor_{Q_l} overline{Q}_l or on (V/W) tensor_{Q_l} overline{Q}_l, one has |iota(beta)| = q^{w/2}.
proof:
This is a statement of pure linear algebra over $\mathbb Q_\ell$; no geometry is used, and no semisimplicity/diagonalizability of $T$ is assumed.

**Notation.** Put $K=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, and write $V_K=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K$ and $T_K=\mathrm{id}_K\otimes T\in\mathrm{End}_K(V_K)$. For a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space $E$ (with $F=\mathbb Q_\ell$ or $F=K$) and an endomorphism $u$, let $\chi_u(t)\in F[t]$ denote its characteristic polynomial $\det(t\,\mathrm{id}-u)$, computed in any $F$-basis of $E$. By hypothesis:

($\ast$) for every embedding $\iota:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$ and every root $\alpha\in K$ of $\chi_{T_K}$, one has $|\iota(\alpha)|=q^{w/2}$.

(An eigenvalue of $T$ on $V_K$ is the same thing as a root in $K$ of $\chi_{T_K}$, because $K$ is algebraically closed, so $\chi_{T_K}$ splits over $K$.)

If $V=0$ there is nothing to prove, so assume $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V=n\ge1$, and let $r=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}W$.

**Step 1: the two induced automorphisms are well defined.** The restriction $T|_W:W\to W$ is defined because $W$ is $T$-stable. It is an automorphism of $W$: $T|_W$ is injective (as $T$ is), and an injective endomorphism of the finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space $W$ is surjective. Now define the induced map $\bar T:V/W\to V/W$ by $\bar T(v+W)=T(v)+W$; this is well defined because $T(W)\subseteq W$. To see $\bar T$ is invertible, let $S=T^{-1}\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$. By the preceding sentence $S|_W=W$ is an automorphism, so $S(W)\subseteq W$, hence $S$ induces $\bar S:V/W\to V/W$, and $\bar T\bar S=\overline{TS}=\mathrm{id}_{V/W}=\overline{ST}=\bar S\bar T$. Thus $\bar T\in\mathrm{GL}(V/W)$, as the statement asserts.

**Step 2: base change identifies the three spaces and maps.** $W_K:=W\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K$ maps into $V_K$ by $w\otimes\lambda\mapsto w\otimes\lambda$; since $K/\mathbb Q_\ell$ is flat (every field extension is free, hence flat), this map is injective, and its image is $T_K$-stable. Under this identification $T_K|_{W_K}=\mathrm{id}_K\otimes(T|_W)$: both sides send $w\otimes\lambda$ to $T(w)\otimes\lambda$. Moreover the natural map
$$\phi:(V/W)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K\longrightarrow V_K/W_K,\qquad (v+W)\otimes\lambda\longmapsto (v\otimes\lambda)+W_K$$
is an isomorphism: choosing a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-complement $U$ of $W$ in $V$, the map $W\oplus U\xrightarrow{\sim}V$ is an isomorphism, base change gives $W_K\oplus U_K\xrightarrow{\sim}V_K$, and $U\cong V/W$ as $\mathbb Q_\ell$-spaces, so $\dim_K(V_K/W_K)=n-r=\dim_K((V/W)_K)$ and $\phi$ is an isomorphism by dimension count. Under $\phi$, the automorphism $\mathrm{id}_K\otimes\bar T$ corresponds exactly to the automorphism of $V_K/W_K$ induced by $T_K$, since both send $(v+W)\otimes\lambda$ to $(T(v)+W)\otimes\lambda$.

**Step 3: characteristic polynomials are unchanged by this scalar extension.** If $A\in M_m(\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is the matrix of an endomorphism $u$ of $\mathbb Q_\ell^m$ in a basis $e_1,\dots,e_m$, then $e_1\otimes1,\dots,e_m\otimes1$ is a $K$-basis of $\mathbb Q_\ell^m\otimes K$, the matrix of $\mathrm{id}_K\otimes u$ in it is the same $A$ (viewed in $M_m(K)$), and $\det(tI-A)$ is computed by the same polynomial expression in the entries of $A$. Hence
$$\chi_{\mathrm{id}_K\otimes u}(t)=\chi_u(t)\ \ \text{in }K[t].$$
Applying this to $u=T|_W$ (using Step 2, $T_K|_{W_K}=\mathrm{id}_K\otimes(T|_W)$) and to $u=\bar T$ (using $\phi$) gives
$$\chi_{T_K|_{W_K}}=\chi_{T|_W}\ \ \text{in }K[t],\qquad \chi_{\text{induced on }V_K/W_K}=\chi_{\bar T}\ \ \text{in }K[t].$$
Consequently an element $\beta\in K$ is an eigenvalue of $T$ on $W\otimes K$ if and only if it is a root of $\chi_{T_K|_{W_K}}$, and similarly for the quotient.

**Step 4: block triangular form and factorization of the characteristic polynomial.**

*Case $0<r<n$.* Choose a $K$-basis $e_1,\dots,e_r$ of $W_K$ and extend it to a $K$-basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$ of $V_K$. Write $T_K(e_j)=\sum_{i=1}^n m_{ij}e_i$ with $M=(m_{ij})\in M_n(K)$. For $j\le r$ one has $T_K(e_j)\in W_K$ by stability, so $m_{ij}=0$ for all $i>r$ and all $j\le r$: $M$ is block upper triangular,
$$M=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\ 0&C\end{pmatrix},\qquad A=(m_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le r},\ B=(m_{ij})_{i\le r<j},\ C=(m_{ij})_{r<i,j\le n}.$$
By Step 2 and the choice of basis, $A$ is exactly the matrix of $T_K|_{W_K}$ in $e_1,\dots,e_r$; and since the classes $\bar e_{r+1},\dots,\bar e_n$ form a $K$-basis of $V_K/W_K$ and $T_K(e_j)\bmod W_K=\sum_{i>r}m_{ij}\bar e_i$ for $j>r$, $C$ is exactly the matrix of the automorphism induced on $V_K/W_K$. Thus $\chi_{T|_W}=\det(tI_r-A)$ and $\chi_{\bar T}=\det(tI_{n-r}-C)$ by Step 3.

Now $tI_n-M=\begin{pmatrix}tI_r-A&-B\\ 0&tI_{n-r}-C\end{pmatrix}$ is again block upper triangular. For any block upper triangular matrix $N=\begin{pmatrix}N_1&N_2\\ 0&N_3\end{pmatrix}$ over the commutative ring $K$, with $N_1\in M_r(K)$ and $N_3\in M_{n-r}(K)$, the Leibniz formula gives $\det N=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak S_n}\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_i N_{i,\sigma(i)}$. If $\sigma$ does not preserve $\{1,\dots,r\}$, then some $i>r$ has $\sigma(i)\le r$, and the factor $N_{i,\sigma(i)}$ lies in the zero block, so that term vanishes. Hence only the $\sigma$ preserving both $\{1,\dots,r\}$ and $\{r+1,\dots,n\}$ contribute, and the sum factors as
$$\det N=\Big(\sum_{\sigma_1\in\mathfrak S_{\{1,..,r\}}}\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma_1)\prod_{i\le r}(N_1)_{i,\sigma_1(i)}\Big)\Big(\sum_{\sigma_3}\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma_3)\prod_{i>r}(N_3)_{i,\sigma_3(i)}\Big)=\det N_1\cdot\det N_3.$$
Applying this to $N=tI_n-M$ yields
$$\chi_{T_K}(t)=\det(tI_n-M)=\det(tI_r-A)\cdot\det(tI_{n-r}-C)=\chi_{T|_W}(t)\cdot\chi_{\bar T}(t)\quad\text{in }K[t].$$

*Case $r=0$.* Then $W=0$, so $W\otimes K=0$ and $\chi_{T|_W}=1$ (determinant of the empty matrix, i.e. the characteristic polynomial of the identity on the zero space); there is no eigenvalue on $W\otimes K$, so the conclusion concerning $W$ is vacuous. The quotient is $V/W=V$ with $\bar T=T$, and the conclusion there is exactly the hypothesis ($\ast$).

*Case $r=n$.* Symmetrically, $V/W=0$ gives no eigenvalues (vacuous), and $W=V$ with $\bar T$-claim replaced by the $T|_W=T$ claim, which is the hypothesis.

**Step 5: conclusion.** In the case $0<r<n$, Step 4 shows that $\chi_{T|_W}$ and $\chi_{\bar T}$ are divisors of $\chi_{T_K}$ in $K[t]$. Let $\beta\in K$ be an eigenvalue of $T$ on $W\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K$ or on $(V/W)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K$. By Step 3, $\beta$ is a root of $\chi_{T_K}$, hence a root of $\chi_{T|_W}$ or of $\chi_{\bar T}$, hence (Step 4) a root of $\chi_{T_K}$; that is, $\beta$ is an eigenvalue of $T_K$ on $V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K$. Applying ($\ast$) to $\alpha=\beta$ and to the given embedding $\iota:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$ gives
$$|\iota(\beta)|=q^{w/2}.$$
Since $\iota$ and $\beta$ were arbitrary, the same equality holds for every embedding and every eigenvalue on $W\otimes K$ and on $(V/W)\otimes K$. The edge cases $r=0$ and $r=n$ were settled in Step 4. This completes the proof.

**Remark (why no extra input is needed).** The argument used only: (i) flatness of field extensions, to identify $(V/W)\otimes K$ with $V_K/W_K$; (ii) invariance of the characteristic polynomial under scalar extension; (iii) the determinant of a block upper triangular matrix. It did not use that $T$ is semisimple, that $q$ is a prime power, or that $\ell\ne p$; the only role of $q^{w/2}$ is as a fixed non-negative real number that the complex absolute values of all eigenvalues equal. Equivalently: purity of the multiset of eigenvalues with respect to all $\ell$-adic places is inherited by $T$-stable subspaces and quotients, because the eigenvalues of the latter form sub-multisets of the eigenvalues of $T$.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ℓ≠p be prime, let m≥1, and put k=bar(F_q). Let d≥2, let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, let Y⊂X be a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over F_{q^m} that is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d-1, and let i:Y→X be the closed immersion. Let C=coker(i^*:H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ℓ)→H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ℓ)). If the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ℓ), then it induces a semisimple operator on C.
proof: Proof. Put Q=q^m=p^{am}. Then Q is a prime power and k=bar(F_Q)=bar(F_q). Let V=H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_l), U=H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_l), and alpha=i^*:U -> V. Since Y is an effective very ample Cartier divisor, O_X(Y) is very ample, hence ample; thus Y is an effective ample divisor in the sense of Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_283. Apply that lemma with the prime power Q in place of q, with X as the smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_Q, and with the smooth effective ample divisor Y. It gives a long exact sequence of finite-dimensional Q_l-vector spaces whose middle arrow in degree d-1 is alpha, and every map in the sequence commutes with the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms. Denote by F_U and F_V the Q-power (=q^m-power) arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms on U and V. The commutation of alpha with Frobenius is F_V o alpha = alpha o F_U. In particular V is finite-dimensional and F_V is an automorphism of V. Let W=im(alpha) subset V. For any w in W choose u in U with w=alpha(u). Then F_V(w)=F_V(alpha(u))=alpha(F_U(u)) in W, so W is F_V-stable. Therefore F_V descends to a unique Q_l-linear automorphism F_C of C=V/W given by F_C(v+W)=F_V(v)+W. This is well-defined: if v-v' in W, then F_V(v)-F_V(v')=F_V(v-v') in W; its inverse is induced by F_V^{-1}. By hypothesis F_V is semisimple on V. Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_402 with T=F_V and W=im(alpha). Since V is finite-dimensional over Q_l, F_V is in GL(V), and W is F_V-stable, lemma_402 says that the operator induced by F_V on V/W is semisimple. But V/W is canonically C and the induced operator is exactly F_C. Hence the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius induces a semisimple operator on C. QED.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), put \(Q=q^m\) and \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_Q\), and let \(i:Z\hookrightarrow X\) be a smooth geometrically connected closed subvariety of pure codimension \(c\ge1\) defined over \(\mathbb F_Q\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and use it to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); for \(W\in\{X,Z\}\) let \(\operatorname{tr}_W:H^{2\dim W}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell\) be the Poincar\'e duality trace normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_W(\mathrm{cl}_W(w))=[\kappa(w):\mathbb F_Q]\). For \(n\ge0\) let \(i_!:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{n+2c}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the homomorphism characterised by \(\operatorname{tr}_X(i_!a\smile b)=\operatorname{tr}_Z(a\smile i^*b)\) for all \(a\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(b\in H^{2d-n-2c}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then the induced map \(i_!:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-c)\to H^{n+2c}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) commutes with the \(Q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(u)=u^Q\).
proof:
Write Q := q^m = p^{am}; then k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q = \overline{\mathbb F}_Q, and the operator of the statement is the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius. We prove that the duality-adjoint Gysin map i_! satisfies

(\dagger)   F_X \circ i_! = Q^{c}\, i_! \circ F_Z : H^n_{\acute et}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \longrightarrow H^{n+2c}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),

and we then explain why (\dagger) is exactly the asserted Frobenius-equivariance of i_! : H^n(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-c) \to H^{n+2c}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

STEP 0. Dimensions and finiteness. X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over \mathbb F_Q, and Z \hookrightarrow X is a smooth geometrically connected closed subvariety of pure codimension c \ge 1. Since X is smooth over a field it is Cohen--Macaulay and catenary, and \dim Z = d-c: every irreducible component of Z has codimension exactly c in X by "pure codimension c", and Z is equidimensional because it is smooth over \mathbb F_Q. Both X and Z are proper over \mathbb F_Q, so eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob (applied with the prime power Q = p^{am} in the role of its q, and with K = \mathbb Q_\ell with its natural Frobenius structure) shows that H^n_{\acute et}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell for W \in \{X,Z\} and every n, and carries a canonical \mathbb Q_\ell-linear Q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism F_W := (\mathrm{id}_{W_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*, \sigma(u)=u^Q. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a (again with Q in the role of its q) F_W is invertible and F_W^{-1} = (\mathrm{id}_{W_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^{-1})^*; in particular F_W preserves cohomological degree.

STEP 1. Traces, pairings, and the definition of i_!. Fix a nonzero e \in \mathbb Q_\ell(1); since \mathbb Q_\ell(1) is one-dimensional, e is a basis and identifies every \mathbb Q_\ell(-r) with \mathbb Q_\ell. For W \in \{X,Z\}, let \operatorname{tr}_W : H^{2\dim W}_{\acute et}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb Q_\ell(-\dim W) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb Q_\ell be the trace of eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77(a) composed with this identification; it is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism with \operatorname{tr}_W(\mathrm{cl}_W(w)) = [\kappa(w):\mathbb F_Q]. For 0 \le r \le 2\dim W put
   \langle x,y\rangle_W := \operatorname{tr}_W(x \smile y), \qquad x \in H^r(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\ y \in H^{2\dim W - r}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \subset \mathbb Q_\ell.
By lemma_77(b) (with q^m = Q and d = \dim W) each \langle-,-\rangle_W is a PERFECT pairing of \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces, and
   (S_W)   \langle F_W x, F_W y \rangle_W = Q^{\dim W}\, \langle x,y\rangle_W \quad\text{for all }x,y.
Indeed lemma_77(b) gives this intrinsically with values in \mathbb Q_\ell(-\dim W), where F acts as the scalar Q^{\dim W}; applying the \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism \mathbb Q_\ell(-\dim W)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell (which commutes with multiplication by scalars of \mathbb Q_\ell) gives (S_W) in \mathbb Q_\ell.

Fix n \ge 0. For a \in H^n(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) the assignment
   \Lambda_a : H^{2d-n-2c}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \longrightarrow \mathbb Q_\ell, \qquad b \longmapsto \langle a, i^* b\rangle_Z = \operatorname{tr}_Z(a \smile i^* b)
is \mathbb Q_\ell-linear (cup product, pullback and trace are \mathbb Q_\ell-linear). Note that the degrees are compatible: i^*b \in H^{2d-n-2c}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) = H^{2\dim Z - n}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), so a \smile i^*b has degree 2\dim Z and the trace on Z applies.

If n > 2\dim Z = 2d-2c, then H^n(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_projective_cohomology_vanishes_above_twice_dimension applied to the projective equidimensional k-scheme Z_k of dimension d-c; in this case n+2c > 2d, so also H^{n+2c}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0, and we define i_! := 0. The characterising identity then reads 0 = 0 (both sides vanish because a=0 and i_!a=0), and (\dagger) holds trivially.

Assume now 0 \le n \le 2d-2c, so that 0 \le n+2c \le 2d and 0 \le 2d-n-2c \le 2d. Since \langle-,-\rangle_X on H^{n+2c}(X) \times H^{2d-n-2c}(X) is perfect, the map u \mapsto (b \mapsto \langle u,b\rangle_X) is an isomorphism H^{n+2c}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^{2d-n-2c}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\mathbb Q_\ell). Hence there is a UNIQUE u \in H^{n+2c}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) with \langle u,b\rangle_X = \Lambda_a(b) for all b; define i_! a := u. Varying a linearly gives the required \mathbb Q_\ell-linear homomorphism i_! : H^n(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \to H^{n+2c}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) characterised by
   (C)   \operatorname{tr}_X(i_! a \smile b) = \operatorname{tr}_Z(a \smile i^* b) \qquad \forall a \in H^n(Z_k),\ b \in H^{2d-n-2c}(X_k).
(Conversely, (C) for all b determines i_!a uniquely by perfectness, so the map of the statement is exactly this one.)

STEP 2. Frobenius naturality of i^*. Because i : Z \hookrightarrow X is defined over \mathbb F_Q, the square of k-schemes
   Z_k \xrightarrow{\ F_Z\ } Z_k
   \Big\downarrow i_k \qquad \Big\downarrow i_k
   X_k \xrightarrow{\ F_X\ } X_k
commutes: both composites are the morphism whose underlying map on the first factor is i_k and on the second factor is \sigma (this is just the assertion that base change to k of the F_Q-morphism i commutes with the Q-power Frobenius of the k-factor). Functoriality of pullback in \acute etale cohomology therefore gives
   (N)   i^* \circ F_X = F_Z \circ i^*.
Applying (N) to the commutative square defined by \sigma^{-1} (equivalently, using lemma_6a to write F_W^{-1} = (\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^{-1})^*) gives likewise i^* \circ F_X^{-1} = F_Z^{-1}\circ i^*, hence
   (N')   i^* b = F_Z\bigl(i^*(F_X^{-1} b)\bigr) \quad\text{for all } b \in H^{2d-n-2c}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),
and F_X^{-1}b again has degree 2d-n-2c.

STEP 3. The computation. Let a \in H^n(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and b \in H^{2d-n-2c}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell); F_Z a \in H^n(Z_k), so (C) applied to the pair (F_Z a, b) gives
   \operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(i_! F_Z a \smile b\bigr) = \operatorname{tr}_Z\bigl(F_Z a \smile i^* b\bigr).
Using (N') and then (S_Z) with \dim Z = d-c, applied to the pair (a,\ i^*F_X^{-1}b) \in H^n(Z)\times H^{2(d-c)-n}(Z),
   \operatorname{tr}_Z\bigl(F_Z a \smile F_Z(i^*F_X^{-1}b)\bigr) = Q^{d-c}\, \operatorname{tr}_Z\bigl(a \smile i^* F_X^{-1} b\bigr).
By (C) applied to the pair (a,\ F_X^{-1}b) (legal, since F_X^{-1}b has degree 2d-n-2c),
   Q^{d-c}\,\operatorname{tr}_Z(a \smile i^*F_X^{-1}b) = Q^{d-c}\, \operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(i_! a \smile F_X^{-1} b\bigr).
Finally, (S_X) with \dim X = d, applied to the pair (i_!a,\ F_X^{-1}b) \in H^{n+2c}(X)\times H^{2d-n-2c}(X), reads \operatorname{tr}_X(F_X i_! a \smile b) = Q^{d}\operatorname{tr}_X(i_! a \smile F_X^{-1}b); substituting,
   \operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(i_! F_Z a \smile b\bigr) = Q^{d-c}\cdot Q^{-d}\, \operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(F_X i_! a \smile b\bigr) = Q^{-c}\,\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(F_X i_! a \smile b\bigr) = \operatorname{tr}_X\bigl( (Q^{-c} F_X i_! a) \smile b\bigr),
where the last equality uses \mathbb Q_\ell-linearity of the pairing in the first variable. Thus for our fixed a,
   \operatorname{tr}_X\bigl( (i_! F_Z a - Q^{-c} F_X i_! a) \smile b\bigr) = 0 \quad\text{for every } b \in H^{2d-n-2c}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).
Both elements lie in H^{n+2c}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), and the pairing H^{n+2c}(X)\times H^{2d-n-2c}(X)\to\mathbb Q_\ell is perfect, hence non-degenerate in the first variable; therefore i_! F_Z a = Q^{-c} F_X i_! a, i.e. F_X i_! a = Q^{c} i_! F_Z a. Since a was arbitrary, (\dagger) is proved (in the range n > 2d-2c it was already noted to be trivial).

STEP 4. Translation of the scalar into the Tate twist. We use the library's convention, which is part of the assertion of lemma_77(a): applying lemma_77(a) to the smooth projective geometrically connected \mathbb F_Q-variety Y = \mathbb P^c_{\mathbb F_Q} of pure dimension c shows that the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius acts on \mathbb Q_\ell(-c) as multiplication by Q^{c}. (Equivalently, F acts on \mathbb Q_\ell(1) by Q^{-1}, so F(e)=Q^{-1}e and F(e^{-c}) = Q^{c} e^{-c} for the basis e^{-c} of \mathbb Q_\ell(-c) determined by the chosen e.)

The twisted space H^n(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-c) := H^n(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell} \mathbb Q_\ell(-c) carries the diagonal arithmetic Frobenius F_Z \otimes F_{\mathbb Q_\ell(-c)}, so F(a \otimes e^{-c}) = Q^{c} F_Z a \otimes e^{-c}. Under the \mathbb Q_\ell-linear identification H^n(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-c) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^n(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), a \otimes e^{-c} \mapsto a, provided by the fixed nonzero e \in \mathbb Q_\ell(1) (the same identification used to regard the traces as \mathbb Q_\ell-valued in Step 1), the Frobenius of the twisted space corresponds exactly to the operator Q^{c} F_Z on H^n(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

The map of the statement, i_! : H^n(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-c) \to H^{n+2c}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), is thus, after these identifications, the same \mathbb Q_\ell-linear map i_!, but with source operator Q^{c}F_Z and target operator F_X. Equation (\dagger), F_X \circ i_! = i_! \circ (Q^{c} F_Z), says precisely that
   F_{X} \circ i_! = i_! \circ F_{H^n(Z)(-c)},
i.e. that i_! commutes with the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius. This is the desired conclusion.

STEP 5. Consistency check of the sign (not used in the proof). Take Z = \{z\} a rational point of X, so c = d and n = 0. Then H^0(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell\cdot 1, and (C) with b \in H^0(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell (X geometrically connected) gives \operatorname{tr}_X(i_!1 \smile b) = b\,\operatorname{tr}_Z(1) = b = \operatorname{tr}_X(b\,\mathrm{cl}(z)), so i_!1 = \mathrm{cl}(z) since \operatorname{tr}_X is an isomorphism in degree 2d. Our formula predicts F_X\,\mathrm{cl}(z) = Q^{d}\,\mathrm{cl}(z) (as F_Z 1 = 1); this holds because \operatorname{tr}_X is F-equivariant with F acting on \mathbb Q_\ell(-d) by Q^{d} and \operatorname{tr}_X(\mathrm{cl}(z)) = 1, i.e. \operatorname{tr}_X(\mathrm{cl}(z)) is the vector e^{-d}, which F multiplies by Q^{d}. So the scalar Q^{+c} in (\dagger) is the correct one, and the assertion is that the UNTWISTED i_! is a Q^{c}-eigenmap, equivalently that the twist by (-c) makes it Frobenius-equivariant.

No use is made of purity, of the localisation sequence, or of any semisimplicity statement.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ℓ≠p be prime, let m≥1, and put k=bar(F_q). Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d≥1 over F_{q^m}, and write H^n=H^n_et(X_k,Q_ℓ). Fix an identification Q_ℓ(1)≅Q_ℓ, let ξ∈H^2 be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, and let L be cup product by ξ. Suppose L^{d-n}:H^n→H^{2d-n} is an isomorphism for every 0≤n≤d. Put P^d=ker(L:H^d→H^{d+2}), let tr_X:H^{2d}→Q_ℓ be the Poincaré duality trace normalized by tr_X(cl(z))=[κ(z):F_{q^m}], set β(x,y)=tr_X(x∪y), and let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. Then G(x,y)=β(x,Fy)+(-1)^d q^{md}β(x,F^{-1}y) is symmetric on P^d.
proof:
Let Q = q^m and put V = P^d = ker(L:H^d -> H^{d+2}). We first note that V is a finite-dimensional Q_l-vector space. Indeed, X is projective, hence proper, over F_Q. Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob to X viewed over F_Q (whose algebraic closure is k = overline(F_Q)) and to the constant sheaf Q_l gives that H^d_et(X_k,Q_l) is finite-dimensional over Q_l. Since V is a Q_l-subspace of H^d_et(X_k,Q_l), it is finite-dimensional.

The chosen identification Q_l(1) ≅ Q_l also identifies Q_l(-d) with Q_l. Under this identification, the Q_l-valued trace tr_X in the statement is the composite of the Q_l(-d)-valued Poincare trace used in Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_432, and the pairing beta(x,y) = tr_X(x cup y) is the corresponding Q_l-valued pairing B(x,y) = tr_X(x cup y) from that lemma.

By Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_432, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F restricts to an automorphism of V, and for all x,y in V one has
B(Fx,Fy) = q^{md} B(x,y).
After identifying Q_l(-d) with Q_l as above, this becomes
beta(Fx,Fy) = q^{md} beta(x,y)
for all x,y in V. In particular, F belongs to GL(V), and c := q^{md} is a nonzero element of Q_l because l != p.

We next determine the symmetry type of beta. For x,y in V, regarded as elements of H^d, apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_469 to X over F_Q with n = d. It gives
beta(x,y) = tr_X(x cup y) = (-1)^{d(2d-d)} tr_X(y cup x) = (-1)^{d^2} beta(y,x).
Since d^2 and d have the same parity, this is
beta(x,y) = epsilon beta(y,x), where epsilon := (-1)^d.

Now apply the purely algebraic lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/0f7916 with K = Q_l, V = P^d, the bilinear form beta, the sign epsilon = (-1)^d, the automorphism F, and c = q^{md}. Its hypotheses are exactly satisfied: beta(x,y) = epsilon beta(y,x) and beta(Fx,Fy) = c beta(x,y) for all x,y in V. The lemma concludes that the form
G(x,y) = beta(x,Fy) + epsilon c beta(x,F^{-1}y)
is symmetric on V. Substituting epsilon = (-1)^d and c = q^{md} gives precisely
G(x,y) = beta(x,Fy) + (-1)^d q^{md} beta(x,F^{-1}y).
Therefore G is symmetric on P^d.

The hard Lefschetz isomorphism hypothesis in the statement is not needed for this particular symmetry; it is compatible with the definitions of P^d and the trace pairing, and the argument above proves the desired symmetry from the Frobenius similitude and graded commutativity of the cup product.

statement: Let X be a scheme, let Z \subseteq X be a closed subscheme, let j:X\setminus Z\hookrightarrow X be the complementary open immersion, and let V\subseteq X be an open subscheme containing Z. Let F be a sheaf of abelian groups on X_{\mathrm{\acute et}} and put K:=\ker\bigl(F\to j_{*}j^{*}F\bigr). For an object U\to X of X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}, let U_{V}:=U\times_{X}V, regarded as an object of X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}. Then for every U\to X the restriction map K(U)\to K(U_{V}) is an isomorphism.
proof:
Write $W:=X\setminus Z$ for the open complement of the closed subscheme $Z$ (so $|W|=|X|\setminus |Z|$), and $j:W\hookrightarrow X$ for the open immersion. For an $X$-scheme $T$ put $T_W:=T\times_X W$ and $T_V:=T\times_X V$. The claim is that for every $U\in X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$ the restriction homomorphism
$$\rho:K(U)=\ker\bigl(F(U)\to (j_*j^*F)(U)\bigr)\longrightarrow K(U_V)=\ker\bigl(F(U_V)\to (j_*j^*F)(U_V)\bigr)$$\nis an isomorphism of abelian groups. The proof is a purely topos-theoretic computation; no cohomology and no coefficients are involved.

**Step 1. $U_V$ and $U_W$ are objects of $X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$, and the relevant fibre products.** \'Etale morphisms are stable under base change and under composition, and open immersions are \'etale. Since $U_V\to V$ is the base change of the \'etale map $U\to X$, it is \'etale, and $V\to X$ is \'etale, so $U_V\to X$ is \'etale; thus $U_V\in X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$, and likewise $U_W\in X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$. The projections $U_V\to U$, $U_W\to U$ are base changes of open immersions, hence themselves open immersions, i.e. morphisms of $X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$ over $U$. Open immersions are monomorphisms of schemes, so $U_V\times_U U_V\cong U_V$, $U_W\times_U U_W\cong U_W$, and
$$U_V\times_U U_W\;\cong\;U\times_X(V\times_X W)\;=\;U\times_X(V\cap W)\;=\;U_{V\cap W}.$$
Moreover $U_V\times_X W\cong (U\times_X V)\times_X W\cong U_V\times_U U_W\cong U_{V\cap W}$, the last identifications being the ones just written down.

**Step 2. $W_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$ as a full subsite, and restriction of sheaves.** An object $T\to X$ of $X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$ factors (topologically) through $W$ if and only if the induced map $T\to W$ is \'etale: if $T\to W$ is \'etale then $T\to X$ is a composite of \'etale maps, hence \'etale; conversely, if $T\to X$ is \'etale and factors through $W\to X$, then the graph $\Gamma:T\to T\times_X W$ is the base change of the diagonal $W\to W\times_X W$, which is an isomorphism because $W\to X$ is a monomorphism, while $T\times_X W\to W$ is the base change of the \'etale map $T\to X$; hence $T\to W$ is \'etale. Thus $W_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$ identifies with the full subcategory of $X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$ on the objects factoring through $W$. Fibre products in $W_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$ are the scheme-theoretic fibre products, hence agree with those in $X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$, and a covering family $\{T_a\to T\}$ in $W_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$ (jointly surjective family of \'etale $W$-maps) is again jointly surjective and \'etale over $X$, hence a covering family in $X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$. It follows that for a sheaf $F$ on $X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$ the restricted presheaf $R(F):=F|_{W_{\mathrm{\acute et}}}$ is a sheaf on $W_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$: for a covering $\{T_a\to T\}$ in $W_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$ the sequence
$$R(F)(T)\longrightarrow \prod_a R(F)(T_a)\rightrightarrows \prod_{a,b}R(F)(T_a\times_T T_b)$$\nis the equalizer expressing that $F$ is a sheaf for the same covering in $X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$, the terms being identical by the agreement of fibre products. So restriction gives a functor $R:\mathrm{Sh}(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}})\to\mathrm{Sh}(W_{\mathrm{\acute et}})$.

**Step 3. Objectwise formula for $j_*$ and for $j^*$, and hence for the canonical map $F\to j_*j^*F$.** Define $j_*^{\#}:\mathrm{Sh}(W_{\mathrm{\acute et}})\to\mathrm{Sh}(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}})$ by $(j_*^{\#}G)(T):=G(T_W)$; this is a functor because $T\mapsto T_W$ is functorial. We claim $R\dashv j_*^{\#}$. Given $\varphi:RF\to G$, set $\psi_\varphi(T):F(T)\to F(T_W)=RF(T_W)\xrightarrow{\varphi_{T_W}}G(T_W)=(j_*^{\#}G)(T)$, using the restriction map of the sheaf $F$ along $T_W\to T$. Given $\psi:F\to j_*^{\#}G$, set $\varphi_\psi(T):=\psi_T:F(T)\to G(T)$ for $T\in W_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$ (where $(j_*^{\#}G)(T)=G(T_W)=G(T)$ since $T_W=T$). These two constructions are mutually inverse: $\varphi_{\psi_\varphi}(T)=\psi_\varphi(T)=\varphi_{T_W}\circ\mathrm{res}=\varphi_T$ for $T\in W_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$ because then $T_W=T$ and $\mathrm{res}$ is the identity; and $\psi_{\varphi_\psi}(T)=\varphi_{\psi,T_W}\circ\mathrm{res}_{T,T_W}=\psi_{T_W}\circ\mathrm{res}_{T,T_W}=\psi_T$, the last equality being the naturality of $\psi$ with respect to the morphism $T_W\to T$ of $X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$, whose induced map $(j_*^{\#}G)(T_W)=G((T_W)_W)\cong G(T_W)\to (j_*^{\#}G)(T)=G(T_W)$ is the identity under $(T_W)_W\cong T_W$. Both directions are natural in $F$ and $G$, so $R\dashv j_*^{\#}$.

The morphism of sites $j:W_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\to X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$ attached to the open immersion is induced by the continuous left-exact functor $u:X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\to W_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$, $T\mapsto T_W$; its direct image is $G\mapsto(G\circ u)=j_*^{\#}$, and its pullback $j^*$ is, by definition, a left adjoint to $j_*$. Since $R$ is left adjoint to $j_*^{\#}$, we obtain a canonical isomorphism $j^*\cong R$; explicitly $j^*F(T)=F(T)$ for $T\in W_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$. Consequently, for every $T\in X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$,
$$(j_*j^*F)(T)=(j^*F)(T_W)=F(T_W),\qquad\text{and}\qquad j_*j^*F\cong j_*^{\#}RF.$$
Under this identification the component at $T$ of the unit $\eta_F:F\to j_*j^*F$ of the adjunction is the map $\psi_{\mathrm{id}}(T)$ constructed above with $\varphi=\mathrm{id}_{RF}$, namely the restriction homomorphism
$$\eta_F(T)=\mathrm{res}_{T,T_W}:F(T)\longrightarrow F(T_W).$$
(One may also see this directly: the above bijection $\mathrm{Hom}(F,j_*^{\#}G)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(RF,G)$ sends a transformation to its components at objects of $W_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$, and the unique element mapping to $\mathrm{id}_{RF}$ has $T$-component $\mathrm{res}_{T,T_W}$.)

**Step 4. Objectwise description of $K$.** Kernels in $\mathrm{Sh}(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}})$ are computed objectwise. Indeed, for $\alpha:B\to C$ the presheaf $T\mapsto\ker(B(T)\to C(T))$ is a sheaf: given a covering $\{T_a\to T\}$ and compatible sections $b_a\in\ker(B(T_a)\to C(T_a))$, the sheaf property of $B$ gives a unique $b\in B(T)$ with $b|_{T_a}=b_a$; the image of $b$ in $C(T)$ restricts to $0$ on every $T_a$, and since $C$ is a sheaf the map $C(T)\to\prod_a C(T_a)$ is injective, so that image is $0$, i.e. $b\in\ker(B(T)\to C(T))$. This presheaf has the universal property of the categorical kernel. Applying this to $\alpha=\eta_F$ and using Steps 1 and 3, for every $T\in X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$
$$K(T)=\ker\bigl(F(T)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{res}}F(T_W)\bigr)=\{\,s\in F(T): s|_{T_W}=0\,\},$$\nand the restriction maps of the subsheaf $K\subseteq F$ are those of $F$. In particular $\rho:K(U)\to K(U_V)$ is just $s\mapsto s|_{U_V}$, well defined because $\mathrm{res}_{U,U_V}$ carries sections vanishing on $U_W$ to sections vanishing on $U_V\times_X W$.

**Step 5. $\{U_V\to U,\;U_W\to U\}$ is an \'etale covering of $U$ in $X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$.** Both maps are open immersions by Step 1, hence \'etale $U$-morphisms. They are jointly surjective on underlying topological spaces: for $u\in|U|$ with image $x\in|X|$, the underlying space of $U_V$ (resp. $U_W$) is the inverse image of $|V|$ (resp. $|W|$) under $|U|\to|X|$, because $V,W\subseteq X$ are open subschemes. If $x\in|V|$ then $u\in|U_V|$; if $x\notin|V|$, then $x\notin|Z|$ since $|Z|\subseteq|V|$ by hypothesis, so $x\in|X|\setminus|Z|=|W|$ and $u\in|U_W|$. Hence the family is a covering family. Its Cech double overlaps are as computed in Step 1, so the sheaf equalizer for this cover reads: $F(U)\to F(U_V)\times F(U_W)$ is the equalizer of $F(U_V)\times F(U_W)\rightrightarrows F(U_{V\cap W})$, where, as the two projections $U_{V\cap W}\to U_V$ and $U_{V\cap W}\to U_W$ are open immersions arising from a cover by two opens, the two comparison maps send $(x,y)$ to $x|_{U_{V\cap W}}$ and $y|_{U_{V\cap W}}$ respectively. Thus:
(i) $F(U)\to F(U_V)\times F(U_W)$ is injective; and
(ii) if $x\in F(U_V)$, $y\in F(U_W)$ satisfy $x|_{U_{V\cap W}}=y|_{U_{V\cap W}}$, there is $s\in F(U)$ with $s|_{U_V}=x$ and $s|_{U_W}=y$.

**Step 6. Injectivity of $\rho$.** Let $s\in K(U)$ with $\rho(s)=0$. Then $s|_{U_V}=0$ in $K(U_V)$, hence in $F(U_V)$ (as $K(U_V)\subseteq F(U_V)$). Also $s|_{U_W}=0$ in $F(U_W)$ because $s\in K(U)$ (Step 4). By (i) applied to the cover of Step 5, $s=0$ in $F(U)$, hence $s=0$ in $K(U)$.

**Step 7. Surjectivity of $\rho$.** Let $t\in K(U_V)\subseteq F(U_V)$. By Step 4 applied to $T=U_V$, $t|_{U_V\times_X W}=0$ in $F(U_V\times_X W)=F(U_{V\cap W})$ (Step 1). Take $y:=0\in F(U_W)$; then $y|_{U_{V\cap W}}=0=t|_{U_{V\cap W}}$. By (ii) there is $s\in F(U)$ with $s|_{U_V}=t$ and $s|_{U_W}=0$. The second equality says $s\in\ker(F(U)\to F(U_W))=K(U)$ by Step 4, and then $\rho(s)=s|_{U_V}=t$. So $\rho$ is surjective.

Steps 6 and 7 show that $\rho:K(U)\to K(U_V)$ is a bijective group homomorphism, hence an isomorphism, for every $U\to X$ in $X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$.

**Edge cases.** The argument is uniform, but for completeness: if $Z=\varnothing$ then $W=X$, $U_W=U$, and Step 4 gives $K(T)=\ker(F(T)\to F(T))=0$ for all $T$, so $\rho:0\to0$ is an isomorphism. If $Z=X$ then $W=\varnothing$, $T_W=\varnothing$ and $F(\varnothing)=0$ (the terminal/zero object of abelian groups, since $\varnothing$ is covered by the empty family), so $K=F$ and $\rho$ is $F(U)\to F(U_V)$, which is bijective by Steps 6-7 with $U_W=\varnothing$. If $V=X$ then $U_V=U$ and $\rho=\mathrm{id}$. In all cases the only property of $V$ used is $|Z|\subseteq|V|$, as stated.

This proves the lemma. (No previously proved lemma is needed: the statement is an elementary computation with the direct/inverse image of an open immersion and the sheaf axiom.)

statement: Let \(q=p^{a}\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q}\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_{q}\), let \(Y\subseteq X\) be a nonempty closed subscheme defined over \(\mathbb F_{q}\) that is geometrically integral and satisfies \(H^{1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})=0\), and let \(j:U=X\setminus Y\hookrightarrow X\) be the open complement. Then the arrow \(H^{1}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})\to H^{1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})\) of the localisation long exact sequence of the pair \((X,Y)\) is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}[F]\)-modules, where \(F=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^{*}\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q}\), is the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius.
proof:
Let \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) and \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) be the closed and open immersions, and write \(i_k:Y_k\hookrightarrow X_k\) and \(j_k:U_k\hookrightarrow X_k\) for their base changes to \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Put \(F_Z=(\operatorname{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), for \(Z=X,Y,U\).

1. Frobenius-equivariant localization sequence. By Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_localization_les_finite_type there is a long exact sequence
\[\cdots\to H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{i_k^*}H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{m+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\cdots.\]
All of \(X,Y,U\) are defined over \(\mathbb F_q\). The complexes \(j_{k,!}\mathbb Q_\ell\), \(\mathbb Q_\ell\), and \(i_{k,*}\mathbb Q_\ell\) on \(X_k\) are constructible and carry natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphisms: pullback by \(F_X\) commutes with \(j_!\) and \(i_*\), and the constant sheaf has the canonical Frobenius structure. Since \(X\) is proper over \(\mathbb F_q\), applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob to these Frobenius-stable constructible complexes gives finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces \(H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \(H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), and \(H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=H^m(X_k,i_{k,*}\mathbb Q_\ell)\), each equipped with its canonical arithmetic Frobenius automorphism. The localization long exact sequence is the cohomology long exact sequence of the functorial distinguished triangle \(j_{k,!}\mathbb Q_\ell\to\mathbb Q_\ell\to i_{k,*}\mathbb Q_\ell\to\cdots\), and this triangle is compatible with the Frobenius structures. Hence every map in the sequence commutes with \(F\); for the pullback maps \(i_k^*\) this is also explicitly given by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_214, while eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a identifies these operators with the usual \(q\)-power Frobenius pullbacks and their inverses. Thus the sequence is exact in the category of \(\mathbb Q_\ell[F]\)-modules.

2. The degree-zero terms. Because \(X\) is geometrically connected, \(X_k\) is connected. Because \(Y\) is nonempty and geometrically integral, \(Y_k\) is integral, hence nonempty and connected. For any connected scheme \(Z\) of finite type over \(k\) and any finite abelian group \(A\), the global sections of the constant sheaf \(A\) on \(Z_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\) are exactly \(A\): a global section is a locally constant \(A\)-valued function on the connected étale topos of \(Z\), hence constant. Applying this to \(A=\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z\) and passing to the inverse limit/tensor product defining \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-coefficients gives \(H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell\). Therefore \(H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell\). Under these canonical identifications the pullback \(i_k^*:H^0(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^0(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is the identity, because pullback of a constant sheaf sends the constant section with value \(c\) to the constant section with value \(c\). (Equivalently, choose a \(k\)-point of \(Y_k\); it exists since \(Y_k\) is nonempty projective over the algebraically closed field \(k\), and evaluation at that point gives the same constant value.)

3. Exactness at the first cohomology groups. The relevant portion of the localization sequence is
\[H^0(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{i_k^*}H^0(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\delta}H^1_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\alpha}H^1(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{i_k^*}H^1(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).\]
By Step 2 the first arrow is an isomorphism. Exactness at \(H^0(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) therefore implies \(\delta=0\). Exactness at \(H^1_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) then gives \(\ker(\alpha)=\operatorname{im}(\delta)=0\), so \(\alpha\) is injective. By hypothesis \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\), so the map \(H^1(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^1(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is zero. Exactness at \(H^1(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) gives \(\operatorname{im}(\alpha)=\ker(0)=H^1(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), so \(\alpha\) is surjective. Hence \(\alpha\) is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces.

4. Conclusion as a Frobenius module. The arrow \(\alpha\) is the map \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) appearing in the localization long exact sequence, and Step 1 showed that this sequence is an exact sequence of \(\mathbb Q_\ell[F]\)-modules. Therefore \(\alpha\) is \(F\)-equivariant. Since it is bijective and \(F\)-equivariant, it is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell[F]\)-modules.

statement: Let \(k\) be a field, let \(X\) be a smooth \(k\)-scheme, let \(Z\subset X\) be a closed subscheme smooth over \(k\) of pure codimension \(c\ge1\) with ideal sheaf \(\mathcal I\), and let \(\pi:\operatorname{Bl}_{Z}X\to X\) be the blow-up of \(Z\). Let \(E\subset\operatorname{Bl}_{Z}X\) be the effective Cartier divisor cut out by \(\mathcal I\cdot\mathcal O_{\operatorname{Bl}_{Z}X}\) and let \(p=\pi|_{E}:E\to Z\). Then \(E\) is isomorphic over \(Z\) to the projective bundle \(\mathbb P_{Z}(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^{2})\) of one-dimensional quotients of the locally free \(\mathcal O_{Z}\)-module \(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^{2}\), and under such an isomorphism \(\mathcal O_{E}(E)\cong\mathcal O_{\mathbb P_{Z}(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^{2})}(-1)\).
proof:
Let \(B=\operatorname{Bl}_{Z}X=\operatorname{Proj}_{X}(\bigoplus_{n\ge 0}\mathcal I^{n})\) and write \(S=\bigoplus_{n\ge 0}\mathcal I^{n}\). If \(Z=\varnothing\) the assertion is vacuous, so assume \(Z\) is nonempty. All assertions are local on \(X\); first work on an affine open \(U=\operatorname{Spec}A\) with \(J=\mathcal I(U)\).

1. Regularity of the immersion. Since \(X\) and \(Z\) are smooth over the field \(k\), their local rings are regular. For \(x\in Z\), put \(A_x=\mathcal O_{X,x}\), \(J_x=\mathcal I_x\), and \(B_x=A_x/J_x=\mathcal O_{Z,x}\). These are regular local rings, and pure codimension \(c\) means \(\dim A_x-\dim B_x=c\). A standard local criterion for regular quotients of regular local rings says that if \(A_x\) is regular and \(A_x/J_x\) is regular of dimension \(\dim A_x-c\), then \(J_x\) is generated by part of a regular system of parameters of \(A_x\). Hence locally on \(X\) the ideal \(J\) is generated by a regular sequence \(f_1,\dots,f_c\), and the classes of \(f_1,\dots,f_c\) form an \(A/J\)-basis of \(J/J^2\). Thus \(Z\hookrightarrow X\) is a regular immersion and \(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2\) is locally free of rank \(c\).

2. The associated graded algebra. On \(U\) choose a regular sequence \(f_1,\dots,f_c\) generating \(J\), as in step 1. The Rees algebra \(R=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}J^n\) has the standard presentation
\[
R\cong A[T_1,\dots,T_c]/(f_iT_j-f_jT_i\mid 1\le i<j\le c).
\]
Indeed, the map \(A[T_1,\dots,T_c]\to R\), \(T_i\mapsto f_i\), is surjective, and exactness of the Koszul complex on the regular sequence shows that its kernel is generated by the Koszul relations \(f_iT_j-f_jT_i\). Tensoring with \(A/J\) gives
\[
R/JR\cong (A/J)[T_1,\dots,T_c].
\]
But \(R/JR=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}J^n/J^{n+1}=\operatorname{gr}_J A\), and under the isomorphism \(T_i\) maps to the class of \(f_i\) in \(J/J^2\). Therefore
\[
\operatorname{gr}_J A\cong \operatorname{Sym}_{A/J}(J/J^2).
\]
These local isomorphisms are the sheafification of the canonical map \(\operatorname{Sym}_{\mathcal O_Z}(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)\to\operatorname{gr}_{\mathcal I}\mathcal O_X\), so they glue to a global isomorphism of graded \(\mathcal O_Z\)-algebras
\[
\operatorname{gr}_{\mathcal I}\mathcal O_X\cong \operatorname{Sym}_{\mathcal O_Z}(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2).
\]

3. Identification of \(E\). The blow-up is \(B=\operatorname{Proj}_X S\). Its inverse image of \(Z\) is
\[
E=B\times_X Z\cong \operatorname{Proj}_Z(S\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}\mathcal O_Z)
=\operatorname{Proj}_Z(\operatorname{gr}_{\mathcal I}\mathcal O_X).
\]
Using the isomorphism from step 2,
\[
E\cong \operatorname{Proj}_Z(\operatorname{Sym}_{\mathcal O_Z}(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2))
=\mathbb P_Z(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2),
\]
where, by convention, \(\mathbb P_Z(F)=\operatorname{Proj}_Z(\operatorname{Sym}_{\mathcal O_Z}F)\) is the bundle of one-dimensional quotients of \(F\). The projection to \(Z\) is the bundle projection, so the isomorphism is over \(Z\).

4. The sign of the exceptional line bundle. Let \(S=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathcal I^n\) and \(B=\operatorname{Proj}_X S\). The degree-one part \(S_1=\mathcal I\) generates \(S\) over \(S_0=\mathcal O_X\), so the principal opens \(D_+(f)\) with \(f\in\mathcal I\) cover \(B\). The graded map \(S(1)\to S\), whose degree-\(n\) component is the inclusion \(S(1)_n=S_{n+1}=\mathcal I^{n+1}\hookrightarrow \mathcal I^n=S_n\), induces a morphism
\[
\varphi:\mathcal O_B(1)\longrightarrow \mathcal O_B.
\]
By \(Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_proj_principal_open_affine\), \(D_+(f)=\operatorname{Spec}S_{(f)}\). On \(D_+(f)\), the sheaf \(\mathcal O_B(1)\) is free with generator \(f\), and \(\varphi\) is multiplication by \(f\). Its image is therefore \(fS_{(f)}\). For every \(g\in\mathcal I\), one has \(g=(g/f)f\) with \(g/f\in S_{(f)}\), so \(fS_{(f)}=\mathcal I S_{(f)}\). Hence the image sheaf of \(\varphi\) is \(\mathcal I\cdot\mathcal O_B\). Since \(E\) is the effective Cartier divisor cut out by \(\mathcal I\cdot\mathcal O_B\), this ideal is \(\mathcal O_B(-E)\) and is invertible. Thus \(\varphi\) is a surjection from the invertible sheaf \(\mathcal O_B(1)\) to the invertible sheaf \(\mathcal O_B(-E)\), hence an isomorphism:
\[
\mathcal O_B(1)\cong\mathcal O_B(-E),\qquad \mathcal O_B(E)\cong\mathcal O_B(-1).
\]

Let \(e:E\hookrightarrow B\) be the closed immersion. The graded algebra defining \(E\) is \(T=S/IS\), and twisting sheaves are compatible with this quotient:
\[
e^*\mathcal O_B(1)\cong\mathcal O_E(1)
\]
because \(S(1)\otimes_S T\cong T(1)\). Therefore
\[
\mathcal O_E(E)=e^*\mathcal O_B(E)\cong e^*\mathcal O_B(-1)\cong\mathcal O_E(-1).
\]
Under the isomorphism \(E\cong\mathbb P_Z(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)\) constructed above, \(\mathcal O_E(1)\) is the tautological quotient line bundle, so \(\mathcal O_E(-1)\) is its dual, denoted \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P_Z(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)}(-1)\). This is exactly the required identification.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(Y\subset X\) be a nonempty smooth very ample divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and put \(U=X\setminus Y\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\xi\) be the cycle class of \(Y\) and let \(L\) be cup product by \(\xi\). Suppose \(L^{d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for all \(0\le n\le d\). If the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on \(H^d_{c,\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and on \(H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), then it is semisimple on \(H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
proof:
Set Q=q^m and regard F_Q as the base field. Since Q=p^(am) is a prime power, the lemmas stated for a prime power q may be applied with q replaced by Q. Let F denote the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius (id x Spec sigma)^*, where sigma(c)=c^Q. All cohomology groups below are etale cohomology over k=overline F_q with Q_l coefficients. Define P^d=ker(L:H^d_et(X_k,Q_l)->H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_l)).

Because Y is a very ample divisor, it is an effective ample Cartier divisor, smooth of pure dimension d-1 over F_Q. The hard Lefschetz hypothesis in the statement says that for every 0<=n<=d the map L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_l)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_l) is an isomorphism. Taking n=d-2 gives that L^2:H^{d-2}_et(X_k,Q_l)->H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_l) is an isomorphism. Consequently L:H^{d-2}_et(X_k,Q_l)->H^d_et(X_k,Q_l) is injective: if x is in H^{d-2} and Lx=0, then L^2x=0, and since L^2 is an isomorphism, x=0.

Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_primitive_middle_decomposition_criterion to the smooth projective geometrically connected variety X over F_Q and the very ample divisor Y. Its hypotheses are satisfied: L:H^{d-2}->H^d is injective as just proved, and L^2:H^{d-2}->H^{d+2} is an isomorphism. The lemma gives a direct-sum decomposition of Q_l-vector spaces
H^d_et(X_k,Q_l)=P^d ⊕ L(H^{d-2}_et(X_k,Q_l)).
Put W=L(H^{d-2}_et(X_k,Q_l)).

Next apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable to X over F_Q and the very ample divisor Y. It gives F∘L=Q L∘F on every cohomological degree. For m=d, the primitive space defined there is P^d=ker L, and the lemma states that P^d is stable under F. The subspace W is also stable under F, because if w=Lx with x in H^{d-2}, then Fw=Q L(Fx), which lies in L(H^{d-2})=W. Hence the decomposition H^d=P^d ⊕ W is a decomposition into F-stable Q_l-subspaces.

We now prove that F is semisimple on each summand.

First consider P^d. Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_514 with q replaced by Q. Its hypotheses are exactly those of the present situation: X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d>=2 over F_Q, Y is a smooth effective ample divisor of pure dimension d-1 over F_Q, U=X-Y, and the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^d_{c,et}(U_k,Q_l) by assumption. The lemma concludes that F is semisimple on P^d=ker(L:H^d->H^{d+2}).

Now consider W. Let V=H^{d-2}_et(X_k,Q_l), let T=F|V, and let S=F|W. The map L:V->W is a Q_l-linear isomorphism because L is injective and W is defined as its image. The relation F∘L=Q L∘F says precisely that S∘L=Q L∘T. Equivalently, (Q^{-1}S)∘L=L∘T. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8, T is semisimple on V if and only if Q^{-1}S is semisimple on W. By assumption T is semisimple, hence Q^{-1}S is semisimple on W.

It remains to pass from Q^{-1}S to S. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5, semisimplicity is equivalent to diagonalizability over an algebraic closure of Q_l. If A is a diagonalizable linear operator and c is a nonzero scalar, then cA is diagonalizable in the same eigenbasis, with eigenvalues multiplied by c. Taking A=Q^{-1}S and c=Q, which is nonzero in Q_l, we conclude that S=Q(Q^{-1}S) is semisimple on W.

Finally, apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9 to the F-stable direct sum H^d_et(X_k,Q_l)=P^d ⊕ W. We have shown that F is semisimple on P^d and on W. The lemma states that the direct-sum operator is semisimple if and only if each summand operator is semisimple. Therefore F is semisimple on H^d_et(X_k,Q_l), which is exactly the desired conclusion.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let l != p be a prime, and put k=overline(F_q). Let X be a proper scheme of finite type over F_q admitting a finite filtration by closed subschemes empty = X_{-1} subset X_0 subset ... subset X_s = X such that each U_i = X_i - X_{i-1} is isomorphic over F_q to a finite disjoint union of affine spaces over F_q. Then H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) = 0 for every odd integer n >= 0.
proof:
We prove that every cohomology group of $X_{\bar{\mathbb F}_q}$ in an odd degree vanishes, by induction along the given filtration. The only inputs are the localisation long exact sequence, the computation of $H^\bullet_c$ of an affine space, and additivity of $H^\bullet_c$ over open-and-closed decompositions.

STEP 0. Notation and the base-changed filtration. Write $k=\overline{\mathbb F_q}$, $\Lambda=\mathbb Q_\ell$. For an $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $Z$ write $Z_k=Z\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k$. The given filtration
$$\varnothing=X_{-1}\subset X_0\subset\cdots\subset X_s=X,\qquad U_i=X_i\setminus X_{i-1}$$
by closed $\mathbb F_q$-subschemes base-changes to a filtration of $X_k$ by closed $k$-subschemes
$$\varnothing=(X_{-1})_k\subset (X_0)_k\subset\cdots\subset (X_s)_k=X_k,$$
because base change preserves closed immersions, open immersions and complements: $k$-points aside, $(X_i)_k\setminus (X_{i-1})_k=(U_i)_k$ as open subschemes of $(X_i)_k$. Moreover, since each $U_i$ is $\mathbb F_q$-isomorphic to a finite disjoint union $\coprod_{t\in T_i}\mathbb A^{m_{i,t}}_{\mathbb F_q}$, base change gives a $k$-isomorphism
$$(U_i)_k\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;\coprod_{t\in T_i}\mathbb A^{m_{i,t}}_{k},\qquad T_i\ \text{finite},\ m_{i,t}\ge 0.$$
Since $X$ is of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$, each $(X_i)_k$ is of finite type over the algebraically closed field $k$, and $\ell\neq p=\operatorname{char}k$.

STEP 1. The two definitions of cohomology with compact support agree. The localisation lemma (Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_localization_les_finite_type) uses, for an open immersion $j\colon V\hookrightarrow Z$ with $Z$ of finite type over an algebraically closed field, the notation $H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(V,\mathbb Q_\ell):=H^m(Z_{\mathrm{\acute et}},j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)$. The lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_hc_affine_space uses $H^m_c(V_k')=H^m(\operatorname{Spec}k,Rf_!\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for $f\colon V_k'\to\operatorname{Spec}k$. These coincide in the situation we need: if $f\colon V\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ factors as $V\xrightarrow{\;j\;}\bar V\xrightarrow{\;g\;}\operatorname{Spec}k$ with $j$ an open immersion and $g$ proper, then $Rf_!\cong Rg_*Rj_!$ (compatibility of $f_!$ with composition, together with $g_!=g_*$ for $g$ proper), and $j_!$ is exact on étale sheaves of abelian groups, hence
$$H^m\bigl(\operatorname{Spec}k,Rf_!\mathbb Q_\ell\bigr)=H^m\bigl(\bar V_{\mathrm{\acute et}},Rj_!\mathbb Q_\ell\bigr)=H^m\bigl(\bar V_{\mathrm{\acute et}},j_!\mathbb Q_\ell\bigr).$$
Applied to $V=\mathbb A^m_k$ with $\bar V=\mathbb P^m_k$, this identifies the groups whose vanishing is given by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_hc_affine_space with the groups appearing in the localisation long exact sequence; and since $(U_i)_k\hookrightarrow (X_i)_k$ is an open immersion into a scheme proper over $k$, the group $H^m((X_i)_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}},j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is exactly $H^m_c((U_i)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ in the standard sense. In particular it depends only on $(U_i)_k$, so we may compute it on each affine-space summand.

STEP 2. Odd compactly supported cohomology of a finite disjoint union of affine spaces vanishes. Let $W=\coprod_{t\in T}\mathbb A^{m_t}_k$ with $T$ finite. We claim $H^n_c(W,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ for every odd $n\ge 0$.
