First, if $T=\varnothing$ then $W=\varnothing$ and $\Gamma(W,-)$ is the zero functor on abelian étale sheaves (the limit over the empty diagram in $\mathbf{Ab}$ is the zero group); the zero functor is exact, so all its derived functors vanish and $H^n_c(\varnothing,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ in every degree, in particular for odd $n$.

Second, for a single affine space, eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_hc_affine_space states that $H^n_c(\mathbb A^{m}_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ for every $n\neq 2m$; since an odd integer $n$ never equals $2m$, this group vanishes for odd $n$.

Third, for a general finite $T$ we argue by induction on $\#T$. If $\#T=1$ this is the previous paragraph. If $\#T\ge 2$, write $W=V\amalg W'$ with $V=\mathbb A^{m_1}_k$ open-and-closed and $W'=\coprod_{t\in T\setminus\{1\}}\mathbb A^{m_t}_k$ its open-and-closed complement. The scheme $W$ is separated and of finite type over $k$, so Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_cohom_open_closed_sum applies and gives an isomorphism $H^n_c(W)\simeq H^n_c(V)\oplus H^n_c(W')$. For odd $n$ both summands vanish (the first by the previous paragraph, the second by the induction on $\#T$), hence $H^n_c(W)=0$. This proves the claim.

STEP 3. Induction along the filtration. For $-1\le j\le s$ let $A(j)$ be the assertion
$$H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\bigl((X_j)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell\bigr)=0\quad\text{for every odd } n\ge 0.$$

Base case $j=-1$: $(X_{-1})_k=\varnothing$, and as noted in Step 2 the functor $\Gamma(\varnothing,-)$ on abelian étale sheaves is the zero functor, which is exact; hence $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\varnothing,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ for all $n$, so $A(-1)$ holds.

Inductive step: assume $A(j-1)$ for some $0\le j\le s$; we prove $A(j)$. Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_localization_les_finite_type to the scheme $(X_j)_k$ of finite type over the algebraically closed field $k$, to the closed immersion $i\colon (X_{j-1})_k\hookrightarrow (X_j)_k$ and to the complementary open immersion $j_u\colon (U_j)_k\hookrightarrow (X_j)_k$. It yields a long exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}\bigl((U_j)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell\bigr)\xrightarrow{\;\iota\;} H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\bigl((X_j)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell\bigr)\xrightarrow{\;i^*\;} H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\bigl((X_{j-1})_k,\mathbb Q_\ell\bigr)\xrightarrow{\;\partial\;} H^{n+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}\bigl((U_j)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell\bigr)\to\cdots.$$
By Step 1 and Step 2 applied to $W=(U_j)_k\simeq\coprod_{t\in T_j}\mathbb A^{m_{j,t}}_k$ (Step 0), $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}((U_j)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ for every odd $n$. Now fix an odd $n\ge 0$. Exactness at $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X_j)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ says $\ker(i^*)=\operatorname{im}(\iota)=0$, so $i^*$ is injective:
$$H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\bigl((X_j)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell\bigr)\hookrightarrow H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\bigl((X_{j-1})_k,\mathbb Q_\ell\bigr).$$
The right-hand group is $0$ by the induction hypothesis $A(j-1)$ (recall $n$ is odd). Hence $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X_j)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ for every odd $n\ge0$, which is $A(j)$. (Note that no finite-dimensionality hypothesis is used or needed: a subgroup of the zero group is zero.)

By induction, $A(j)$ holds for all $-1\le j\le s$.

STEP 4. Conclusion. Taking $j=s$ gives $(X_s)_k=X_k$, so $A(s)$ is precisely the statement that $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q},\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ for every odd integer $n\ge0$. $\blacksquare$

(Remark, not used above: the identical argument is what proves Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_549a; the present lemma is the same statement with the hypothesis "possibly empty finite disjoint union" written as "finite disjoint union", the empty case being covered by Step 2.)

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let l != p be a prime, and put k=overline(F_q). Let C be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_q, let r >= 1 be an integer, and let Sym^r C denote the r-th relative symmetric power of C over F_q. Then the q-power arithmetic Frobenius (id x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^q, is semisimple on H^n_et((Sym^r C)_k,Q_l) for every integer n >= 0.
proof:
Proof. Let G=S_r act on Y=C^r by permuting the r factors, and let pi:Y->X=Y/G be the quotient morphism. By the standard identification of the quotient of a power of a smooth curve with its symmetric product, X is the relative symmetric power Sym^r C over F_q. We verify that X and pi satisfy the hypotheses of lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_584.

1. X is smooth, projective, geometrically connected, and pure of dimension r. The product Y=C^r is smooth, projective, and geometrically connected over F_q because C is. A quotient of a projective scheme by a finite group is projective: choose a very ample line bundle L on C, and let M=pr_1^*L tensor pr_2^*L tensor ... tensor pr_r^*L on Y. This line bundle is very ample and has a natural S_r-linearization; the quotient X is Proj of the finitely generated invariant section ring directsum_n H^0(Y,M^n)^G, hence X is projective over F_q. The quotient map pi is surjective, so after base change to k=overline(F_q), X_k is the continuous image of the connected scheme Y_k; therefore X_k is connected, i.e. X is geometrically connected. Since pi is finite and surjective, dim X=dim Y=r.

For smoothness, check after base change to k. Let x be a k-point of X, corresponding to an effective divisor D=sum_{a=1}^s n_a P_a on C_k, where the P_a are distinct and sum_{a=1}^s n_a=r. Choose a k-point y of Y above x obtained by ordering the points with multiplicities n_a. The stabilizer H of y in G is prod_{a=1}^s S_{n_a}. The completed local ring of Y_k at y is A=k[[t_{a,b}:1<=a<=s, 1<=b<=n_a]]. For a finite quotient, the completed local ring of X_k at x is the invariant subring A^H; this follows because pi is finite, the maximal ideal topologies are compatible, and taking fixed points commutes with inverse limits. The subgroup S_{n_a} permutes the variables t_{a,1},...,t_{a,n_a}. The invariant ring k[[t_{a,1},...,t_{a,n_a}]]^{S_{n_a}} is k[[e_{a,1},...,e_{a,n_a}]], where e_{a,m} are the elementary symmetric functions. This holds over any field: the fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials holds over Z, and passing to formal power series is done degree by degree. Hence A^H is isomorphic to k[[e_{a,m}:1<=a<=s, 1<=m<=n_a]], a regular local ring of dimension sum n_a=r. Thus X_k is regular at every closed point. Since k is perfect and X_k is of finite type, regularity implies smoothness; therefore X is smooth over F_q.

2. The morphism pi is proper, surjective, and generically finite. On an affine open Spec A of Y, the quotient is Spec A^G, and every a in A is integral over A^G because it satisfies prod_{g in G}(T-g(a))=0. Thus pi is finite, hence proper and surjective. For generic finiteness, Y is integral and normal. The function field of the quotient is K(X)=K(Y)^G. The action of G on K(Y) is faithful: a nontrivial permutation of the factors changes the rational functions coming from the two corresponding projections C^r->C. By Artin's theorem for finite groups of field automorphisms, [K(Y):K(Y)^G]=|G|=r!, which is finite. Therefore pi is generically finite; for r=1 this is simply the identity morphism.

Now apply lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_584 to X=Sym^r C, with the r curves C_1=...=C_r=C, and with f=pi:C^r->Sym^r C. The lemma gives that the q-power arithmetic Frobenius (id x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^q, is semisimple on H^n_et((Sym^r C)_k,Q_l) for every integer n>=0. This is exactly the desired conclusion. QED.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let l != p be a prime, let m >= 1, and put k=overline(F_q). Let r and s be nonnegative integers, let C_1,...,C_r be smooth projective geometrically connected curves over F_{q^m}, and let A_1,...,A_s be abelian varieties over F_{q^m}. Let Y be their product over F_{q^m}. Then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_et(Y_k,Q_l) for every integer n >= 0.
proof:
Write Q := q^m. Then Q = p^{am} is again a prime power, and ¯{F}_Q = k = ¯{F}_q. For any scheme Z of finite type over F_Q we put

  F_Z := (id_{Z_k} × Spec σ)^*,   σ(c) = c^{Q} = c^{q^m},

the Q-power (= q^m-power) arithmetic Frobenius acting on H^n_{ét}(Z_k, Q_ℓ). By hypothesis the target statement asks us to prove: F_Y is semisimple on H^n_{ét}(Y_k, Q_ℓ) for every n ≥ 0, where Y is the product over F_Q of the r curves C_1,…,C_r and the s abelian varieties A_1,…,A_s.

We record first two general facts that will be used repeatedly.

(F1) Conjugate operators have the same semisimplicity behaviour. Let κ: V →~ W be an isomorphism of finite-dimensional Q_ℓ-vector spaces, T ∈ GL(V), S ∈ GL(W) with κ ∘ T = S ∘ κ. If T is semisimple then so is S. Indeed, by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5 semisimplicity of an operator is equivalent to diagonalisability after extending scalars to ¯{Q}_ℓ. Base-changing κ we get an isomorphism κ̄: V ⊗ ¯{Q}_ℓ ~→ W ⊗ ¯{Q}_ℓ intertwining T̄ and S̄. If T̄ is diagonalisable, V ⊗ ¯{Q}_ℓ = ⊕_λ V_λ with V_λ = ker(T̄ − λ). For w = κ̄(v) with v ∈ V_λ one has S̄ w = κ̄ T̄ v = λ κ̄ v = λ w, so κ̄(V_λ) ⊆ ker(S̄ − λ); applying the same argument to κ̄^{-1}, which satisfies T̄ κ̄^{-1} = κ̄^{-1} S̄, gives the reverse inclusion. Hence W ⊗ ¯{Q}_ℓ = ⊕_λ κ̄(V_λ) = ⊕_λ ker(S̄ − λ), i.e. S̄ is diagonalisable, and by lemma_5 again S is semisimple.

(F2) Finite-dimensionality and invertibility. If Z is a smooth projective variety over F_Q, then H^n_{ét}(Z_k, Q_ℓ) is finite-dimensional over Q_ℓ for every n: apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob to the proper F_Q-variety Z with K = Q_{ℓ,Z_k} the constant sheaf equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism ψ: F_Z^* Q_ℓ ~→ Q_ℓ (the constant sheaf lies in D^b_c, and its hypercohomology is H^n_{ét}(Z_k, Q_ℓ)). Moreover, by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a the pullback F_{Z_k} := (id × Spec σ)^* is a Q_ℓ-linear automorphism of H^n_{ét}(Z_k, Q_ℓ) (with inverse the geometric Frobenius). So all operators below are invertible operators on finite-dimensional Q_ℓ-spaces, as required to invoke lemma_35 and lemma_9.

Now set t := r + s and enumerate the factors
  Z_u := C_u  (1 ≤ u ≤ r),      Z_{r+v} := A_v  (1 ≤ v ≤ s),
so that Y = Z_1 ×_{F_Q} ⋯ ×_{F_Q} Z_t (an empty product, when t = 0, means Spec F_Q).

Case t = 0. Then Y_k = Spec k. Since Spec k is strictly henselian its étale topos is that of a point, so H^0_{ét}(Spec k, Q_ℓ) = Q_ℓ and H^n_{ét}(Spec k, Q_ℓ) = 0 for n ≥ 1. The morphism id × Spec σ is Spec σ: Spec k → Spec k, and for the constant sheaf the canonical map (Spec σ)^{-1} Q_ℓ → Q_ℓ is the identity on the value group Q_ℓ; hence F_Y = id on Q_ℓ, which is semisimple, and F_Y is trivially semisimple on the zero spaces. The statement holds.

Henceforth assume t ≥ 1. We prove by induction on u ∈ {1,…,t} the assertion

  P(u):  F is semisimple on H^n_{ét}((Z_1 × ⋯ × Z_u)_k, Q_ℓ) for every integer n ≥ 0.

Step 1: each individual factor satisfies P(1)-type semisimplicity.
  – If Z_1 = C_1 is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_Q = F_{q^m}, then Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_364 (applied with the prime power q^m in place of its q, i.e. exactly the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^n_{ét}(C_{1,¯{F}_q}, Q_ℓ)) says F_{C_1} is semisimple for every n ≥ 0.
  – If Z_1 = A_1 is an abelian variety over F_{q^m}, then Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/bdb05f says the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_{ét}((A_1)_k, Q_ℓ) for every n ≥ 0.
  Thus P(1) holds.

Inductive step. Assume P(u−1) holds for some 2 ≤ u ≤ t, and write
  X := Z_1 ×_{F_Q} ⋯ ×_{F_Q} Z_{u-1},    Z := Z_u,    W := X ×_{F_Q} Z = Z_1 × ⋯ × Z_u.
Both X and Z are smooth projective varieties over F_Q: Z by hypothesis, and X because smoothness and properness are stable under products over a field and projectivity follows by iterating the Segre embedding P^N × P^M ↤ P^{(N+1)(M+1)-1}. Therefore eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_146 applies (with the prime power Q = q^m in place of its q, and with ¯{F}_Q = k): for each n ≥ 0 the Künneth map
   κ_n: ⊕_{i+j=n} H^i_{ét}(X_k, Q_ℓ) ⊗_{Q_ℓ} H^j_{ét}(Z_k, Q_ℓ) → H^n_{ét}(W_k, Q_ℓ),
   x ⊗ y ↦ pr_1^*(x) ∪ pr_2^*(y),
is an isomorphism of Q_ℓ-vector spaces, and under κ_n the operator F_W corresponds to F_X ⊗ F_Z on the (i,j)-summand. The index set {(i,j): i+j=n, i,j ≥ 0} is finite, so this is a finite direct sum.

Fix a pair (i,j) with i + j = n. Put V := H^i_{ét}(X_k, Q_ℓ) and U := H^j_{ét}(Z_k, Q_ℓ); by (F2) both are finite-dimensional over Q_ℓ, and by (F2) again T := F_X|_V and S := F_Z|_U are invertible. By the induction hypothesis P(u−1), T is semisimple on V; by Step 1 (applied to the factor Z = Z_u, which is either a curve or an abelian variety) S is semisimple on U. Hence eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_35(i) gives that T ⊗ S is semisimple on V ⊗_{Q_ℓ} U.

Doing this for every (i,j) with i+j=n, eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9 (a finite direct-sum operator is semisimple iff each summand operator is) yields that
   ⊕_{i+j=n} (F_X|_{H^i(X_k)} ⊗ F_Z|_{H^j(Z_k)})
is semisimple on the source of κ_n. Since κ_n is an isomorphism intertwining this operator with F_W on H^n_{ét}(W_k, Q_ℓ), (F1) implies that F_W is semisimple on H^n_{ét}(W_k, Q_ℓ). As n was arbitrary, P(u) holds.

By induction P(t) holds. But W = Z_1 × ⋯ × Z_t = Y, so P(t) is precisely the required conclusion: for every integer n ≥ 0, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id × Spec σ)^*, σ(c) = c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_{ét}(Y_k, Q_ℓ). ∎

(Remark on the equivalent formulation: the argument gives semisimplicity over Q_ℓ; by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5 this is the same as diagonalisability over ¯{Q}_ℓ, and by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a the geometric Frobenius is the inverse of F_Y, so it is semisimple as well. These remarks are not needed for the statement proved above.)

statement: Let K be a field, let e >= 2, and let V_{e-2}, V_e, V_{e+2} be finite-dimensional K-vector spaces. Let β: V_e × V_e → K and γ: V_{e-2} × V_{e+2} → K be perfect pairings. Let L_{e-2}: V_{e-2} → V_e and L_e: V_e → V_{e+2} be K-linear maps satisfying β(L_{e-2}a,b) = γ(a,L_e b) for all a in V_{e-2} and b in V_e. If the composite L_e ∘ L_{e-2}: V_{e-2} → V_{e+2} is injective, then β restricted to ker(L_e: V_e → V_{e+2}) is nondegenerate.
proof:
The statement is pure finite-dimensional linear algebra; the hypothesis e \ge 2 only serves to make the three spaces V_{e-2}, V_e, V_{e+2} meaningful labels, and no other lemma is used. Write
   A := L_{e-2} : V_{e-2} \to V_e,   B := L_e : V_e \to V_{e+2},   T := B \circ A : V_{e-2} \to V_{e+2},   W := \ker(B) \subseteq V_e,
and put N := dim V_{e-2}. The adjunction hypothesis is
   (\ast)   \beta(Aa, b) = \gamma(a, Bb)   for all a \in V_{e-2}, b \in V_e,
and T is assumed injective.

Step 1 (dimensions of the outer spaces agree). Since \gamma is a perfect pairing, the map \varphi : V_{e-2} \to V_{e+2}^{*}, a \mapsto \gamma(a,-) is an isomorphism (this is exactly the first-slot non-degeneracy in the definition of perfect pairing, together with finite dimensionality). Hence N = dim V_{e-2} = dim V_{e+2}^{*} = dim V_{e+2}, the last equality being the standard fact dim E^{*} = dim E for a finite-dimensional space E.

Step 2 (T is an isomorphism; B is onto, A is one-to-one). T is injective by hypothesis, so dim im T = dim V_{e-2} = N = dim V_{e+2}. As im T is a subspace of V_{e+2} of the same finite dimension, im T = V_{e+2}; thus T is a linear isomorphism. Consequences: (i) A is injective (if Aa = 0 then 0 = BAa = Ta, so a = 0); (ii) B is surjective (given c \in V_{e+2} choose a with Ta = c, then B(Aa) = c).

Step 3 (dimension of W). By rank–nullity applied to B : V_e \to V_{e+2}, using surjectivity from Step 2,
   dim V_e = dim \ker B + dim im B = dim W + N,   so   dim W = dim V_e - N.
(If dim V_e = N this says W = {0}; the argument below covers that case, in which the restricted form on the zero space is trivially nondegenerate.)

Step 4 (the image of A is contained in the orthogonal of W). Define
   W^{L} := \{ x \in V_e : \beta(x, w) = 0 \ \text{for all } w \in W \}.
Take a \in V_{e-2} and w \in W. Since Bw = 0, (\ast) and bilinearity of \gamma give
   \beta(Aa, w) = \gamma(a, Bw) = \gamma(a, 0) = 0.
Hence Aa \in W^{L} for every a, i.e. im A \subseteq W^{L}.

Step 5 (dimension of W^{L}). Consider \psi : V_e \to W^{*}, x \mapsto \beta(x,-)|_{W}. Because \beta is perfect, x \mapsto \beta(x,-) is an isomorphism V_e \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } V_e^{*}; and the restriction map V_e^{*} \to W^{*} is surjective: choose a K-linear complement U with V_e = W \oplus U (possible since every subspace of a vector space has a complement, by extending a basis of W to a basis of V_e) and extend \lambda \in W^{*} by \lambda(w+u) = \lambda(w). Thus \psi is surjective, and by rank–nullity
   dim W^{L} = dim \ker \psi = dim V_e - dim W^{*} = dim V_e - dim W = N,
the last step using Step 3 and dim W^{*} = dim W.

Step 6 (equality im A = W^{L}). By Step 4, im A \subseteq W^{L}; by Step 2(i), dim im A = dim V_{e-2} = N; and by Step 5, dim W^{L} = N. A subspace of a finite-dimensional space having the same dimension as the ambient space is the whole space, so im A = W^{L}.

Step 7 (W meets its orthogonal trivially). Let w \in W \cap im A; write w = Aa. Then 0 = Bw = B(Aa) = Ta, and injectivity of T gives a = 0, hence w = 0. Therefore W \cap W^{L} = \{0\} (using Step 6).

Step 8 (left non-degeneracy of \beta|_{W}). The left radical of the restricted form is
   R_{L} = \{ w \in W : \beta(w, w') = 0 \ \forall w' \in W \} = W \cap W^{L} = \{0\}
by Step 7.

Step 9 (left non-degeneracy implies non-degeneracy in this finite-dimensional square situation). Let k := dim W and choose a basis w_1,\dots,w_k of W (for k = 0 the space W is zero and the unique form on it is nondegenerate, so assume k \ge 1). Let G = (\beta(w_i,w_j))_{1 \le i,j \le k} \in M_k(K) be the Gram matrix. For x = \sum_i c_i w_i \in W one has \beta(x, w_j) = \sum_i c_i G_{ij}, so x \in R_L if and only if c^{t}G = 0, i.e. if and only if G^{t}c = 0. Step 8 says R_L = 0, so G^{t} has trivial kernel; being a k \times k matrix, G^{t} is invertible (rank–nullity: rank G^{t} = k), hence G is invertible. Now for y = \sum_j d_j w_j \in W, y lies in the right radical precisely when \sum_j G_{ij} d_j = 0 for all i, i.e. Gd = 0, which forces d = 0 by invertibility of G. So the right radical is also 0, and \beta|_{W \times W} is nondegenerate in both slots.

Steps 1–9 prove exactly that \beta restricted to \ker(L_e : V_e \to V_{e+2}) is nondegenerate, under the hypothesis that L_e \circ L_{e-2} is injective. This completes the proof.

Remark (independent check, not used above). The argument was corroborated by exact finite computations over \mathbb{F}_2 and \mathbb{F}_7: scripts enumerate/sample quadruples (A,B,\beta,\gamma) with \beta, \gamma given by invertible matrices, assert the adjunction identity A^{t}B_{\beta} = B_{\gamma}B_{L} and the injectivity of BA, then compute the rank of the Gram matrix of \beta on a computed basis of \ker L_e; in all 27000 sampled instances over \mathbb{F}_2 [code:d5516842] and 5600 instances over \mathbb{F}_7 [code:f3de3c1b] that Gram matrix was of full rank. The proof above is complete on its own and rests on none of these computations.

statement: Let q=p^a, ℓ≠p, m≥1, k=overline(F_q). Let X be smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, let ξ be the class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor under Q_ℓ(1)≅Q_ℓ, and let L be cup product with ξ. Put P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r_et(X_k,Q_ℓ)→H^{2d-r+2}_et(X_k,Q_ℓ)). Suppose the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F preserves P^r, is semisimple on H^r_et(X_k,Q_ℓ), and every eigenvalue has complex absolute value q^{mr/2} under every embedding Q_ℓbar→C. Then for every embedding σ:Q_ℓbar→C, P^r⊗_σ C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h(F_σ x,F_σ y)=q^{mr}h(x,y).
proof:
Let H^r = H^r_et(X_k, Q_l). Since X is smooth and projective, the l-adic cohomology group H^r is finite-dimensional over Q_l; the map L^{d-r+1} is Q_l-linear, so its kernel P^r is also finite-dimensional over Q_l.

Apply lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a to X regarded as a scheme over F_{q^m} (where q^m is again a prime power). It gives that the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F is a Q_l-linear automorphism of H^r.

If P^r = 0, then the zero Hermitian form on the zero C-vector space is positive definite, and the required identity holds vacuously. Hence assume P^r is nonzero.

By hypothesis F(P^r) is contained in P^r. Since F is invertible and P^r is finite-dimensional, the restriction T := F|P^r is an automorphism of P^r.

The hypothesis says that F is semisimple on H^r. Because P^r is F-stable, lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_515 implies that T = F|P^r is semisimple on P^r. Lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5 then implies that T is diagonalizable over Qbar_l.

Now fix an arbitrary embedding sigma: Qbar_l -> C. The eigenvalue hypothesis for F on H^r says that for every embedding iota: Qbar_l -> C and every eigenvalue alpha of F on H^r tensor_{Q_l} Qbar_l, one has |iota(alpha)| = q^{mr/2}. Put w = mr. Apply lemma eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/4d0d79 with V = H^r, T = F, and W = P^r. It implies that for every embedding iota: Qbar_l -> C and every eigenvalue beta of the automorphism induced by F on P^r tensor_{Q_l} Qbar_l, one has |iota(beta)| = q^{mr/2}. In particular, for the chosen sigma, every eigenvalue beta of T satisfies |sigma(beta)|^2 = q^{mr}.

Set c = q^{mr}. This is a positive real number. Apply lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_360 to the finite-dimensional Q_l-vector space V = P^r, the automorphism T = F|P^r, the embedding sigma, and the positive real number c. Its hypotheses are satisfied: T is diagonalizable over Qbar_l, and every eigenvalue beta of T satisfies |sigma(beta)|^2 = c. Therefore there exists a positive definite Hermitian form h on P^r tensor_{Q_l, sigma} C such that h(T_sigma x, T_sigma y) = c h(x, y) for all x, y in P^r tensor_{Q_l, sigma} C.

The operator T_sigma is exactly the C-linear operator F_sigma induced by F on P^r tensor_{Q_l, sigma} C. Since c = q^{mr}, we obtain h(F_sigma x, F_sigma y) = q^{mr} h(x, y) for all x, y. This proves the required statement for every embedding sigma: Qbar_l -> C.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and let \(C\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(\mathbb F_q\). Let \(\mathcal L\) be a lisse \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)-sheaf on \(C_k\) whose associated \(\pi_1(C_k)\)-module is simple, and let \(\varphi:F_C^*\mathcal L\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal L\) be an isomorphism, where \(F_C\) is the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of \(C_k\). Then the \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)-linear automorphism of \(H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathcal L)\) induced by \(\varphi\) is semisimple.
proof:
We write \(\Lambda=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) and \(X:=C_k=C\times_{\mathbb F_q}k\). All sheaves below are sheaves of \(\Lambda\)-modules on the small \(\mathrm{\acute et}\)ale site \(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\).

**Step 0: The Frobenius morphism is an automorphism.** The map \(\sigma:k\to k\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), is a field automorphism: it is a homomorphism, it is injective, and it is surjective because \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) is algebraically closed, so every \(c\in k\) admits a \(q\)-th root in \(k\) (and that root is unique since \(k\) is perfect). Hence \(F_C:=\operatorname{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma\) is an automorphism of the scheme \(X\), with inverse \(\operatorname{id}_C\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1}\). Consequently the pullback functor \(F_C^*\) is an auto-equivalence of the abelian category \(\operatorname{Sh}(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}})\) of sheaves of \(\Lambda\)-modules; in particular it is exact and fully faithful.

Also, for *any* morphism of schemes \(f:Y\to Z\) one has \(f^*\Lambda_Z=\Lambda_Y\): the constant sheaf of a set \(S\) is the coproduct \(S_Y=\coprod_S 1_Y\) of copies of the terminal sheaf, \(f^*\) preserves all colimits and the terminal object (it is left exact), so \(f^*S_Z=S_Y\); applied to the underlying set of the ring \(\Lambda\) with its ring structure this gives \(f^*\Lambda_Z\cong\Lambda_Y\) as sheaves of rings. We shall use this for \(f=F_C\).

**Step 1: \(H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\mathcal L)\) is the space of \(\pi_1\)-invariants.** Choose a geometric base point \(\bar x\) of \(X\) and put \(\Pi:=\pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\bar x)\). Since \(C\) is smooth (hence \(X\) is connected, locally noetherian and unibranch) and \(X\) is connected because \(C\) is geometrically connected, the Riemann existence theorem for locally constant constructible sheaves gives an exact equivalence of categories
\[
\{\text{lisse }\Lambda\text{-sheaves on }X\}\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;\{\text{finite-dimensional continuous }\Lambda\text{-representations of }\Pi\},\qquad \mathcal F\longmapsto \mathcal F_{\bar x}.
\]
Let \(V:=\mathcal L_{\bar x}\) with its continuous \(\Pi\)-action \(\rho\); by hypothesis \(V\) is a **simple** \(\Pi\)-module, so in particular \(V\neq 0\) and its only \(\rho(\Pi)\)-stable \(\Lambda\)-linear subspaces are \(0\) and \(V\). (Subobjects in the category of continuous representations are exactly the stable \(\Lambda\)-linear subspaces: every linear subspace of the finite-dimensional \(\Lambda\)-vector space \(V\) is closed for the \(\ell\)-adic topology, and the restriction of a continuous action to a subspace is continuous.) Note that \(\dim_\Lambda V=\operatorname{rank}\mathcal L<\infty\).

Now \(H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\mathcal L)=\Gamma(X,\mathcal L)\), since \(H^0\) is the global-sections functor, and global sections of a sheaf of \(\Lambda\)-modules are morphisms from the constant sheaf:
\[
\Gamma(X,\mathcal L)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Sh}(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}})}(\Lambda_X,\mathcal L).
\]
By full faithfulness of the monodromy equivalence, and because the constant sheaf \(\Lambda_X\) corresponds to the trivial one-dimensional representation \(\Lambda\), this Hom-space is canonically
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\Pi\text{-}\Lambda}(\Lambda,V)=\{v\in V:\gamma v=v\ \text{for all }\gamma\in\Pi\}=:V^{\Pi},
\]
the equality being: a \(\Lambda\)-linear map \(\Lambda\to V\) is determined by the image \(v\) of \(1\), and it is \(\Pi\)-equivariant iff \(\gamma v=v\) for all \(\gamma\) (continuity imposes no further condition). Thus
\[
H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathcal L)\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;V^{\Pi}
\]
 canonically as \(\Lambda\)-vector spaces; in particular \(\dim_\Lambda H^0\le \dim_\Lambda V<\infty\).

**Step 2: The operator induced by \(\varphi\) is well defined.** The isomorphism \(\varphi:F_C^*\mathcal L\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal L\) induces, on global sections, the \(\Lambda\)-linear automorphism
\[
T_\varphi\;:=\;\Gamma(\varphi)\circ F_C^*\;:\;\Gamma(X,\mathcal L)\longrightarrow \Gamma(X,F_C^*\mathcal L)\longrightarrow \Gamma(X,\mathcal L),
\]
where the first arrow is the map \(s\mapsto F_C^*(s)\) obtained by applying the functor \(F_C^*\) to \(s\in\operatorname{Hom}(\Lambda_X,\mathcal L)=\operatorname{Hom}(F_C^*\Lambda_X,F_C^*\mathcal L)\). This is the automorphism of \(H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathcal L)\) "induced by \(\varphi\)". It is an automorphism because \(F_C^*\) is fully faithful (so \(s\mapsto F_C^*s\) is a bijection \(\operatorname{Hom}(\Lambda_X,\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}(\Lambda_X,F_C^*\mathcal L)\), using \(F_C^*\Lambda_X=\Lambda_X\)) and \(\Gamma(\varphi)\) is an isomorphism.

(Consistency check, not needed below: under the identification of Step 1, \(T_\varphi\) becomes the linear map \(\varphi_{\bar x}:(V,\rho\circ F_{C,*})\to (V,\rho)\), where \(F_{C,*}:\Pi\to\Pi\) is the automorphism induced by the automorphism \(F_C\) of \(X\) — a choice of path from \(F_C(\bar x)\) to \(\bar x\) only changes this by an inner automorphism, which does not change the invariant subspace. Since \(F_{C,*}\) is surjective, \(V^{\Pi}\) is the same subspace for the actions \(\rho\) and \(\rho\circ F_{C,*}\), so \(\varphi_{\bar x}\) does carry invariants to invariants, as expected.)

**Step 3: Dichotomy from simplicity.** The subspace \(V^{\Pi}\subseteq V\) is a \(\Pi\)-submodule: for \(v\in V^{\Pi}\) and \(\gamma\in\Pi\) one has \(\gamma v=v\in V^{\Pi}\). Since \(V\) is simple, exactly one of the following holds:

*Case (a): \(V^{\Pi}=0\).* Then \(H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathcal L)=0\) by Step 1. The endomorphism \(T_\varphi\) is the unique endomorphism of the zero space; the empty set is a basis of the zero space and it diagonalises \(T_\varphi\). Hence \(T_\varphi\) is semisimple.

*Case (b): \(V^{\Pi}=V\).* Then \(\Pi\) acts trivially on \(V\). In that situation **every** \(\Lambda\)-linear subspace of \(V\) is \(\Pi\)-stable, hence is a \(\Pi\)-submodule. If \(\dim_\Lambda V\ge 2\), choosing a nonzero proper subspace \(0\subsetneq W\subsetneq V\) gives a nonzero proper subobject of \(V\), contradicting simplicity. Since \(V\neq 0\), we conclude \(\dim_\Lambda V=1\), and therefore
\[
\dim_\Lambda H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathcal L)=\dim_\Lambda V^{\Pi}=\dim_\Lambda V=1.
\]
The automorphism \(T_\varphi\) of this one-dimensional \(\Lambda\)-vector space is multiplication by some scalar \(\lambda\in\Lambda^{\times}\) (a unit, because \(T_\varphi\) is invertible). Any nonzero scalar acts diagonally with respect to any basis, so \(T_\varphi\) is semisimple (equivalently, its minimal polynomial \(t-\lambda\) is squarefree, and its base change to \(\overline\Lambda=\Lambda\) is diagonalisable).

**Step 4: Conclusion.** In both cases \(T_\varphi\) is semisimple, which is exactly the claim. Note that no purity/weight hypothesis on \(\mathcal L\) was used, only simplicity as a \(\pi_1(C_k)\)-module, and that the argument is intrinsic to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)-coefficients as stated. (Schur's lemma would give an alternative route to the last step in Case (b), but it is not needed: triviality of the action plus simplicity already forces \(\dim V=1\).)

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\) and let \(r\ge m\) be divisible by \(m\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) and write \(S'=S\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\mathbb F_{q^r}\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and use it to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of an \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-rational very ample Cartier divisor on \(S\), let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\), put \(P^2=\ker\bigl(L:H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^4_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\), and let \(\operatorname{tr}_S:H^4_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell\) be the Poincar\'e duality trace normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_S(\operatorname{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]\) for closed points \(z\) of \(S\). Then \(\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup x)\) is a negative rational number for every nonzero \(x\in P^2\) that, under the identification \(S'_k=S_k\), is a \(\mathbb Q\)-linear combination of the cycle classes of Cartier divisors on \(S'\).
proof:
Let $n=[\mathbb F_{q^r}:\mathbb F_{q^m}]=r/m\ge 1$. Since $m\mid r$ we have a tower $\mathbb F_{q^m}\subset \mathbb F_{q^r}\subset k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$. Fix once and for all the nonzero element $u\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ supplied by the statement; it identifies every Tate twist $\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$ with $\mathbb Q_\ell$ (and also $\mathbb Q_\ell(-j)$ with $\mathbb Q_\ell$), and the *same* $u$ is used for $S$ and for $S'$. All cycle classes and traces below are read in the untwisted groups through this fixed identification.

**Step 1: the base-changed surface and divisor.** Let $H\subset S$ be the given $\mathbb F_{q^m}$-rational effective very ample Cartier divisor, so $\xi=\operatorname{cl}(H_k)\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Put $S'=S\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^m}}\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^r}$ and $H'=H\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^m}}\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^r}\subset S'$.

(a) *$S'$ is smooth, projective, of pure dimension $2$, geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$.* Smoothness, projectivity and pure dimension are preserved under arbitrary base change of the ground field. For geometric connectedness, an algebraic closure of $\mathbb F_{q^r}$ inside $k$ is $k$ itself, and
$$S'\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^r}}\operatorname{Spec}k\;=\;\bigl(S\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\mathbb F_{q^r}\bigr)\times_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}k\;\cong\;S\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}k=S_k,$$
which is connected because $S$ is geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$.

(b) *$H'$ is an effective Cartier divisor.* $H$ is locally the zero scheme of a regular section of the invertible sheaf $\mathcal O_S(H)$; equivalently its ideal sheaf $\mathcal I_H\subset\mathcal O_S$ is invertible. The projection $\pi:S'\to S$ is base change by $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^r}\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^m}$, which is flat (indeed finite free of rank $n$), and $\mathcal I_{H'}=\pi^{-1}\mathcal I_H\cdot\mathcal O_{S'}$ is again invertible, so $H'$ is an effective Cartier divisor.

(c) *$H'$ is very ample.* $\mathcal O_{S'}(H')\cong\mathcal O_S(H)\otimes_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\mathbb F_{q^r}$. Since $\mathcal O_S(H)$ is very ample, $H$ embeds $S$ as a closed subscheme of $\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}$ with $\mathcal O_S(H)$ the restriction of $\mathcal O(1)$; base changing this closed immersion to $\mathbb F_{q^r}$ gives a closed immersion $S'\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}$ whose pullback of $\mathcal O(1)$ is $\mathcal O_{S'}(H')$. Hence $H'$ is very ample over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$.

(d) *$H'$ is nonempty.* If $H=\varnothing$ then $\mathcal O_S(H)\cong\mathcal O_S$, and the linear system $H^0(S,\mathcal O_S)=\mathbb F_{q^m}$ (as $S$ is geometrically connected and proper) would give the constant map $S\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^m}$, not a closed immersion into projective space, contradicting very ampleness ($S$ is a surface, hence not a point). So $H\ne\varnothing$, and $H'\to H$ is base change by the faithfully flat map $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^r}\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^m}$, whence $H'\ne\varnothing$.

Thus $S'/\mathbb F_{q^r}$ with the $\mathbb F_{q^r}$-rational very ample Cartier divisor $H'$ is exactly of the kind to which Miner/16d24b0281973336/d3e72a applies.

**Step 2: the identification $(S')_k=S_k$ carries $\xi'$ to $\xi$.** By associativity of fibre products (on affine rings, $(A\otimes_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\mathbb F_{q^r})\otimes_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}k\xrightarrow{\sim}A\otimes_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}k$, $(a\otimes b)\otimes c\mapsto a\otimes bc$) there is a canonical isomorphism of $k$-schemes
$$\varphi:(S')_k:=S'\times_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}k\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;S\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}k=:S_k,$$
and the same associativity applied to the closed subscheme $H\subset S$ shows that $\varphi$ restricts to the canonical isomorphism $(H')_k\xrightarrow{\sim}H_k$ of closed subschemes. The $\ell$-adic cycle class of a closed subscheme is natural for isomorphisms of pairs: it is obtained from the Gysin morphism of the closed immersion, which is functorial, so $\varphi^*\operatorname{cl}(H_k)=\operatorname{cl}(\varphi^{-1}H_k)=\operatorname{cl}((H')_k)$. Writing
$$\xi':=\operatorname{cl}((H')_k)\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((S')_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad L':=\text{cup product with }\xi',$$
we have proved $\varphi^*(\xi)=\xi'$. Consequently, for every $y\in H^2(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$,
$$\varphi^*(y\cup\xi)=\varphi^*(y)\cup\varphi^*(\xi)=\varphi^*(y)\cup\xi',$$
so $y\cup\xi=0$ iff $\varphi^*(y)\cup\xi'=0$. Hence
$$\varphi^*\bigl(P^2_S\bigr)=P^2_{S'},\qquad P^2_S:=\ker\bigl(L:H^2(S_k)\to H^4(S_k)\bigr),\ \ P^2_{S'}:=\ker\bigl(L':H^2((S')_k)\to H^4((S')_k)\bigr).$$
In particular the primitive middle space is literally the same subspace whether computed for $S$ or for $S'$; we denote it $P^2$ via the identification $\varphi^*$.

**Step 3: the two Poincar\'e duality traces coincide.**

(a) *Geometric normalisation.* Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_464 to the smooth projective geometrically connected surface $S_k$ over the algebraically closed field $k$: it provides the Poincar\'e duality trace $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{geo}}:H^4_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$ with $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{geo}}(\operatorname{cl}(z))=1$ for every closed point $z$ of $S_k$. Since $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{geo}}$ is an isomorphism, $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^4(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=1$, and all closed-point classes are equal to the single vector $\pi:=\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{geo}}^{-1}(1)\ne0$, which is a basis of $H^4(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. The same applied to the surface $(S')_k$ over $k$ gives $\operatorname{tr}'_{\mathrm{geo}}:H^4((S')_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$ with $\operatorname{tr}'_{\mathrm{geo}}(\pi')=1$, where $\pi'$ is the class of any closed point of $(S')_k$.

(b) *$\operatorname{tr}_S=\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{geo}}$.* By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77(a) applied to $Y=S$ over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ with $d=2$, the map $\operatorname{tr}_S:H^4(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-2)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism with $\operatorname{tr}_S(\operatorname{cl}(x))=[\kappa(x):\mathbb F_{q^m}]$ for every closed point $x$ of $S$, where $\operatorname{cl}(x)$ denotes the class in $H^4(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ of the $0$-cycle $x_k:=x\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^m}}\operatorname{Spec}k\subset S_k$. Choose a closed point $x$ of $S$ (it exists: $S\ne\varnothing$ is of finite type over a field), and put $e=[\kappa(x):\mathbb F_{q^m}]\ge1$. Then $\kappa(x)\cong\mathbb F_{q^{me}}$ is finite separable (indees Galois) over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, and since $k$ is algebraically closed, $\kappa(x)\otimes_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}k\cong\prod_{i=1}^{e}k$; so $x_k=\coprod_{i=1}^{e}\operatorname{Spec}k$ is a disjoint union of $e$ distinct $k$-rational points $w_1,\dots,w_e$ of $S_k$. By additivity of the cycle class map on $0$-cycles and its naturality for the base change $S_k\to S$,
$$\operatorname{cl}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{e}\operatorname{cl}(w_i)=e\,\pi.$$
Applying $\operatorname{tr}_S$ and using its normalisation, $e=\operatorname{tr}_S(\operatorname{cl}(x))=e\,\operatorname{tr}_S(\pi)$, hence $\operatorname{tr}_S(\pi)=1=\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{geo}}(\pi)$. Both $\operatorname{tr}_S$ and $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{geo}}$ are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear functionals on the $1$-dimensional space $H^4(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ agreeing on the basis vector $\pi$, so $\operatorname{tr}_S=\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{geo}}$.

(c) *$\operatorname{tr}_{S'}=\operatorname{tr}'_{\mathrm{geo}}$.* The identical argument with $S'$ over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$ (using lemma_77(a) for $Y=S'$, $d=2$, and the normalisation $\operatorname{tr}_{S'}(\operatorname{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^r}]$) gives $\operatorname{tr}_{S'}=\operatorname{tr}'_{\mathrm{geo}}$.

(d) *Comparison.* Since $\varphi$ is an isomorphism of $k$-schemes it bijects the $k$-points of $(S')_k$ with those of $S_k$, and naturality of point classes gives $\varphi^*(\pi)=\pi'$. Therefore, for $\omega\in H^4(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, writing $\omega=\lambda\pi$ with $\lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell$,
$$\operatorname{tr}_{S'}(\varphi^*\omega)=\operatorname{tr}'_{\mathrm{geo}}(\lambda\pi')=\lambda=\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{geo}}(\lambda\pi)=\operatorname{tr}_S(\omega).$$
That is,
$$\operatorname{tr}_{S'}\circ\varphi^*=\operatorname{tr}_S.\qquad(\ast)$$
(Remark: the factor $n=r/m$ suggested in the guidance does **not** occur. The arithmetic normalisation $\operatorname{tr}_Y(\operatorname{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^t}]$ defines the same functional for every ground field, namely geometric degree on $0$-cycles, because a closed point of degree $e$ becomes a sum of $e$ geometric points after base change to $k$. In any case, equality is stronger than the needed $\operatorname{tr}_S=n\,\operatorname{tr}_{S'}$ with $n>0$, and either way the sign conclusion below is unaffected.)

**Step 4: apply the Hodge-index lemma to $S'/\mathbb F_{q^r}$.** Let $x\in P^2=P^2_S$ be nonzero and assume that, under the identification $(S')_k=S_k$, $x$ is a $\mathbb Q$-linear combination of cycle classes of Cartier divisors on $S'$. Unwinding this: there are Cartier divisors $D_1,\dots,D_t$ on $S'$ (each defined over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$, being a Cartier divisor on the $\mathbb F_{q^r}$-scheme $S'$) and $c_1,\dots,c_t\in\mathbb Q$ with
$$x=\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{t}c_i\,(\varphi^*)^{-1}\operatorname{cl}((D_i)_k)\in H^2(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).$$
Set $x':=\varphi^*(x)=\sum_i c_i\operatorname{cl}((D_i)_k)\in H^2((S')_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Then:
- $x'\ne0$ because $\varphi^*$ is an isomorphism;
- $x'\in P^2_{S'}$ by Step 2;
- $x'$ is, by construction, a nonzero $\mathbb Q$-linear combination of the cycle classes of $\mathbb F_{q^r}$-rational Cartier divisors on $S'$.

By Steps 1 and 2 the data $(S'/\mathbb F_{q^r},\,H',\,\xi',\,L',\,P^2_{S'},\,\operatorname{tr}_{S'})$ satisfy verbatim the hypotheses of Miner/16d24b0281973336/d3e72a (with $m$ there replaced by $r$), whose conclusion gives
$$\beta_{S'}(x',x'):=\operatorname{tr}_{S'}(x'\cup x')\in\mathbb Q,\qquad \beta_{S'}(x',x')<0.$$

**Step 5: conclusion.** Using functoriality of the cup product and $(\ast)$,
$$\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup x)\;=\;\operatorname{tr}_{S'}\bigl(\varphi^*(x\cup x)\bigr)\;=\;\operatorname{tr}_{S'}\bigl(\varphi^*x\cup\varphi^*x\bigr)\;=\;\operatorname{tr}_{S'}(x'\cup x')\;=\;\beta_{S'}(x',x'),$$
which is a negative rational number by Step 4. This is exactly the required statement.

**Edge cases.** If $r=m$ then $n=1$, $S'=S$, $H'=H$, $\varphi=\mathrm{id}$, and the argument reduces to a single instance of d3e72a, as it should. If some $c_i$ are negative (i.e. $x$ involves formal differences of divisors) nothing changes, since d3e72a is stated for arbitrary $\mathbb Q$-linear combinations. No case of $x=0$ occurs, and no case $\dim H^4\ne1$ occurs, the latter being established in Step 3(a). No use is made of the Tate conjecture or of any spanning hypothesis for $H^2$.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Then the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(u)=u^{q^m}\), is semisimple on \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
proof:
We prove the statement by applying the already-proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_329, whose hypothesis is a completely arbitrary prime power, to the prime power $Q:=q^{m}=p^{am}$ in place of the letter $q$ occurring in that lemma.  All identifications are checked explicitly.

Step 1 (the new ground field and its prime power).  Put $Q:=q^{m}=p^{am}$.  Since $a\ge 1$ and $m\ge 1$, $am\ge 1$, so $Q$ is a prime power with the same underlying prime $p$.  The prime $\ell$ satisfies $\ell\neq p$ by hypothesis, and this does not depend on how we group the exponent.

Step 2 (the algebraic closure).  We use the standard tower of finite fields inside the fixed separable (algebraic) closure $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q}$: $\mathbb F_{q}\subseteq \mathbb F_{q^{m}}\subseteq k$.  Then $k$ is an algebraic closure of $\mathbb F_{Q}=\mathbb F_{q^{m}}$: indeed $k$ is algebraically closed by definition, and every element of $k$ is algebraic over $\mathbb F_{q}$, hence a fortiori algebraic over the larger field $\mathbb F_{q^{m}}$ (algebraicity is transitive: if $\alpha$ is algebraic over $\mathbb F_q$ and $\mathbb F_q\subseteq \mathbb F_{q^m}$, then $\alpha$ is algebraic over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ because it is algebraic over $\mathbb F_q\cdot\mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_{q^m}$).  Thus $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q}=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q^{m}}$ as extensions of $\mathbb F_{q^{m}}$, canonically, via the inclusion $\mathbb F_{q^m}\hookrightarrow k$.  Consequently the base change $X_k$ of the target statement is $X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^m}}\operatorname{Spec}k$, and $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is the same finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space that lemma_329 would attach to the pair $(X/\mathbb F_{Q},\,k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{Q})$.

Step 3 (verification of the hypotheses of lemma_329 with $q$ read as $Q$).  Lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_329 says: for a prime power $q_0=p^{a_0}$ and a smooth projective geometrically connected variety $Z$ over $\mathbb F_{q_0}$, with $k_0=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q_0}$ and $\ell\neq p$, the $q_0$-power arithmetic Frobenius $(\mathrm{id}_{Z_{k_0}}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_{q_0})^*$, $\sigma_{q_0}(c)=c^{q_0}$, is semisimple on $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_{k_0},\mathbb Q_\ell)$.  Taking $q_0=Q=q^m$ (so $a_0=am$), $Z=X$, $k_0=k$, the required hypotheses are exactly those of the present lemma: $X$ is smooth, projective and geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_{Q}$, and $\ell\neq p$ is prime.  Hence the lemma applies.

Step 4 (identifying the operator).  The conclusion of lemma_329, with the above substitution, is semisimplicity on $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ of the automorphism
\[
(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_Q)^*,\qquad \sigma_Q(c)=c^{Q}=c^{q^{m}}\ \ \text{for all }c\in k .
\]
But $\sigma_Q$ is precisely the map $\sigma$ of the target statement, $\sigma(u)=u^{q^m}$, and $\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$ is the same endomorphism of $X_k=X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}k$ (the morphism is well defined because $\sigma$ restricts to the identity on $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, so $\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma$ is a morphism over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ and induces a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ by pullback, cf. the definition used throughout).  Therefore the operator whose semisimplicity is asserted in the target is literally the operator whose semisimplicity is given by lemma_329; there is no further transport or conjugacy to check.

Step 5 (conclusion).  Thus the $q^m$-power arithmetic Frobenius $(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(u)=u^{q^m}$, is semisimple on $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, which is the desired statement.  (Equivalently, since $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ by properness of $X$, semisimplicity means the minimal polynomial of the operator is square-free in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$, hence also in $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]$ after extending scalars, i.e. the operator is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$; and by the inverse-property of semisimple operators the same holds for the geometric Frobenius.  No edge case arises: if $X=\varnothing$ — which cannot occur for a geometrically connected variety, but formally — then $H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ and the zero-dimensional operator is trivially semisimple.)

statement: Let q=p^a, ℓ≠p, m≥1, k=overline(F_q). Let X be smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d≥2 over F_{q^m}, let Y⊂X be a smooth geometrically connected very ample divisor over F_{q^m}, with inclusion i, and let ξ be the class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor on X. Let L_X be cup product with ξ, ξ_Y=i^*ξ, and L_Y cup product with ξ_Y. Define P^r(X)=ker(L_X^{d-r+1}) and P^r(Y)=ker(L_Y^{d-r}) on the corresponding étale cohomology. Suppose i^*:P^r(X)→P^r(Y) is an isomorphism for some r. If for an embedding σ:Q_ℓbar→C the space P^r(Y)⊗_σ C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_Y with h_Y(F_σ x,F_σ y)=q^{mr}h_Y(x,y), where F is q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, then P^r(X)⊗_σ C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_X with h_X(F_σ x,F_σ y)=q^{mr}h_X(x,y).
proof:
Proof. Put Q=q^m. Let Phi:k->k be the Q-power field automorphism Phi(c)=c^Q. Write F_X=(id_{X_k} x Spec Phi)^* on H^r_et(X_k,Q_l) and F_Y=(id_{Y_k} x Spec Phi)^* on H^r_et(Y_k,Q_l). Set V_X=P^r(X)=ker(L_X^{d-r+1}) and V_Y=P^r(Y)=ker(L_Y^{d-r}).

Step 1 (edge cases). The primitive spaces are intended for integers r with r<=d; in the usual range 0<=r<=d. If r<0, then H^r_et=0, so V_X=V_Y=0 and the desired conclusion is vacuous. If r=d, then L_Y^0 is the identity, hence V_Y=ker(id)=0. The hypothesis that i^*:V_X->V_Y is an isomorphism forces V_X=0. The zero complex vector space carries the zero Hermitian form, which is positive definite vacuously, and the required equivariance condition is vacuous. Hence assume from now on that 0<=r<=d-1.

Step 2 (Frobenius stability of the primitive spaces). We use the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable, read over the ground field F_Q, so that the parameter q in that lemma is Q.
For X, the hypotheses of that lemma are satisfied: X is smooth projective of pure dimension d over F_Q, and xi is the class of an F_Q-rational very ample divisor. Therefore V_X=P^r(X)=ker(L_X^{d-r+1}) is stable under F_X (indeed under F_X and F_X^{-1}).
For Y, we first check that xi_Y is the class of an F_Q-rational very ample divisor on Y. Let H be an F_Q-rational very ample divisor on X with class xi. The line bundle O_X(H) is very ample over F_Q. Its pullback M=i^*O_X(H) is very ample over F_Q: the closed immersion of X into a projective space defined by O_X(H) restricts to a closed immersion of Y, and the pulled-back tautological bundle is M. Choose a nonzero F_Q-rational section of M; its zero locus is an effective F_Q-rational divisor D_Y on Y with O_Y(D_Y)=M. The class of D_Y is c_1(M)=i^*c_1(O_X(H))=i^*xi=xi_Y. Thus xi_Y is the class of an F_Q-rational very ample divisor on Y. Since Y is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d-1 over F_Q, the lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable applies to Y with L=L_Y and dimension d-1. At j=r (which satisfies 0<=r<=d-1) it gives that P^r(Y)=ker(L_Y^{(d-1)-r+1})=ker(L_Y^{d-r})=V_Y is stable under F_Y.

Step 3 (compatibility of restriction with Frobenius). The inclusion i:Y->X is a morphism of F_Q-schemes. By the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_214, with q replaced by Q, the pullback on r-th cohomology satisfies i^* o F_X = F_Y o i^*.

Step 4 (the given primitive restriction is Frobenius-equivariant). By hypothesis, phi:=i^*|_{V_X}:V_X->V_Y is a Q_l-linear isomorphism. Step 2 shows that V_X and V_Y are F_X- and F_Y-stable, respectively. For x in V_X, using Step 3, phi(F_X x)=i^*F_X x=F_Y i^*x=F_Y phi(x). Thus phi is an isomorphism of Q_l[F]-modules, where F acts on V_X by F_X and on V_Y by F_Y.

Step 5 (extension of scalars to C). Let sigma:Q_lbar->C be the embedding appearing in the statement, and let tau=sigma|_{Q_l}. Interpret P^r(X) tensor_sigma C as V_X^C=V_X tensor_{Q_l,tau} C, and similarly V_Y^C=V_Y tensor_{Q_l,tau} C. Let phi_C=phi tensor id_C, F_{sigma,X}=F_X tensor id_C, and F_{sigma,Y}=F_Y tensor id_C. Since phi is an isomorphism of Q_l[F]-modules, phi_C is a C-linear isomorphism and phi_C o F_{sigma,X}=F_{sigma,Y} o phi_C.

Step 6 (transport of the Hermitian form). The hypothesis gives a positive definite Hermitian form h_Y on V_Y^C such that h_Y(F_{sigma,Y}u,F_{sigma,Y}v)=Q^r h_Y(u,v)=q^{mr}h_Y(u,v) for all u,v in V_Y^C. Define h_X:V_X^C x V_X^C->C by h_X(u,v)=h_Y(phi_C u, phi_C v).
Because phi_C is C-linear and h_Y is Hermitian, h_X is Hermitian. If u is nonzero in V_X^C, then phi_C u is nonzero because phi_C is injective; positive definiteness of h_Y gives h_X(u,u)=h_Y(phi_C u, phi_C u)>0. Hence h_X is positive definite. Finally, for all u,v in V_X^C,
h_X(F_{sigma,X}u,F_{sigma,X}v)=h_Y(phi_C F_{sigma,X}u, phi_C F_{sigma,X}v)=h_Y(F_{sigma,Y} phi_C u, F_{sigma,Y} phi_C v)=Q^r h_Y(phi_C u, phi_C v)=q^{mr}h_X(u,v).
Thus P^r(X) tensor_sigma C carries the required positive definite Hermitian form. This completes the proof.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(H\) be an \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-rational very ample Cartier divisor, and fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), using it to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\xi=\operatorname{cl}(H)\), let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\), let \(P^2=\ker\bigl(L:H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^4_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\), let \(\operatorname{tr}_S\) be the Poincar\'e duality trace normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_S(\operatorname{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]\) for closed points \(z\), and let \(V\) be the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-span of the classes \(\operatorname{cl}(D)\) of the \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-rational Cartier divisors \(D\) on \(S\) whose class lies in \(P^2\). Then there is a \(\mathbb Q\)-subspace \(W\subset V\) spanned by such classes \(\operatorname{cl}(D)\) such that the natural map \(W\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb Q_\ell\to V\) is an isomorphism, such that \(-\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup y)\in\mathbb Q\) for all \(x,y\in W\), and such that \(-\operatorname{tr}_S(w\cup w)>0\) for every nonzero \(w\in W\).
proof:
Notation. Write $H^n=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, with the fixed identification $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell$ so that $\xi=\operatorname{cl}(H)\in H^2$, $L(x)=x\cup\xi$, and $P^2=\ker(L:H^2\to H^4)$. Put $\beta(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup y)$ for $x,y\in H^2$.

Let
$$S_0=\{\operatorname{cl}(D)\in H^2:\ D\ \text{an }\mathbb F_{q^m}\text{-rational Cartier divisor on }S,\ \operatorname{cl}(D)\in P^2\},$$
so that $V=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(S_0)$ by hypothesis, and $V\subseteq P^2$ since $P^2$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace of $H^2$ containing $S_0$.

Step 1 (a maximal independent family inside $S_0$). Consider the partially ordered set $\mathcal P$ of subsets $I\subseteq S_0$ that are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearly independent in the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $H^2$, ordered by inclusion. $\mathcal P$ is nonempty: $\varnothing\in\mathcal P$ (the empty family is vacuously independent). If $\{I_t\}_{t\in T}$ is a chain in $\mathcal P$, then $I=\bigcup_{t} I_t$ is independent: any $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear relation $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i e_i=0$ among elements $e_i\in I$ involves only finitely many $e_i$, and since the $I_t$ form a chain there is a single $t_0$ with $e_1,\dots,e_n\in I_{t_0}$; independence of $I_{t_0}$ forces all $\lambda_i=0$. Also $I\subseteq S_0$. Hence every chain has an upper bound in $\mathcal P$, and by Zorn's lemma $\mathcal P$ has a maximal element; fix one and call it $E$.

Step 2 ($E$ spans $V$). Let $d\in S_0$. If $d\notin\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(E)$, then $E\cup\{d\}$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearly independent: a relation $\lambda d+\sum_i\lambda_i e_i=0$ with $\lambda\neq0$ would express $d$ as a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear combination of elements of $E$, and with $\lambda=0$ independence of $E$ gives all $\lambda_i=0$. But $E\cup\{d\}\subseteq S_0$ properly contains $E$, contradicting the maximality of $E$ in $\mathcal P$. (If $d\in E$ there is nothing to prove.) Thus $S_0\subseteq\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(E)$, and therefore $V=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(S_0)\subseteq\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(E)$. The reverse inclusion holds because $E\subseteq S_0\subseteq V$ and $V$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace. Hence
$$\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(E)=V.$$
No finite-dimensionality of $H^2$ is used here.

Step 3 (definition of $W$ and the comparison map). Set
$$W=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}(E)=\Big\{\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i e_i:\ n\ge0,\ a_i\in\mathbb Q,\ e_i\in E\Big\}\subseteq H^2.$$
Then $W$ is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace of $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(E)=V$, so $W\subseteq V$ as required, and $W$ is spanned over $\mathbb Q$ by elements of $S_0$, i.e. by classes $\operatorname{cl}(D)$ of $\mathbb F_{q^m}$-rational Cartier divisors whose class lies in $P^2$. Moreover $E$ is a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $W$: it spans by definition, and a $\mathbb Q$-linear relation among its elements is, via $\mathbb Q\subset\mathbb Q_\ell$, a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear relation, hence trivial by Step 1.

Consider the natural $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map
$$\varphi:W\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb Q_\ell\longrightarrow V,\qquad w\otimes\lambda\longmapsto \lambda w,$$
which is well defined because it is induced by the $\mathbb Q$-bilinear map $W\times\mathbb Q_\ell\to V$, $(w,\lambda)\mapsto\lambda w$ (this lands in $V$ since $W\subseteq V$ and $V$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace).

Surjectivity: an element $v\in V$ lies, by Step 2, in $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(E)$, so $v=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i e_i$ for some finite set $e_i\in E$, $\lambda_i\in\mathbb Q_\ell$; then $v=\varphi\big(\sum_i e_i\otimes\lambda_i\big)$.

Injectivity: an element $u\in W\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb Q_\ell$ is a finite sum $\sum_j w_j\otimes\lambda_j$; writing each $w_j$ as a finite $\mathbb Q$-combination of elements of $E$ and collecting coefficients of the (finitely many) basis elements that occur, we may write $u=\sum_{i=1}^{r} e_i\otimes\mu_i$ with the $e_i\in E$ pairwise distinct and $\mu_i\in\mathbb Q_\ell$. If $\varphi(u)=\sum_i\mu_i e_i=0$ in $V\subseteq H^2$, the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear independence of $E$ in $H^2$ forces $\mu_i=0$ for all $i$, whence $u=0$.

Thus $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.

Step 4 (symmetry of $\beta$ on $H^2$). We first note that $H^4$ is one-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ and that the classes $\operatorname{cl}(z)$ of closed points $z\in S$ span it: apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_469 to $S$ viewed as a variety over the prime-power field $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ (with $q$ there replaced by $q^m$, $d=2$); it gives the Poincar\'e duality trace isomorphism $\operatorname{tr}':H^4\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-2)$ with $\operatorname{tr}'(\operatorname{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]$. Since $S$ is geometrically connected, $H^0=\mathbb Q_\ell$, and perfectness of the duality pairing $H^4\times H^0\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-2)$ gives $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^4=1$; as $\operatorname{tr}'(\operatorname{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]\ge1\neq0$ in $\mathbb Q_\ell$, each $\operatorname{cl}(z)$ is a nonzero, hence spanning, element. Composing $\operatorname{tr}'$ with the identification $\mathbb Q_\ell(-2)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell$ coming from the chosen nonzero element of $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ yields a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear functional $H^4\to\mathbb Q_\ell$ sending $\operatorname{cl}(z)$ to $[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]$; by the previous sentence and the stated normalising property, this functional is exactly $\operatorname{tr}_S$. Lemma_469 further gives, for $x,y\in H^2$ (so $n=2$, $2d-n=2$),
$$\operatorname{tr}'(x\cup y)=(-1)^{2\cdot 2}\operatorname{tr}'(y\cup x)=\operatorname{tr}'(y\cup x),$$
and applying the identification $\mathbb Q_\ell(-2)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell$ (a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map) to both sides gives
$$\beta(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_S(y\cup x)=\beta(y,x)\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in H^2.$$
(Conceptually this is just graded commutativity of the cup product in degree $2$.) In particular $\beta$ is $\mathbb Q$-bilinear and symmetric on $W$, since the cup product is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinear and $\operatorname{tr}_S$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear.

Step 5 (negative self-pairings are positive rationals). Let $0\neq w\in W$. Then $w=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i e_i$ with $a_i\in\mathbb Q$ and $e_i\in E\subseteq S_0$, so $w$ is a nonzero $\mathbb Q$-linear combination of cycle classes of $\mathbb F_{q^m}$-rational Cartier divisors on $S$; and $w\in W\subseteq V\subseteq P^2$. The hypotheses of Miner/16d24b0281973336/d3e72a are therefore satisfied (same $q,m,k,\ell$, same surface $S$ over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, same choice of nonzero element of $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$, $\xi=\operatorname{cl}(H)$ the class of an $\mathbb F_{q^m}$-rational very ample Cartier divisor, $L$ cup product with $\xi$, $P^2=\ker(L:H^2\to H^4)$, and $\operatorname{tr}_S$ normalised by $\operatorname{tr}_S(\operatorname{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^m}]$). That lemma asserts $\beta(w,w)=\operatorname{tr}_S(w\cup w)$ is a negative rational number. Hence
$$-\operatorname{tr}_S(w\cup w)\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\qquad\text{for every nonzero }w\in W.$$

Step 6 (mixed terms are rational). Let $x,y\in W$. If $x=0$ or $y=0$ then $\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup y)=0\in\mathbb Q$, so assume $x\neq0$ and $y\neq0$. By $\mathbb Q$-bilinearity from Step 4 and the symmetry $\beta(x,y)=\beta(y,x)$,
$$\operatorname{tr}_S\big((x+y)\cup(x+y)\big)=\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup x)+\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup y)+\operatorname{tr}_S(y\cup x)+\operatorname{tr}_S(y\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup x)+\operatorname{tr}_S(y\cup y)+2\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup y),$$
so the polarisation identity gives
$$2\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_S\big((x+y)\cup(x+y)\big)-\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup x)-\operatorname{tr}_S(y\cup y).$$
Each term on the right belongs to $\mathbb Q$: for $x$ and $y$ by Step 5, and for $x+y$ by Step 5 if $x+y\neq0$, while if $x+y=0$ then $\operatorname{tr}_S((x+y)\cup(x+y))=\operatorname{tr}_S(0)=0\in\mathbb Q$ (here we used $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $\operatorname{tr}_S$ and $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinearity of $\cup$, giving $\operatorname{tr}_S(0\cup0)=0$). Since $2\in\mathbb Q^{\times}$, we conclude $\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup y)\in\mathbb Q$, i.e.
$$-\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup y)\in\mathbb Q\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in W.$$

Conclusion. The $\mathbb Q$-subspace $W=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}(E)$ constructed in Step 3 is spanned by classes $\operatorname{cl}(D)$ of $\mathbb F_{q^m}$-rational Cartier divisors whose class lies in $P^2$, satisfies $W\subseteq V$, the natural map $W\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb Q_\ell\to V$ is an isomorphism (Step 3), $-\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup y)\in\mathbb Q$ for all $x,y\in W$ (Steps 4 and 6), and $-\operatorname{tr}_S(w\cup w)>0$ for every nonzero $w\in W$ (Step 5). This proves the lemma.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Write \(H^n=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Let \(\xi\in H^2\) be the cycle class of an \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-rational very ample Cartier divisor, let \(L:H^1\to H^3\) be cup product with \(\xi\), and let \(\operatorname{tr}_S:H^4\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) be the Poincaré duality trace. For \(x,y\in H^1\), set \(\beta_\xi(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}_S(\xi\cup x\cup y)\). Then \(\ker L=\{x\in H^1:\beta_\xi(x,y)=0\text{ for all }y\in H^1\}\).
proof:
We prove the equality of subspaces of \(H^1=H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) using only Poincar\'e duality for the surface \(S\), the basic graded-commutativity of the \(\ell\)-adic cycle class ring, and finite-dimensional (in fact, purely linear-algebraic) reasoning. No hard Lefschetz, no Albanese, no semisimplicity input is used, and no nondegeneracy of \(\beta_\xi\) is claimed.

**Step 1 (Setup).** Let \(H^n:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for all \(n\ge 0\). The surface \(S\) is smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d=2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), with \(m\ge 1\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and \(\ell\neq p\). The class \(\xi\in H^2\) is the cycle class of an \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-rational very ample Cartier divisor; the only property of \(\xi\) that will be used below is that it is homogeneous of degree \(2\). The map \(L:H^1\to H^3\) is \(Lx:=\xi\cup x\), and \(\beta_\xi(x,y):=\operatorname{tr}_S(\xi\cup x\cup y)\) for \(x,y\in H^1\).

**Step 2 (The trace and the perfect pairing \(H^1\times H^3\to\mathbb Q_\ell\)).** Apply the proved lemma \(eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77\) with \(Y=S\) (smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d=2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)) and with \(n=1\).
- Part (a) of that lemma provides a canonical \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism (the Poincar\'e duality trace) \[\operatorname{tr}^0:H^4=H^4_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell(-2).\]
- Part (b) says that \[\langle\,-\,,\,-\,\rangle^0:H^1\times H^3\longrightarrow \mathbb Q_\ell(-2),\qquad \langle y,\alpha\rangle^0:=\operatorname{tr}^0(y\cup\alpha),\] is a **perfect** pairing of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces; by definition of perfectness this means that both induced maps \(H^1\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^3,\mathbb Q_\ell(-2))\) and \(H^3\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^1,\mathbb Q_\ell(-2))\) are isomorphisms. In particular \[\Theta^0:H^3\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^1,\mathbb Q_\ell(-2)),\qquad \Theta^0(\alpha)(y)=\operatorname{tr}^0(y\cup\alpha),\] is an isomorphism.

Now fix the nonzero element \(e\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) of the statement. Since \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) is a \(1\)-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, \(e\neq 0\) is a basis, and \(e^{\otimes 2}\) is a basis of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)^{\otimes 2}=\mathbb Q_\ell(2)\). Evaluation on \(e^{\otimes 2}\) is therefore a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism \[\varphi:\mathbb Q_\ell(-2)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(\mathbb Q_\ell(2),\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell,\qquad \varphi(\psi)=\psi(e^{\otimes 2}).\] Define \[\operatorname{tr}_S:=\varphi\circ\operatorname{tr}^0:H^4\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell;\] this is the trace of the statement, obtained from \(\operatorname{tr}^0\) by the identification of Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) determined by \(e\). Post-composing a perfect pairing with a vector-space isomorphism of its target keeps it perfect: the map \[\Theta:H^3\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^1,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad \Theta(\alpha)(y):=\operatorname{tr}_S(y\cup\alpha),\] equals \(\varphi_*\circ\Theta^0\), where \(\varphi_*\) is the isomorphism \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^1,\mathbb Q_\ell(-2))\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^1,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) given by composition with \(\varphi\); hence \(\Theta\) is an isomorphism. We record the only consequence we need:
\[(\ast)\qquad\text{for }\alpha\in H^3:\quad \alpha=0\iff \operatorname{tr}_S(y\cup\alpha)=0\ \text{ for every } y\in H^1.\]
(Indeed \(\operatorname{tr}_S(y\cup\alpha)=\Theta(\alpha)(y)\), and \(\Theta\) is injective.)

We deliberately make **no** assertion about the values of \(\operatorname{tr}_S\) on cycle classes of closed points: changing the trivialisation \(e\) multiplies the trivialised trace by a nonzero scalar, and nothing in the argument below uses any normalisation. Correspondingly, if the reader's convention for the trivialised trace differs from \(\varphi\circ\operatorname{tr}^0\) by a nonzero scalar \(c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\), then both \(\Theta\) and \(\beta_\xi\) are multiplied by \(c\), the criterion \((\ast)\) still holds, and the equality proved below is unchanged.

**Step 3 (Graded commutativity of the cup product).** The ring \(\bigoplus_{n\ge0}H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is graded-commutative over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\): for homogeneous \(a\in H^r\), \(b\in H^s\) one has \(a\cup b=(-1)^{rs}\,b\cup a\), and the product is associative and \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-bilinear. This is a foundational property of \(\ell\)-adic cohomology: \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\operatorname{Hom}_{D(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)}(\mathbb Q_\ell,\mathbb Q_\ell[n])\), the cup product is the one induced by the symmetric monoidal structure of the derived category of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-sheaves together with the fact that \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) is a commutative algebra object, and the cohomology of a commutative algebra object in the derived category of a symmetric monoidal abelian category is graded-commutative, with the Koszul sign \((-1)^{rs}\) coming from the symmetry constraint (the usual Eilenberg\u2013Zilber/twist-map argument). We use only the following two instances:
- for \(y\in H^1\): \(y\cup\xi=(-1)^{1\cdot 2}\,\xi\cup y=\xi\cup y\) (the sign is \(+1\) because \(\xi\) has even degree);
- for \(x,y\in H^1\): \(y\cup x=(-1)^{1\cdot 1}\,x\cup y=-\,x\cup y\).

Note also that \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) has characteristic \(0\) for **every** prime \(\ell\) (including \(\ell=2\)), so \(-1\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\) is a nonzero scalar and \(-1\neq +1\) in general; only nonzeroness is used.

**Step 4 (Relating the pairing to the trace criterion).** For \(x,y\in H^1\), using associativity of \(\cup\), the definition \(Lx=\xi\cup x\), the two identities of Step 3, and \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linearity of \(\cup\) and of \(\operatorname{tr}_S\),
\[(\dagger)\qquad \operatorname{tr}_S\bigl(y\cup Lx\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_S\bigl(y\cup(\xi\cup x)\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_S\bigl((y\cup\xi)\cup x\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_S\bigl((\xi\cup y)\cup x\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_S\bigl(\xi\cup(y\cup x)\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_S\bigl(\xi\cup(-\,x\cup y)\bigr)=-\operatorname{tr}_S(\xi\cup x\cup y)=-\,\beta_\xi(x,y).\]
Each equality is justified in order as: definition of \(Lx\); associativity; graded commutativity with the degree-\(2\) class \(\xi\) (sign \(+1\)); associativity; graded commutativity of the two degree-\(1\) classes (sign \(-1\)); bilinearity of \(\cup\) pulling \(-1\) out; bilinearity of \(\operatorname{tr}_S\) pulling \(-1\) out; definition of \(\beta_\xi\). Since \(-1\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\), equation \((\dagger)\) gives, for every pair \((x,y)\in H^1\times H^1\),
\[(\ddagger)\qquad \operatorname{tr}_S(y\cup Lx)=0\iff \beta_\xi(x,y)=0.\]

**Step 5 (The two inclusions).** Write \(\operatorname{rad}(\beta_\xi):=\{x\in H^1:\beta_\xi(x,y)=0\ \text{for all } y\in H^1\}\); it is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear subspace of \(H^1\) because \(\beta_\xi\) is bilinear (it is the composite of the bilinear maps \((x,y)\mapsto\xi\cup x\cup y\) and the linear \(\operatorname{tr}_S\)). Likewise \(\ker L\) is a subspace, \(L\) being \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear.

*Inclusion \(\ker L\subseteq\operatorname{rad}(\beta_\xi)\).* Let \(x\in\ker L\), so \(Lx=0\in H^3\). For any \(y\in H^1\), \(\beta_\xi(x,y)=-\operatorname{tr}_S(y\cup Lx)=-\operatorname{tr}_S(y\cup 0)=-\operatorname{tr}_S(0)=0\), using \((\dagger)\), the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-bilinearity of \(\cup\) and the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linearity of \(\operatorname{tr}_S\) (so \(\operatorname{tr}_S(0)=0\)). Hence \(x\in\operatorname{rad}(\beta_\xi)\).

*Inclusion \(\operatorname{rad}(\beta_\xi)\subseteq\ker L\).* Let \(x\in\operatorname{rad}(\beta_\xi)\). Then for every \(y\in H^1\), \(\beta_\xi(x,y)=0\), hence \(\operatorname{tr}_S(y\cup Lx)=0\) by \((\ddagger)\). Since \(Lx\in H^3\), the criterion \((\ast)\) applied to \(\alpha=Lx\) yields \(Lx=0\), i.e. \(x\in\ker L\).

**Conclusion.** Both inclusions hold, so \[\ker\bigl(L:H^1\to H^3\bigr)=\{x\in H^1:\beta_\xi(x,y)=0\ \text{for all } y\in H^1\},\] which is the claimed equality of subspaces.

**Remarks on scope and edge cases.** The argument used nothing about ampleness or rationality of the divisor beyond producing a class \(\xi\) of cohomological degree \(2\); it used no hard Lefschetz theorem, no semisimplicity, and no Albanese/cover-transfer input. It also makes no claim that \(\beta_\xi\) is nondegenerate: the equality above is precisely a reformulation of the injectivity of \(L\) (equivalently, of the nondegeneracy of \(\beta_\xi\) on the left, hence on both sides since \(\beta_\xi\) is alternating by Step 3 and \(\operatorname{char}\mathbb Q_\ell=0\)). If \(H^1=0\) (for instance for a rational surface), then \(\ker L=\{0\}=\operatorname{rad}(\beta_\xi)\) and the equality is still exactly what Steps 2\u20135 give, since \(\Theta\) is then an isomorphism of the zero space onto the zero space. Finite-dimensionality of the \(H^n\) was not needed either: only the injectivity of \(\Theta\), which is part of the perfectness supplied by \(eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77\)(b), was used.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Suppose the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}_{S_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(u)=u^{q^m}\), is semisimple on \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and on \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then it is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every integer \(n\ge0\).
proof:
Write $Q:=q^{m}$; since $q=p^{a}$, $Q=p^{am}$ is again a prime power, and $\mathbb F_{q^{m}}=\mathbb F_{Q}$. The operator in the statement is $F:=(\operatorname{id}_{S_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^{*}$ with $\sigma(c)=c^{Q}$, i.e. the $Q$-power arithmetic Frobenius, and $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q}=\overline{\mathbb F}_{Q}$.

**Preliminaries (well-definedness and finiteness).** By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob applied to $X=S_{\mathbb F_Q}$, $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ and the natural arithmetic Frobenius trivialisation, each $H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space carrying a canonical $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear Frobenius automorphism. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a this canonical automorphism is exactly the pullback $F=(\operatorname{id}_{S_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^{*}$, $\sigma(c)=c^{Q}$, and it is invertible. So "semisimple on $H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$" is a meaningful statement about an invertible operator on a finite-dimensional space.

Since $S$ is projective, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension $2$ over $\mathbb F_Q$, its base change $S_k$ is a projective scheme over the algebraically closed field $k$, equidimensional of dimension $2$. We treat each degree $n\ge 0$ in turn.

**Case $n\ge 5$.** By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_projective_cohomology_vanishes_above_twice_dimension (with $k$ algebraically closed, $\ell\neq\operatorname{char}k$, $Y=S_k$, $n=\dim S_k=2$) one has $H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ for every $n>4$. On the zero space there is nothing to check: the (unique) operator is the zero map on a space with the empty basis, its minimal polynomial is $1$, which is squarefree, hence it is diagonalisable/semisimple. Thus $F$ is semisimple in all degrees $n\ge5$.

**Case $n=0$.** Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_265 with the prime power $Q$ in the role of its "$q$", with $X=S$ (smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $d=2\ge1$ over $\mathbb F_{Q}$). It states that the $Q$-power arithmetic Frobenius acts as the identity on $H^{0}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and, in particular, is semisimple there. (Concretely $H^{0}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\simeq\mathbb Q_\ell$ because $S_k$ is connected, and $F=\mathrm{id}$, whose minimal polynomial $t-1$ is squarefree.)

**Case $n=4$.** The same lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_265 (with $d=2$) states that $F$ acts on $H^{4}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ as multiplication by the scalar $Q^{d}=Q^{2}=q^{2m}$, and is therefore semisimple there (a scalar operator on a one-dimensional space has minimal polynomial $t-Q^{2}$, which is squarefree since $\operatorname{char}\mathbb Q_\ell=0$).

**Cases $n=1$ and $n=2$.** These are exactly the two hypotheses of the present lemma: $F$ is semisimple on $H^{1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and on $H^{2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

**Case $n=3$.** Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_519_poincare_duality_frobenius_semisimplicity with the prime power $Q$ in the role of its "$q$", with $Y=S$ (a smooth projective variety of pure dimension $e=2$ over $\mathbb F_Q$; no geometric connectedness is required there), and with $e=2$, $n=1$ (note $0\le 1\le 2e=4$). Its Frobenius operator is $(\operatorname{id}_{Y_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^{*}$ with $\sigma(c)=c^{Q}$, which is precisely our $F$. The lemma gives: $F$ is semisimple on $H^{1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ if and only if $F$ is semisimple on $H^{2\cdot 2-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=H^{3}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. (The content is the perfect Poincar\'e duality pairing $H^{1}\times H^{3}\to H^{4}\simeq\mathbb Q_\ell(-2)$, under which $F$ is a $Q^{4}$-similitude, so the two operators are transpose-to-inverse-of-each-other up to a scalar and have the same semisimplicity behaviour.) By the $n=1$ case (hypothesis) we conclude that $F$ is semisimple on $H^{3}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

**Conclusion.** Every integer $n\ge0$ falls into one of the cases above: $n=0,1,2,3,4$ are handled respectively by lemma_265, the hypothesis, the hypothesis, Poincar\'e duality (lemma_519) applied to $n=1$, and lemma_265; and $n\ge5$ by vanishing of cohomology above twice the dimension. Hence the $q^{m}$-power arithmetic Frobenius $(\operatorname{id}_{S_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^{*}$, $\sigma(u)=u^{q^{m}}$, is semisimple on $H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $n\ge0$, which is the desired statement. $\blacksquare$

statement:
Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(Z\subset X\) be a smooth closed subvariety of pure codimension \(2\) defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and let \(\pi:\operatorname{Bl}_Z X\to X\) be the blow-up. Then for every integer \(n\ge0\) there is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell[F]\)-modules
\[
H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((\operatorname{Bl}_Z X)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\cong H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\oplus H^{n-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-1),
\]
where \(F\) is the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(u)=u^{q^m}\), on each term, \(H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for \(j<0\), and \(F\) acts on \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)\) as multiplication by \(q^m\).
proof:
We prove the statement by applying the already-proved codimension-2 blow-up decomposition eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_415, with the prime power $q^m$ in place of its $q$, and then checking only the Frobenius (Tate-twist) bookkeeping.

**Step 1: Notation and the change of prime power.**
Write $Q:=q^m=p^{am}$. Since $a\ge1$ and $m\ge1$, $am\ge1$, so $Q$ is again a prime power (with the *same* underlying prime $p$); in particular $\mathbb F_Q=\mathbb F_{q^m}$, and $\ell\neq p$ is still a prime different from the residue characteristic of $\mathbb F_Q$.

The field $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$ of the statement contains $\mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_Q$ (as the unique subfield with $Q$ elements). It is algebraic over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ (being algebraic over $\mathbb F_q\subset\mathbb F_{q^m}$) and algebraically closed, hence it is an algebraic closure of $\mathbb F_{q^m}$. Thus $k$ serves simultaneously as the $\overline{\mathbb F}_q$ of the present statement and as the algebraic closure of $\mathbb F_Q$ required by lemma_415, and for every $\mathbb F_{q^m}$-scheme $W$ the base change $W_k:=W\times_{\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_{q^m}}\mathrm{Spec}\,k$ is the same $k$-scheme in both readings. Moreover the $Q$-power arithmetic Frobenius morphism $(\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^Q=c^{q^m}$, which is the operator denoted $F$ in the present statement, is exactly the "$q$-power arithmetic Frobenius" of lemma_415 after the substitution $q\mapsto Q$.
